context: A variety registered act under this Act shall be valid for a period of fifteen years from the date of notification of the variety, subject to the payment of renewal fees as prescribed. The renewal fee shall be payable at intervals of six years beginning after the expiry of the initial fifteen-year period, and failure to pay such fee within the stipulated time may result in the lapse of the registration, provided that a grace period of three months shall be allowed for payment with a late fee. Any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right in a registered variety may apply to the Central Government for redressal. The Central Government may, after conducting an inquiry, issue an order restraining the infringer and awarding damages to the breeder, considering the actual loss suffered and any reasonable royalty due. A farmer, however, shall be permitted to save, use, sow, re-sow and multiply any variety registered under this Act for purposes of propagation on his own land, provided that such farmer does not sell, market or distribute such saved material.

Any person desiring registration of a layout-design shall submit an application to the Intellectual Property Office as provided herein, accompanied by the prescribed fee and all necessary documentation demonstrating originality. The application shall clearly delineate the three-dimensional arrangement of the elements constituting the layout-design, specifying each layer and its function within the semiconductor integrated circuit. A registered layout-design shall confer upon the applicant the exclusive right to reproduce, sell, or commercially exploit the said layout-design for a period of ten years from the date of registration, subject to continued payment of annual renewal fees. However, such rights shall not extend to ideas, procedures, systems, methods of operation, computer programs, or data; protection is strictly limited to the specific layout-design itself. Any unauthorized reproduction or commercial exploitation of a registered layout-design constitutes an infringement under this Act and may be subject to legal remedies including injunctions and damages. A person claiming prior art must submit evidence substantiating its existence before the filing date of the application.

(1) Whoever aggrieved by an order of the adjudicating officer under section 124A may prefer an appeal to the appellate authority, who shall be an officer at least one rank above the adjudicating officer, within a period of sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, as the Central Government may by notification authorise in this behalf.
(2) Every appeal under this section shall be preferred in such form and manner as may be prescribed.
(3) An appeal may be admitted after the expiry of the period of sixty days if the appellant satisfies the appellate authority that he had sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal within that period.
(4) No appeal shall be disposed of unless the appellant has been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark reasonably believes that goods bearing an infringing mark have been imported and are held in possession by any person with intent for sale or distribution within the territory of India, such proprietor may apply to the Customs Authority for orders relating to the confiscation of those goods. The Customs Authority shall, upon receiving such application and after due consideration of evidence presented, determine whether the goods are indeed subject to the confiscation goods clause as provided herein. Any party possessing a license or assignment related to the trademark in question shall be deemed an interested party and entitled to participate fully in any proceedings concerning the determination of confiscation. The proprietor may further grant sub-licenses for the disposal of confiscated goods, subject to conditions prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent shall furnish a detailed specification outlining the scope and boundaries of the claimed invention. The description must clearly articulate all elements encompassed within the claims, ensuring that any matter not explicitly described is understood to be excluded. Where an invention far claimed extends beyond the originally disclosed subject matter, the Controller may require further clarification demonstrating the inventive step relating to each additional element. Such requirements shall be considered met only upon submission of a revised specification and accompanying drawings, if applicable, accurately reflecting the broadened scope. The applicant’s compliance with these stipulations is essential for determining patentability under this Act and preventing subsequent challenges regarding claim interpretation.

For the purposes of this Act, where any sound recording, cinematographic film, or other artistic work is produced by means of an apparatus operated and controlled by a person, that person shall be deemed to be the ‘recording means person’ in relation to such production. Provided that, if the operation and control of said apparatus are undertaken under the direction and supervision of another individual, then the directing individual may also be considered a recording means person, subject to demonstrating substantial creative contribution beyond mere instruction. Further, where multiple persons jointly operate and control an apparatus, the determination of who constitutes a ‘recording means person’ shall be resolved based on their respective roles in the production process, as evidenced by written agreements or other verifiable documentation. This provision applies irrespective of whether such person is employed or engaged under contract.

The holder of a design register relating to a layout-design may grant a license conferring rights to use the registered layout-design, subject to such terms and conditions as are specified in the license agreement. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to manufacture, import, sale, hire, and exhibition of integrated circuits incorporating the design register layout. Assignment of rights pertaining to a registered layout-design is permissible, provided that such assignment is executed in writing and duly stamped as required under relevant laws. Any subsequent licensee or assignee shall be bound by the original terms of registration and any conditions imposed during the initial grant. The Registrar may require submission of details regarding assignments and licenses for record purposes, as provided herein.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication registered under this Act shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of the said geographical indication for goods conforming to the standards specified in the registration certificate, provided that such license agreement expressly stipulates the conditions governing quality control and adherence to production methods as defined within the geographical indication’s code of conduct. Further, any assignment of rights pertaining to a registered geographical indication shall require prior notification to the Registrar, detailing the assignee's undertaking to uphold the integrity and distinctiveness of the geographical indication. The Registrar may, subject to due process, refuse registration of an assignment if it determines that the proposed assignee lacks the requisite capacity or intention to protect the application registration geographical indication’s reputation.

(1) For the purposes of this Act, a record called the Register of Layout-Designs shall be kept at the head office of the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry wherein shall be entered all registered layout-designs with the names, addresses and descriptions of the proprietor and such other matters related to the registered layout-designs as may be prescribed. (2) Subject to the superintendence and direction of the Central Government, the register shall be kept under the control and management of the Registrar. (3) There shall be kept at each Branch office of the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry a copy of the register and other documents as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct.

Any issued breeder desiring to assign, license, or otherwise transfer the rights conferred by a certificate of registration for a new plant variety shall furnish a written instrument of assignment or license, as the case may be, to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, specifying the duration, scope, and territorial extent of such transfer. The instrument shall also clearly identify the transferee and detail any conditions attached to the assignment or license, including royalty rates or benefit-sharing arrangements. Where a license is granted for commercial exploitation, the issued breeder shall ensure that the licensee undertakes to maintain the genetic purity and distinctiveness of the variety, and to comply with all conditions stipulated in the certificate of registration. Failure to register such transfer within ninety days of its execution shall render the transfer void *ab initio* as provided herein. The Authority may, subject to reasonable cause, extend this period by a further thirty days. Any assignment or license shall be subject to the provisions relating to farmers’ rights and research exemptions under this Act.

(1) Every suit or other civil proceeding arising under this Chapter in respect of the infringement of copyright in any work or the infringement of any other right conferred by this Act shall be instituted in the district court having jurisdiction. (2) For the purpose of sub-section ( 1), a “district court having jurisdiction ” shall, notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908) or any other law for the time being in force, include a district court within the local limits of whose juris diction, at the time of the institution of the suit or other proceeding, the person instituting the suit or other proceeding or, where there are more than one such persons, any of them actually and voluntarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain.

The Controller may, at any time during the proceedings relating to an application for patent, require the applicant to furnish such further information or particulars as he deems necessary for the determination of inventiveness. Such requirement shall be made in writing and specify the grounds upon which the request is based, referencing relevant prior art documents where applicable. The applicant shall have a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of such communication within which to comply, subject to extensions granted under this Act. Failure to provide the requested information within the stipulated time may result in the application being deemed abandoned. The adequacy and clarity of the *specification* accompanying the patent application are paramount; any ambiguity or omission rendering the invention not readily reproducible by a person skilled in the art shall be grounds for rejection.

Where a patent is granted and subsequently subject to a challenge regarding its novelty or inventive step, the Controller may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating prior publication that anticipates the claimed invention, issue an order directing the provisional publication of the patent’s expiry date. Such publication shall be deemed conclusive for all purposes under this Act unless within sixty days from the date of such publication, the patentee files a notice of objection disputing the validity of the determination and requesting a review by the Appellate Board. The Controller may require further documentation to substantiate the claim of published expiry. Provided that any decision rendered by the Appellate Board shall be final, subject only to appeal to the High Court on grounds limited to jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice.

(1) If any person is, by reason of minority, lunacy or other disability, incapable of making any statement or doing anything required or permitted by or under this Act, the lawful guardian, committee or manager (if any) of the person subject to the disability, or if there be none, any person appointed by any court possessing jurisdiction in respect of his property, may make such statement or a statement as nearly corresponding thereto as circumstances permit, and do such things in the name and on behalf of the person subject to the disability.
(2) An appointment may be made by the court for the purposes of this section upon the petition of any person acting on behalf of the person subject to the disability or of any other person interested in the making of the statement or the doing of the thing.

(1) Where, in respect of a patent, a compulsory licence has been granted, the Central Government or any person interested may, after the expiration of two years from the date of the order granting the first compulsory licence, apply to the Controller for an order revoking the patent on the ground that the patented invention has not been worked in the territory of India or that reasonable requirements of the public with respect to the patented invention has not been satisfied or that the patented invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price.
(2) Every application under sub-section (1) shall contain such particulars as may be prescribed, the facts upon which the application is based, and, in the case of an application other than by the Central Government, shall also set out the nature of the applicant's interest.
(3) The Controller, if satisfied that the reasonable requirements of the public with respect to the patented invention have not been satisfied or that patented invention have not been worked in the territory of India or that the patented invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price, may make an order revoking the patent.

Where an objection is taken against a patent grant on the ground that the claims are unduly broad or encompass subject matter beyond the scope of the asserted invention far claimed, the Controller shall provide the applicant with a reasoned opportunity to respond and amend the claims accordingly. Such amendment may be permitted only if it does not substantially alter the nature of the invention as originally disclosed in the patent application. The determination of whether an amendment constitutes a substantial alteration shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from the acceptance of the amended claim. This provision applies equally to applications filed under this Act and those claiming priority from an India patent.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any person may apply to the Controller for institution of proceedings requesting restoration of the patent. Such application shall be made within six months from the date of such lapse and shall state fully the grounds upon which the applicant claims that the failure to pay the renewal fee was accidental or arose from circumstances beyond their reasonable control. The Controller may, after affording an opportunity of being heard to the applicant and any other interested party, direct restoration of the patent if satisfied that the grounds alleged are substantiated. Restoration shall revive the patent as if it had not lapsed, subject to payment of all overdue renewal fees together with a surcharge calculated at such rate as may be prescribed by the Central Government. The Controller shall record the order of restoration and publish it in the Patent Journal.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be made to the Controller under this Act in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish with the application a representation of the layout-design in the manner specified by the regulations. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall acknowledge its receipt and assign it a registration number. The Registrar shall maintain a register of applications for registration, noting the date of filing and the assigned registration number. Any person may inspect the register of applications subject to any conditions imposed by the Controller. An entry in the design registry shall be conclusive evidence of the particulars contained therein relating to the layout-design.

Any person dissatisfied with an order adjudicating officer relating to the revocation of a patent, or the imposition of a penalty under this Act, may lodge an objection with the High Court, provided that such objection is filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the said order. The High Court shall, upon receipt of such objection, constitute a Special Bench to examine the merits of the case and may, after hearing the parties concerned and subject to such conditions as it deems fit, confirm, modify, or set aside the order of the adjudicating officer. Further, if the objection concerns a matter of substantial legal complexity, the High Court may refer it to a larger Bench for determination. Any decision of the High Court in such matters shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to appeal permissible under the general laws of the land.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright shall subsist in a literary work for sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the author’s death. Where the author is not an individual, such period shall be reckoned from the beginning of the calendar year following the date on which the work is first published under circumstances indicating an intention to make it available to the public. Any person claiming infringement of copyright may file a suit in the district court having jurisdiction over the cause of action. The Court may, upon application made by any party to the proceedings, grant such temporary injunction as appears to the Court just and equitable. An appeal from the order of the District Court shall lie to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Any dispute concerning ownership of copyright arising under this Act may be referred for arbitration as agreed upon by the parties involved, provided that both parties consent in writing.

A provisional specification submitted under this Act shall be treated as a document establishing an early filing date for an invention, subject to the subsequent filing of a complete specification as provided herein. The provisional specification must describe the invention with sufficient detail to allow a person skilled in the relevant art to understand the concept and its potential application. Any disclosure within the provisional specification relating to a best mode contemplated by the inventor shall not be a condition for validity, but must be consistent with the overall description. A request for examination, accompanied by the complete specification, shall be filed within the time prescribed, failing which the provisional application shall lapse. Where a complete specification is filed claiming priority from a provisional specification, the complete specification must adequately support the claims made and disclose all information material to the invention as it existed on the date of filing of the provisional specification.

(1) Every application for a patent shall be for one invention only and shall be made in the prescribed form and filed in the patent office.
(1A) Every international application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty for a patent, as may be filed designating India, shall be deemed to be an application under this Act, if a corresponding application has also been filed before the Controller in India.
(1B) The filing date of an application referred to in sub-section (1A) and its complete specification processed by the patent office as designated office or elected office shall be the international filing date accorded under the Patent Cooperation Treaty.
(2) Where the application is made by virtue of an assignment of the right to apply for a patent for the invention, there shall be furnished with the application, or within such period as may be prescribed after the filling of the application, proof of the right to make the application.

A geographical indication, once registered under this Act, shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the said geographical indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered. Any use of a registered geographical indication by a person other than the registered proprietor, or a person duly authorized by him, shall constitute an infringement of the exclusive right. However, an honest use of a descriptive term corresponding to a geographical indication, not constituting an act of unfair competition, shall not be deemed to be an infringement. 

Where a geographical indication has fallen into disuse in relation to the goods for which it was registered, the Registrar may, upon application made in the prescribed manner and after giving the registered proprietor an opportunity to be heard, revoke the registration. A used geographical indication, even if not registered, may be protected under common law principles of passing off, subject to demonstrating sufficient goodwill and likelihood of deception. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications and related particulars.

The registration of a trade mark shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any rights prior existing. An application for registration may be assigned or transmitted by way of mortgage, pledge or otherwise, provided that such assignment or transmission does not affect the validity of the registration itself. Where a trade mark has been used continuously by the previous proprietor and the subsequent assignee or transferee ceases such use within the period specified under this Act, the right to use the trade mark may revert to the original registered proprietor. A transmissible case arises when an application for registration is assigned before its acceptance, and the assignor retains a continuing interest in the outcome of that application.

Any person who, by virtue of being a director of a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, has exercised control over the creation of a cinematograph film, shall be deemed the first owner of the copyright in that film, subject to any agreement to the contrary executed prior to the commencement of the film’s production. However, such ownership shall not extend to any underlying literary or musical work incorporated within the film, the copyright in which shall remain vested in the author or authors thereof, unless expressly assigned as provided herein. A director may, by written instrument, assign all or any of their rights in the copyright of the cinematograph film to another person or entity, and such assignment shall be effective upon registration with the Registrar of Copyrights. Where a director is appointed by a producer solely for the purpose of directing the film, and receives consideration therefor, it shall be presumed that any copyright arising from the direction is owned by the producer, unless otherwise stipulated in a written contract. Any dispute regarding the ownership of copyright between a director and a producer shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to licensing and royalty payments.

For the purposes of determining patentability under this Act, an invention shall be considered to possess substance only if it demonstrates novelty and involves an inventive step. An application for a patent may be filed disclosing the matter referred to in section 10, provided that such disclosure adequately describes the manner in which the invention can be performed. The Controller General shall have power to require amendment of any claim where it is found not to clearly define the scope of protection sought. Where an applicant has previously published particulars of the invention, a period of twelve months from the date of first publication shall apply for claiming priority under this Act. An invention which consists essentially of a substance means new and lacks inventive step shall be deemed unpatentable as provided herein.

(1) If any person refuses or fails to furnish—
(a) to the Central Government any information which he is required to furnish under sub-section (5) of section 100,
(b) to the Controller any information or statement which he is required to furnish by or under section 146, he shall be liable to penalty which may extend to one lakh rupees, and in case of the continuing refusal or failure, a further penalty of one thousand rupees for every day after the first during which such refusal or failure continues.
(2) If any person, being required to furnish any such information as is referred to in sub-section (1), furnishes information or statement which is false, and which he either knows or has reason to believe to be false or does not believe to be true, 3he shall be liable to penalty for a sum equal to one half per cent. of the total sale or turnover, as the case may be, of business or of the gross receipts in profession as computed in the audited accounts of such person, or a sum equal to five crore rupees, whichever is less.

For the purposes of this Act, "proceeding infringement" shall mean an action undertaken by any party which creates a reasonable apprehension in the mind of another that their trade mark rights are being, or are likely to be, infringed. Such actions include, but are not limited to, the publication of false or misleading statements concerning the quality or origin of goods or services; the use of signs identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services not authorized by the proprietor; and any other conduct calculated to deceive or confuse consumers regarding the source or affiliation of products. Provided that mere advertising, devoid of such deceptive intent, shall not constitute proceeding infringement as provided herein.

(1) No court shall take cognizance of an offence under section 107 or section 108 or section 109 except on complaint in writing made by the Registrar or any officer authorised by him in writing: Provided that in relation to clause ( c) of sub-section
(1) of section 107, a court shall take cognizance of an offence on the basis of a certificate issued by the Registrar to the effect that a registered trade mark has been represented as registered in respect of any goods or services in respect of which it is not in fact registered.
(2) No court inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class shall try an offence under this Act.
(3) The offences under section 103 or section 104 or section 105 shall be cognizable.

Where an aggrieved party alleges infringement of patent rights granted under this Act, the remedies available shall be determined according to the principles established herein. Such aggrieved parties may seek injunctive relief preventing further acts of making, using or importing the patented invention without authorization. The Controller may, upon receiving evidence of wilful infringement, order damages to be paid by the infringer to the patentee, reflecting lost profits and reasonable royalty rates. This determination shall consider the extent of the infringing activity and its impact on the market share previously held by the patentee. Rules carry provisions for expedited hearings in cases involving urgent threats of irreparable harm arising from ongoing infringement. In matters concerning convention applications filed as an invention convention country application, the date of first filing abroad is crucial to establishing priority rights.

Where the proprietor of a registered trademark grants a license permitting the use of their mark upon goods or services, such license may include provisions for assignment of the right to prevent acts of passing off. The licensee shall be entitled to assign the benefit of this protection against unauthorized use creating confusion amongst consumers, provided that such assignment is made in writing and duly executed. Further, where a trademark proprietor enters into an agreement with another party allowing them to utilize their mark under conditions restricting specific commercial activities, any subsequent attempt by a third party to engage in similar activities constituting passing off shall be actionable at the instance of both the original proprietor and the initially licensed party, subject to the terms outlined within the licensing arrangement. The rights granted or assigned hereunder are not transferable without prior written consent from the trademark proprietor.

A farmer aggrieved by the refusal of the Plant Variety Protection Authority to register a farmer’s variety, or by any decision concerning the benefit sharing arising from the commercial exploitation of such variety, may file an appeal before the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed in the Schedule. The Appellate Board shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to both parties, pass an order confirming, modifying or reversing the decision of the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Any person claiming to be a farmer and asserting rights under this Act shall furnish proof of their bona fide agricultural activity to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board. Should the Appellate Board find that the appellant was not a genuine farmer at the time of the original grievance, the appeal shall be dismissed with costs. Further, any delay in filing an appeal beyond the stipulated ninety days may be condoned if sufficient cause is shown.

Any person manufacturing a pharmaceutical substance, whether alone or in combination with other active pharmaceutical ingredients, without a valid patent or license as provided herein, shall be deemed to have committed an infringement and shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five crore rupees or imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or both. Where the infringement relates to a pharmaceutical substance essential for public health, the penalty may be enhanced up to ten crore rupees. Any evidence obtained through search and seizure relating to the illicit manufacture of such substances shall be admissible in court, subject to the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code. A person claiming legitimate manufacture shall bear the burden of proving compliance with this Act, including demonstrating the novelty and non-obviousness of the pharmaceutical substance. Repeated offences shall attract cumulative penalties and potential revocation of manufacturing licenses. All seized materials shall be subject to disposal as directed by a designated court.

The Chairperson shall exercise ultimate authority in matters pertaining to the registration and rectification of semiconductor layout-designs as provided herein, and shall ensure adherence to principles of natural justice in all proceedings. Any decision of the Chairperson regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration may be subject to review by a designated officer, provided that such review shall not exceed thirty days from the date of the Chairperson’s initial order. In cases involving disputes concerning the similarity of a proposed layout-design to an existing registered layout-design, or where allegations of trade mark similarity are raised in relation to the commercial exploitation of a layout-design, the Chairperson may appoint a technical expert to provide an independent assessment. The remuneration of such an expert shall be borne by the applicant, or apportioned between the parties as the Chairperson deems just. The Chairperson shall maintain a register of all registered layout-designs and shall make such register accessible to the public subject to reasonable restrictions. Any appeal against a decision of the Chairperson shall be made to the High Court having territorial jurisdiction.

(1) The examiner to whom an application for a patent is referred under section 12 shall make investigation for the purpose of ascertaining whether the invention so far as claimed in any claim of the complete specification—
(a) has been anticipated by publication before the date of filing of the applicant's complete specification in any specification filed in pursuance of an application for a patent made in India and dated on or after the 1st day of January, 1912;
(b) is claimed in any claim of any other complete specification published on or after the date of filing of the applicant's complete specification, being a specification filed in pursuance of an application for a patent made in India and dated before or claiming the priority date earlier than that date.
(2) The examiner shall, in addition, make such investigation for the purpose of ascertaining whether the invention, so far as claimed in any claim of the complete specification, has been anticipated by publication in India or elsewhere in any document other than those mentioned in sub-section (1) before the date of filing of the applicant's complete specification.

Where any imported goods are suspected of being counterfeit or deceptively misdescribed in relation to a registered trade mark, an officer of customs shall immediately notify the Registrar. The Registrar may, upon receipt of such notification and after affording the proprietor of the trade mark an opportunity to be heard, issue instructions to the Customs authorities regarding the disposition of the goods. Such instructions may direct that the goods be seized and detained pending further investigation or examination. Where the imported goods are determined to be in violation of this Act, they shall be subject to confiscation under the provisions of the Customs Act 1962. The proprietor of the trade mark shall be entitled to recover from the importer any costs incurred by the Registrar in connection with the examination and disposition of the goods, provided that the importer is found to have acted in bad faith or with knowledge of the infringing nature of the goods.

Where a registered layout design owner desires to grant a license or assign their rights relating to a protected integrated circuit layout design, such license or assignment shall be in writing and executed by an authorized representative of the owner. The terms of any license granted under this Act may specify the field of use, duration, and geographical extent of the permitted exploitation. Further, where a license is assigned along with the underlying layout design rights, the assignee shall become the exclusive proprietor subject to any continuing obligations stipulated in the original licensing agreement. Any dispute arising concerning the validity or interpretation of such licenses or assignments may be referred to the Appellate Board sub for adjudication and binding determination, as provided herein. The Board’s decision shall be final and conclusive.

Any order for the grant of a licence under this Chapter shall operate as if it were a deed granting a licence executed by the patentee and all other necessary parties embodying the terms and conditions, if any, settled by the Controller.

Any person claiming infringement of copyright in any work shall, subject to provisions regarding limitation periods, institute civil proceedings in a District Court having jurisdiction over the cause of action. Upon receiving complaint of alleged copyright infringement, the court may issue an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, provided that such restraint is necessary to prevent irreparable injury. The remedies available under this Act include damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the copyright owner as a result of the infringement, and in cases of flagrant or wilful infringement, punitive damages not exceeding ten times the actual damages. Furthermore, any works seized during investigation of alleged infringements shall be held in custody of the Copyright Office until determination of the case by the court.

Any individual or enterprise who knowingly uses a protected geographical indication in relation to goods not originating from the registered geographical territory, or employs such an indication in a manner that misrepresents the true origin of those goods, shall be liable for damages as provided herein. This includes instances where packaging, advertising, or labelling falsely suggests a connection to the registered area. Furthermore, any act which falsifies genuine geographical indications by way of imitation, colourable representation, or misleading association with the registered indication constitutes an infringement under this Act. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may issue cease and desist orders, direct destruction of infringing materials, and impose penalties not exceeding ten times the value of the infringing goods sold.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to the grant, refusal, modification or revocation of registration of a registered breeder variety may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. Failure to comply with prescribed conditions for maintaining a registered breeder variety shall render the registrant liable to pay compensation as determined by the Board, not exceeding five times the annual royalty fees collected during the period of non-compliance. Furthermore, any act of unauthorized propagation or sale of a protected registered breeder variety, discovered through inspection carried out under this Act, constitutes an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine as provided herein.

An applicant desiring to apply patent shall furnish with the prescribed fee a statement of particulars relating to the invention, including its title and a concise description thereof. The statement must further detail the class or classes to which the invention relates, as determined by the controller. Where an application incorporates by reference matter which has previously been made available to the public, whether in India or elsewhere, the applicant shall provide a written explanation of the circumstances under which such matter became available and demonstrate that the claimed invention is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the novelty assessment if deemed necessary for proper examination.

The Central Trademarks Registry shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trademark, conduct such searches as are deemed necessary to ascertain whether the mark is already registered or applied for under this Act. Any person claiming rights in respect of any existing trade name or trademark may, within four months from the date of advertisement of acceptance of the proposed trademark, file notice of opposition with the Registry. Such opposition shall be determined according to the procedures as provided herein. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further particulars relating to the use of the mark and the goods or services in connection therewith. It is a condition precedent that registration ought effected only after due consideration of any such opposition, and where applicable, subsequent hearings.

(1) A registered layout-design is infringed by a person who, not being the registered proprietor of the layout-design or a registered user thereof,— (1)(a) does any act of reproducing, whether by incorporating in a semiconductor integrated circuit or otherwise, a registered layout-design in its entirety or any part thereof, except such act of reproducing any part thereof which is not original within the meaning sub-section (2) of section 7; (1)(b) subject to the provisions of sub-section (5), does any act of importing or selling or otherwise distributing for commercial purposes a registered layout-design or a semiconductor integrated circuit incorporating such registered layout-design or an article incorporating such a semiconductor integrated circuit containing such registered layout-design for the use of which such person is not entitled under this Act. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in section 17, sub-section (1) or sub-section (5), the performance of the act of reproduction referred to in clause (a) of sub-section (1), where such act is performed for the limited purposes of scientific evaluation, analysis, research or teaching, shall not constitute act of infringement within the meaning of that clause.

Any person claiming rights in a trade mark registered in a convention country may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Registrar for the registration of an advertising international registration of that mark in India. The application shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by a certified copy of the basic application or registration and a statement identifying the goods or services for which the mark is registered in the country of origin. Should the Registrar object to the registration on grounds of conflict with prior Indian trade marks, the applicant may file a response within sixty days, demonstrating distinctiveness and lack of deceptive similarity. Any decision of the Registrar in this regard shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Registrar’s order. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, except where a substantial question of law is involved, allowing for further recourse to the High Court.

Any application for the registration of a geographical indication shall be examined by the Registrar, and such examination shall be conducted as provided herein, with due regard to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the goods meet the criteria for registration, and that the application complies with all procedural requirements, the geographical indication shall be registered in the Register. Registration shall apply to the goods originating from a defined geographical area and possessing qualities or a reputation linked to that origin, and no registration shall be granted if it is likely to mislead the public or be contrary to public order or morality. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, require the applicant to furnish further evidence or clarification regarding the geographical area, the qualities of the goods, or the link to their origin. A register of geographical indications shall be maintained, open to inspection by interested parties upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any alteration to the registered geographical indication shall require a separate application and be subject to the same scrutiny as the original registration.

(2) The date of every patent shall be entered in the register.

Where a complaint alleging infringement of layout-design rights is received, the Controller shall initiate a procedure investigation to ascertain the facts and circumstances surrounding the alleged violation. Such investigation shall include examination of relevant documents, recording statements from interested parties including the complainant, the accused, and any witnesses identified during the process. The Controller may issue summons requiring attendance and production of evidence as deemed necessary for the purpose of this investigation. Any person failing to comply with a summons issued under this Act is liable to penalties as provided herein. The findings of the procedure investigation shall form the basis for subsequent proceedings relating to infringement claims.

(3) Opposition to the registration under sub-section (2) may be made on any of the following grounds, namely:— (a) that the person opposing the application is entitled to the breeder's right as against the applicant; or (b) that the variety is not registrable under this Act; or (c) that the grant of certificate of registration may not be in public interest; or (d) that the variety may have adverse effect on the environment. (4) The Registrar shall serve a copy of the notice of opposition on the applicant for registration and, within two months from the receipt by the applicant of such copy of the notice of opposition, the applicant shall send to the Registrar in the prescribed manner a counter-statement of the grounds on which he relies for his application, and if he does not do so, he shall be deemed to have abandoned his application.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered Geographical Indication relating to “placed houses parliament” may file an application with the Registrar, subject to demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from the registration. Such applications shall specify the particulars of the alleged error or omission and provide supporting evidence establishing the distinctiveness of the goods or services originating from the geographical territory claimed. The Registrar shall afford the applicant and any opposing party a reasonable opportunity for argument under this Act. An aggrieved party may appeal against an order passed by the Registrar to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is made within sixty days of the date of communication of the order. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein.

Where a patent india has been granted and the proprietor thereof becomes aware that any person other than himself or his licensee has infringed or is infringing the invention in respect of which the patent has been granted, he may institute suit for damages against such person. The measure of damages recoverable under this Act shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringement and the profits made by the infringer attributable to the making, use or sale of the patented invention. Provided that in determining the said profits, due account shall be taken of any expenditure incurred by the infringer in making, using or selling the invention. Subject to this, damages may include reasonable royalties which the infringer would have been willing to pay. The proprietor shall also be entitled to an injunction restraining the infringing activity as provided herein.

Any person who,— (a) makes or causes to be made a false entry in the Register of Copyrights kept under this Act, or (b) makes or causes to be made a writing falsely purporting to be a copy of any entry in such register, or (c) produces or tenders or causes to be produced or tendered as evidence any such entry or writing, knowing the same to be false, shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.

Upon expiry term patent, any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to compulsory licensing or revocation may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the Appellate Board shall not entertain any appeal if it is shown that the appellant failed to make a timely application for relief under this Act. Further, where a patent has expired and another patent claiming priority from the same earlier application is subsequently granted, the rights conferred by the later patent shall be subject to any prior compulsory licenses previously issued or applications pending under this Act relating to the invention claimed in the earlier patent. The Controller may, upon receiving an application demonstrating substantial prejudice due to the expiry term patent, grant interim relief pending determination of the appeal.

Any officer of the patent office who, having authority to examine an application for a patent, wilfully and with intent to cause delay rejects such application without reasonable grounds shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years or with fine, or with both. Should any person present to the patent office forged documents as part of a claim for inventorship, that person shall forfeit all rights relating to said invention and be liable to prosecution under the Indian Penal Code. The Controller of Patents, subject to directions issued by the Central Government, may establish regional offices of the patent office to facilitate access for applicants residing in remote areas. Any false representation made to obtain an expedited hearing before the patent office will attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. All records maintained by the patent office shall be deemed public documents and open to inspection as provided herein.

(1) Subject to the other provisions of this Act, a certificate of registration for a variety issued under this Act shall confer an exclusive right on the breeder or his successor, his agent or licensee, to produce, sell, market, distribute, import or export the variety: Provided that in the case of an extant variety, unless a breeder or his successor establishes his right, the Central Government, and in cases where such extant variety is notified for a State or for any area thereof under section 5 of the Seeds Act, 1966 (54 of 1966), the State Government, shall be deemed to be the owner of such right. (2) A breeder may authorise any person to produce, sell, market or otherwise deal with the variety registered under this Act subject to such limitations and conditions as may be specified by regulations.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a patent has been granted, the patentee shall be entitled to grant exclusive licenses in respect thereof, and may assign his rights and interest therein to any person or persons, either wholly or partially, and either for the whole duration of the term of the patent or for any lesser period. Any such assignment or license shall take effect only upon registration with the Controller, and the prescribed fee shall be paid at the time of such registration. Where an exclusive license has been granted, the licensee shall have all the rights and powers which the patentee might have exercised under this Act. The patentee may also grant non-exclusive licenses, provided that such licenses do not unreasonably restrain trade or competition. Upon assignment, the assignee shall be deemed to be the holder of the patent for all purposes as if he were the original patentee.

Where any person, being the registered proprietor of a trade mark, or having been previously refused registration thereof, institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, and such proceedings are found to be frivolous or vexatious, the Court may impose sentence imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year. For the purposes of determining whether proceedings are frivolous, the Court shall consider whether the specification claim in the plaint accurately reflects the scope of the registered trade mark and whether reasonable grounds existed for believing that infringement has occurred. This provision applies irrespective of any subsequent amendment or withdrawal of the said proceedings.

A geographical indication shall be considered to be falsified when goods are offered for sale, or otherwise presented to the public, in a manner which suggests a connection to a geographical indication, when no such connection exists. Any representation, direct or indirect, that goods originate from a region associated with a registered geographical indication, but do not, shall constitute an indication falsified as provided herein. Where a collective or qualifying mark is used in conjunction with a geographical indication, any misrepresentation regarding adherence to the standards or criteria for use of that mark shall also be deemed an indication falsified. The Registrar may, subject to such inquiry as may be deemed necessary, issue a notice to any person suspected of engaging in such practices, requiring them to demonstrate the veracity of their claims regarding the geographical origin of goods. Failure to adequately demonstrate such veracity may result in the initiation of enforcement proceedings under this Act.

The registered owner of an integrated circuit layout-design shall be permitted to grant licenses conferring rights relating to reproduction and use, subject to the terms specified therein. Such licenses may be assigned to any person or entity with the prior written consent of the original registrant, provided that such assignment is recorded with the Registrar within thirty days. Where a license agreement involves alterations to the registered layout-design which substantially affect its functionality or appearance, the assignee shall apply for an alteration certificate registration demonstrating the nature and extent of those changes. The Registrar may require submission of technical documentation substantiating these modifications before processing the application. Failure to obtain such certification prior to commercial exploitation of the altered design renders the assignee liable for infringement proceedings under this Act.

Any act done in contravention of the provisions relating to revocation of a patent, as provided herein, shall constitute a commission offence, attracting penalties as specified in the Schedules to this Act. Where such a commission offence involves fraudulent intent, the penalty shall be enhanced by an amount not exceeding twice the value of the damages suffered by the patent holder, subject to a minimum fine of five thousand rupees. A person abetting the commission of such an offence, or attempting to commit such an offence, shall be deemed to have committed the commission offence and shall be liable to the same penalties. Provided that, if the offence is committed by a partnership firm, each partner shall be held jointly and severally liable for the penalties imposed. The burden of proving due diligence to prevent the commission offence shall lie with the accused.

Where an application for a patent has been laid open for public inspection and the complete specification is subsequently amended, such amendment shall only be permissible if it does not substantially alter the nature claimed for the invention. Any party aggrieved by the acceptance of an amended specification may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of publication of the amended specification under this Act. The Board shall consider whether the amendment introduces matter which goes beyond the disclosure in the original application, and if so, determine that the patent should not be granted or, alternatively, require further examination. It is provided that the Controller may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct a fresh search relating to the invention as affected by the specification amended.

(1) Save as provided in sub -section (2), nothing in this Act shall authorise the registration of two or more persons who use a trade mark independently, or propose so as to use it, as joint proprietors thereof.
(2) Where the relations between two or more persons interested in a trade mar k are such that no one of them is entitled as between himself and the other or others of them to use it except— (a) on behalf of both or all of them; or\ (b) in relation to an article or service with which both or all of them are connected in the course of trade, those persons may be registered as joint proprietors of the trade mark, and this Act shall have effect in relation to any rights to the use of the trade mark vested in those persons as if those rights had been vested in a single person.

A musical work shall be deemed to include not only compositions fixed permanently in a tangible medium but also improvisations performed live, provided that such improvisation is recorded and subsequently reproduced with the authorization of the practitioner person responsible for its creation. Such authorization shall be evidenced by a written agreement specifying the terms of reproduction, including royalty rates payable to the practitioner person. The right of copyright under this Act in respect of any musical work shall vest initially in the composer or arranger unless otherwise stipulated within a contractual arrangement executed prior to the first public performance. Any subsequent assignment of such rights must adhere to principles of transparency and fair dealing as provided herein.

The Register of Copyrights shall be prima facie evidence of the particulars entered therein and documents purporting to be c opies of any entries therein, or extracts therefrom, certified by the Registrar of Copyrights and sealed with the seal of the Copy right Office shall be admissible in evidence in all courts without further proof or production of the original.

(1) A registered trade mark may be taken off the register in respect of the goods or services in respect of which it is registered on application made in the prescribed manner to the Registrar or the High Court by any person aggrieved on the ground either—
(a) that the trade mark was registered without any bona fide intention on the part of the applicant for registration that it sh ould be used in relation to those goods or services by him or, in a case to which the provisions of section 46 apply, by the company concerned or the registered user, as the case may be, and that there has, in fact, been no bona fide use of the trade mark in relation to those goods or services by any proprietor thereof for the time being up to a date three months before the date of the application; or

A registered proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the goodwill of the trade mark with or without any part of the business in which it is used. Any assignment of a reference use mark shall be accompanied by a detailed statement outlining the scope of permitted use, including the specific goods or services for which the mark is assigned and any geographical limitations applicable to such use. Where an assignment involves a complex licensing arrangement, the Trade Marks Registry may, at the request of either party, appoint a chairperson judicial member to facilitate a fair and equitable determination of the terms. Such a member shall have the power to direct mediation or, failing that, to make recommendations regarding the assignment, which shall be binding unless successfully appealed. The assignee shall be entitled to all rights and remedies as if they were the original proprietor, subject to the terms of the assignment and any conditions imposed by the Registry. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment voidable.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct an examination as provided herein to ascertain whether the mark satisfies the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder. The registrar may require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information or documents, subject to a reasonable timeframe specified by the registrar. Where the application is found to be deficient, the application registrar shall communicate the objections to the applicant in writing, detailing the grounds for such objection. Provided that, if the applicant fails to address the objections within the stipulated period, the application shall be deemed to be abandoned. The registrar shall maintain a register of all applications received and their current status.

(1) On receipt of copy of the certificate of registration under sub-section (8) of section 23 or sub-section (2) of section 24, the Authority shall publish such contents of the certificate and invite claims of benefit sharing to the variety registered under such certificate in the manner as may be prescribed. (2) On invitation of the claims under sub-section (1), any person or group of persons or firm or governmental or non-governmental organisation shall submit its claim of benefit sharing to such variety in the prescribed form within such period, and accompanied with such fees, as may be prescribed: Provided that such claim shall only be submitted by any— (i) person or group of persons, if such person or every person constituting such group is a citizen of India; or (ii) firm or governmental or non-governmental organisation, if such firm or organisation is formed or established in India.

A services trade mark shall be registrable under this Act, notwithstanding that it is not used in relation to goods, where the applicant intends to use it, or authorize its use, in connection with the provision of services. For the purposes of this Act, ‘services’ include, but are not limited to, financial, banking, insurance, transport, educational, construction, and medical services. An application for the registration of a services trade mark shall be subject to the same conditions and requirements as an application for a trade mark for goods, provided that the specification of services must be clearly and accurately defined. The Registrar may, however, require further clarification if the specified services are vague or overly broad. Registration of a services trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the specified services.

(1) Where a person is convicted of an offence under section 56, the court convicting him may direct the forfeiture to Government of all goods and things by means of, or in relation to, which the offence has been committed. (2) When a forfeiture is directed on a conviction and an appeal lies against the conviction, an appeal shall lie against the forfeiture also. (3) When a forfeiture is directed on a conviction, the court, before whom the person is convicted, may order any forfeited articles to be destroyed or otherwise disposed of as the court thinks fit.

(1) Whoever aggrieved by an order of the adjudicating officer under sect ion 112A may prefer an appeal to the appellate authority, who shall be an officer at least one rank above the adjudicating officer, within a period of sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, as the Central Government may by notification authorise in this behalf
(2) Every appeal under this section shall be preferred in such form and manner as may be prescribed.
(3) An appeal may be admitted after the expiry of the period of sixty days if the appellant satisfies the appellate authority that he had sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal within that period.
(4) No appeal shall be disposed of unless the appellant has been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
(5) The appellate authority referred to in sub -section
(1) shall dispose of th e appeal within sixty days from the date of filing.
(6) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, if the person fails to comply with the order of the adjudicating officer under section 112A or the order of the appellate authority under this section, as the case may be, within ninety days of such order, he shall, in addition to the penalty, be punishable with fine of one lakh rupees or imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with both.

Where any person is found to have made a false statement or suppressed material information during proceedings before the Controller relating to the grant, revocation or maintenance of a patent, an inquiry imposing penalty shall be initiated by the Controller. Such inquiry may be conducted by the Controller personally or through an officer duly authorised under this Act. The amount of the penalty shall not exceed one million rupees and is subject to adjustments as determined by the Central Government based on prevailing economic conditions. Any appeal against an order made during such inquiry imposing penalty shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

A breeder variety registered under this Act shall confer upon the breeder the exclusive right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import, export, and stock propagable material of the variety in India. However, such exclusive right shall be subject to the provisions relating to research and breeding, and shall not extend to acts done solely for private and non-commercial purposes. Any farmer who is in possession of seeds of a registered breeder variety may save, use, sow, re-sow, multiply, and propagate such seeds for his own purposes, provided that he does not sell, market, or distribute such saved seeds or propagable material. The Authority may, upon application by any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right, initiate an inquiry and, if satisfied that an infringement has occurred, issue a cease and desist order. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Authority may appeal to the High Court. A registered breeder shall maintain a record of all transactions relating to the sale and distribution of the variety, as provided herein, and make such record available for inspection upon demand by an officer authorized by the Central Government.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent resulting from a falsely marked application patent shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where any person, by way of fraud or misrepresentation, obtains registration of an application patent for an invention which is not new, or does not involve an inventive step, or does not relate to a patentable subject matter as provided herein, such registration shall be void ab initio and the Controller may revoke the patent forthwith. The aggrieved party may initiate proceedings before the High Court seeking damages commensurate with actual loss suffered due to the fraudulent application. Provided that no action for recovery of damages shall lie against any person who proves reasonable diligence in ascertaining the novelty and inventive step prior to filing the application patent. Any false representation concerning the scope of a granted patent, including claims not supported by the specification, will attract similar penalties.

Notwithstanding anything contained under this Act relating to the ownership of copyright in cinematographic films, where the film sound exclusively comprises musical works and literary works created independently of the filming process, the author or authors of such works shall be deemed the first owners of copyright therein. This determination is subject to the condition that the producers demonstrate, through documented evidence presented before an adjudicating officer appointed by the Central Government, that they were not party to any agreement assigning said rights prior to the commencement of film production. Any dispute arising from this provision may be appealed to a High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose, provided such appeal is made within ninety days of the order of the adjudicating officer.

(b) that such other complete specification was published on or after the priority date of the applicant's claim, then, unless it is shown to the satisfaction of the Controller that the priority date of the applicant's claim is not later than the priority date of the claim of that specification, the provisions of sub-section (2) shall apply thereto in the same manner as they apply to a specification published on or after the date of filing of the applicant's complete specification.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under sub-section (2) of section 64 or section 66 may, within thirty days of the date of such order appeal to the Court to which appeals from the court making the order ordinarily lie, and such appellate court may direct that execution of the order be stayed pending disposal of the appeal.

(1) For the purposes of this Act, a record called the Register of Trade Marks shall be kept at the head office of the Trade Marks Registry, wherein shall be entered all registered trade marks with the names, addresses and description of the propri etors, notifications of assignment and transmissions, the names, addresses and descriptions of registered users, conditions, limitations and such other matter relating to registered trade marks as may be prescribed.
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), it shall be lawful for the Registrar to keep the records wholly or partly in computer floppies diskettes or in any other electronic form subject to such safeguards as may be prescribed.
(3) Where such register is maintained wholly or par tly on computer under sub -section ( 2) any reference in this Act to entry in the Register shall be construed as the reference to any entry as maintained on computer or in any other electronic form.
(4) No notice of any trust, express or implied or construct ive, shall be entered in the register and no such notice shall be receivable by the Registrar.
(5) The register shall be kept under the control and management of the Registrar.

Where a company is proved to have committed an offence relating to the unauthorized reproduction of a copyrighted work, and it is demonstrated that such reproduction occurred with the knowledge or consent of a directing mind of the company, both the company and such individual shall be held liable for damages and injunctive relief as provided herein. Should the alleged infringement concern a patented invention, and the company asserts the validity of a corresponding patent application pending before the Patent Office, proceedings regarding the alleged copyright offence shall be stayed pending a final determination by the Patent Office on the matter of patent validity. However, such stay shall not exceed a period of six months, and the aggrieved party may petition the High Court for expedited resolution if the Patent Office fails to render a decision within said timeframe. Any appeal arising from a decision concerning a company proved offence shall lie before the appellate authority designated under this Act, subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods.

Any person claiming to have essentially derived a variety, as defined under this Act, shall submit an application for registration to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application shall include a detailed description of the characteristics of the derived variety, demonstrating its distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability, and a clear indication of the initial variety from which it was derived. A declaration affirming that the applicant possesses legitimate access to the initial variety and has complied with the provisions relating to benefit sharing, where applicable, shall also be furnished. The Authority may, subject to verification of the claims and conformity with the established criteria for essentially derived varieties, register the variety and issue a certificate of registration. Provided that, registration shall not be granted if the derived variety lacks substantial novelty or if its production and propagation would be detrimental to the maintenance of the initial variety. The registrar may request additional information or samples as deemed necessary for a thorough evaluation of the crop sciences involved.

Any person desiring registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller of Designs in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee as provided herein. The application shall disclose all essential features of the layout-design including its topological arrangement and dimensions, and must clearly identify the semiconductor material utilized in its fabrication. A representation, being a graphical depiction of the layout-design, shall also be furnished with such application; said representation may be in black and white or colour as deemed appropriate by the applicant. 

Where an applicant claims priority from an earlier application filed in a convention country, details thereof including the filing date and country must be stated within the prescribed period. The Controller, upon examination of the application and finding it to be complete and compliant with the provisions of this Act, shall register the layout-design subject to verification of novelty and originality; however, registration may be refused if the layout-design is found to be plagiarized or lacking in distinctive character. Any registered semiconductor layout-design shall confer upon the applicant exclusive rights as stipulated herein.

Any person who knowingly imports, manufactures, distributes, displays for sale, or offers for sale any layout-design infringing the rights of the design registered proprietor shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to ten times the number of infringed integrated circuits. Such liability may be enforced by way of civil suit in the District Court having jurisdiction over the territory where the infringement occurred. Further, under this Act, a design registered proprietor aggrieved by an act of infringement may apply for an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing such acts. The court shall consider evidence presented demonstrating actual or threatened loss to the design registered proprietor as a consequence of the infringement and may award costs reflective of that harm.

(1) Subject to the provisions of section 9, at any time after the filing of an application and 3before the grant of the patent under this Act, the Controller may, at the request of the applicant made in the prescribed manner, direct that the application shall be post-dated to such date as may be specified in the request, and proceed with the application accordingly:
Provided that no application shall be post-dated under this sub-section to a date later than six months from the date on which it was actually made or would, but for the provisions of this sub-section, be deemed to have been made.
(2) Where an application or specification (including drawings) or any other documents is required to be amended under section 15, the application or specification or other document shall, if the Controller so directs, be deemed to have been made on the date on which the requirement is complied with or where the application or specification or other document is returned to the applicant, on the date on which it is refiled after complying with the requirement.

All proceedings before the Authority or the Registrar, as the case may be, relating to registration of variety or essentially derived variety, registration of agent, registration of licence or registration of compulsory licensing under this Act shall be deemed to be judicial proceedings within the meaning of sections 193 and 228, and for the purpose of section 196 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) and the Authority or the Registrar, as the case may be, shall be deemed to be a civil court for the purposes of section 195 and Chapter XXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974).

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant exclusive licenses under their patent for an invention, specifying the field of use, territory, or other limitations as they deem fit. Such license shall be assignable by the patentee, either wholly or partially, and such assignment shall vest in the assignee the right to exercise the licensed rights to the extent specified therein. Where a patentee has granted multiple licenses relating to the same invention, the Controller may intervene if disputes arise concerning priority of enjoyment of the patented invention amongst the licensees, acting as an arbiter to ensure equitable distribution of benefits derived from exploitation of the intellectual property. Further, any licensee may, with prior written consent of the patentee and subject to conditions prescribed herein, sub-license their rights pertaining to the granted invention.

(1) Where it is proposed that a person should be registered as a registered user of a trade mark, the registered proprietor and the proposed registered user shall jointly apply in writing to the Registrar in the prescribed manner, and every suc h applic ation shall be accompanied by—
