(iv) stating whether the permitted use is to be for a period or without limit of period, and, if for a period, the duration thereof; and
(c) such further documents or other evidence as may be required by the Reg istrar or as may be prescribed. (2) When the requirements of sub-section (1) have been complied with, the Registrar shall register the proposed registered user in respect of the goods or services as to which he is so satisfied. (3) The Registrar shall issue notice in the prescribed m anner of the registration of a person as a registered user, to other registered users of the trade mark, if any. (4) The Registrar shall, if so requested by the applicant, take steps for securing that information given for the purposes of an application under this section (other than matters entered in the register) is no t disclosed to rivals in trade.

Any person who, without reasonable cause, makes any false representation concerning the registration of a trade mark or the identity of the proprietor thereof shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a public record of all registered trade marks and associated applications; access to this record is subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning acceptance or rejection of an application under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, any person found to be using a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark shall be liable for damages as determined by civil court, consistent with section 21 Indian principles of fair use and consumer protection.

The Authority may, by general or special order in writing, delegate to the Chairperson, any member or officer of the Authority subject to such conditions or limitations, if any, as may be specified in the order, such of its powers and functions (except the power to make regulations under section 95) under this Act as it may deem necessary.
Reports of or to the Controller made under this Act other than the report referred to in section 45 shall not in any case be published or be open to public inspection.

An application for registration of a design shall be deemed invalid if the proposed design incorporates elements that compromise the security india explanation as determined by the Controller, acting on information received from designated national agencies. The Registrar may require an applicant to submit detailed technical specifications and manufacturing processes relating to the design, particularly where it pertains to articles intended for use in critical infrastructure or defense applications. Such submissions are subject to confidentiality agreements binding upon the applicant and their representatives. Furthermore, designs referencing plant varieties registered under the Plant Varieties Registry shall include a declaration confirming compliance with relevant biosafety regulations and acknowledging any intellectual property rights held by the variety’s breeder. Failure to provide this declaration will result in rejection of the application.
(5) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to empower the Controller to make any such order cancelling the registration of a design as is provided for in section 19.

Where a proprietor elects to have a mark separately registered under this Act, and such registration has been completed, the proprietor shall retain exclusive rights pertaining solely to the elements comprising said mark as individually delineated in the certificate of registration. Assignment of the parent trademark shall not automatically extend to the mark separately registered unless expressly stated within the assignment documentation. Any license granted by the proprietor relating to the use of the main trade mark may be extended to cover the use of the mark separately registered, provided that such extension is clearly articulated and documented in writing, specifying the permitted scope of usage and duration. Further, sub-licensing of the mark separately registered shall require prior written consent from the original proprietor, subject to conditions as they deem fit.

The Copyright Act provides that any society registered under this Act shall, within three months of the close of each financial year, remit to the Office prescribed fees as determined by the Central Government. Failure to remit such fees in full and on time constitutes a breach of the terms of registration and renders the society liable for penalties as may be specified through notification. Any aggrieved party, including but not limited to authors or beneficiaries entitled to royalties, may file an appeal against any assessment of copyright society fee deemed excessive or improperly levied. Such appeals shall be heard by a designated officer appointed by the Central Government, whose decision is final subject to judicial review under established principles of law.

For the purpose of this Act, “filed registry fee” means the sum prescribed under regulations framed by the Central Government and required to be remitted at the time of presenting an application for registration of a trade mark, or for any subsequent proceeding requiring formal entry upon the register. This fee is distinct from renewal fees or advertisement costs incurred during examination. The amount constituting the filed registry fee shall be determined based on the class of goods or services covered by the application and may be adjusted periodically as deemed necessary to account for administrative expenses. Failure to remit the correct filed registry fee will render an application voidable, subject to provisions regarding rectification.

(2) Without prejudice to the provisions contained in the General Clauses Act, 1897 (10 of 1897) with respect to repeals, any notification, rule, order, requirement, registration, certificate, notice, decis ion, determination, direction, approval, authorisation, consent, application, request or thing made, issued, given or done under the Designs Act, 1911 (2 of 1911), shall, in force at the commencement of this Act, continue to be in force and have effect as if made, issued, given or done under the corresponding provisions of this Act.

Subject to the other provisions of this Act, any holder of a variety registered act shall be entitled to grant licenses for the commercial exploitation of their protected plant variety. Such licenses may be granted on such terms and conditions as the licensing authority deems fit, including royalty rates, duration, and geographical scope. The license agreement shall clearly define the permitted uses of the propagating material derived from the registered variety. Assignment of a variety registered act is permissible with the prior approval of the Central Government, which may impose conditions to ensure continued benefit to farmers and preservation of genetic resources. Further, any binding government undertaking involved in agricultural research or development may enter into non-exclusive licenses under this Act for public service purposes, provided that such use does not unduly prejudice the rights of the registered breeder.

(1) No person, either alone or in partnerships with any other person, shall practise, describe or hold himself out as a patent agent, or permit himself to be so described or held out, unless he is registered as a patent agent or, as the case may be, unless he and all his partners are so registered.
(2) No company or other body corporate shall practise, describe itself or hold itself out as patent agents or permit itself to be so described or held out.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this section, practise as a patent agent includes any of the following acts, namely:—
(a) applying for or obtaining patents in India or elsewhere;

For the purposes of this Act, a "later publication application" means an application for patent relating to an invention which is disclosed in a document laid open to public inspection, whether by way of printed publication or otherwise, prior to the date of filing of the said application; provided that such disclosure did not contain sufficient particulars as to enable the invention to be performed. An applicant shall be deemed to have knowledge of any matter contained in a later publication application if it is readily available and accessible under this Act. The existence of a geographical indication applied for, but not registered, does not preclude consideration of a later publication application.

An officer of the Government whose duty it is to take part in the enforcement of the provisions of this Chapter, shall not be compelled in any court to say when he got any information as to the commission of any offence against this Act.

(1) If an assignee fails to make sufficient exercise of the rights assigned to him, and such failure is not at tributable to any act or omission of the assignor, then, the Appellate Board may, on receipt of a complaint from the assignor and after holding such inquiry as it may deem necessary, revoke such assignment. (2) If any dispute arises with respect to the assignment of any copyright, the Appellate Board may, on receipt of a complaint from the aggrieved party and after holding such inquiry as it considers necessary, pass such order as it may deem fit including an order for the recovery of any royalty payable: Provided that the Appellate Board shall not pass any order under this sub -section to revoke the assignment unless it is satisfied that the terms of assignment are harsh to the assignor in case the assignor is also the author: Provided further that, pending the disposal of an application for revocation of assignment under this sub-section, the Appellate Board may pass such order, as it deems fit regarding implementation of the terms and conditions of assignment including any consideration to be paid for the enjoyment of the rights assigned:— Provided also that, no order of revocation of assignment under this sub-section, shall be made within a period of five years from the date of such assignment. (3) Every complaint received under sub -section (2) shall be dealt with by the Appellate Board as far as possible and efforts shall be made to pass the final order in the matter within a period of six months from the date of receipt of the complaint and any delay in compliance of the same, the Appellate Board shall record the reasons thereof.

Any person who, without authorisation from the owner of the sound recording, reproduces the said sound recording in any medium, including but not limited to digital formats for distribution or commercial use, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount equivalent to three times the reasonable licensing fee that would have been payable had the reproduction been authorised, subject to a minimum penalty of fifty thousand rupees. Further, where such infringement is committed with the intent to deceive or cause undue gain, the offender may also face imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years. The owner of the sound recording shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement as provided herein.

Where any person considers that another has infringed his patent, he may institute proceedings for relief under this Act. Such proceedings shall be brought before the appropriate civil court having jurisdiction, and the aggrieved party must demonstrate to the satisfaction of the Court that the alleged infringing act falls within the scope of the claims as defined in the specification of the patent. The defendant shall have the right to challenge the validity of the patent itself, presenting evidence demonstrating a lack of novelty or an absence of inventive step. Should the Court find infringement and invalidity concurrently, remedies may be limited to injunctive relief preventing further acts of infringement, without entitlement to damages or account of profits. The specification constitutes the sole basis for determining the scope of protection afforded by the patent; any interpretation beyond its clear and unambiguous terms shall not be permitted.

(1) The relief which a court may grant in any suit for infringement or for passing off referred to in section 13 4 includes injunction (subject to such terms, if any, as the court thinks fit) and at the option of the plaintiff, either damages or an account of profits, together with or wit hout any order for the delivery -up of the infringing labels and marks for destruction or erasure. (2) The order of injunction under sub -section ( 1) may include an ex parte injunction or any interlocutory order for any of the following matters, namely:—
(i) that at the time he commenced to use the trade mark complained of in the suit , he was unaware and had no reasonable ground for believing that the trade mark of the plaintiff was on the register or that the plaintiff was a registered user using by way of permitted use; and
(ii) that when he became aware of the existence and nature of the plaintiff’s right in the trade mark, he forthwith ceased to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services in respect of which it was registered; or
(c) where in a suit for passing off, the defendant satisfies the court—
(i) that at the time he commenced to use the trade mark complained of in the suit , he was unaware and had no reasonable ground for believing that the trade mark fo r the plaintiff was in use; and

An action concerning the alleged infringement of a trademark registration may only be commenced before the Commercial Court established under this Act, provided that such Court has territorial jurisdiction over the defendant's place of business. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all pending and disposed-of suits relating to registered trademarks, including details of the marks involved and the nature of the alleged infringement. Further, any party seeking relief against an act of court suit infringement must demonstrate demonstrable similarity between the impugned mark and the registered trademark, considering not only visual appearance but also phonetic resemblance and conceptual meaning. The Court shall have power to grant such remedies as are deemed appropriate under this Act, including injunctions and damages.

Where an application for a patent relates to a process for producing a substance and that substance is used as an ingredient or intermediate in the manufacture of another substance, the determination of novelty and inventive step shall be undertaken with due consideration given to the nature of the process itself. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish particulars relating to the working of the process claimed, including details concerning any equipment utilized and the yield obtained under standard conditions. Any objection raised by a third party regarding the validity of a patent for a process respect patent shall be adjudicated according to the prescribed procedures, with emphasis on demonstrating prior use or public knowledge undermining inventive step. The applicant bears the onus of proving that the claimed process is capable of being performed by a person skilled in the art and produces the desired result consistently.

(a) by the absence or omission from the register of any entry; or
(b) by any entry made in the register without sufficient cause; or

In this Act, a trade description shall mean any description, statement, or indication, including names, marks, signs, figures, letters, words, or combinations thereof, applied to goods or their packaging, signifying the quality, quantity, area, manufacture, or origin of those goods. A trade description may also include any statement relating to the mode of performance of services. Any representation of a trade description, whether graphical or otherwise, shall be deemed to be included within the definition as provided herein. It shall not be necessary for a trade description to be directly applied to the goods if it is displayed prominently in connection with the offering for sale, sale, or distribution of such goods. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a false trade description shall be actionable.

Any person to whom a licence has been granted under section 84 shall be entitled to call upon the patentee to take proceedings to prevent any infringement of the patent, and, if the patentee refuses or neglects to do so within two months after being so called upon, the licensee may institute proceedings for the infringement in his own name as though he were the patentee, making the patentee a defendant; but a patentee so added as defendant shall not be liable for any costs unless he enters an appearance and takes part in the proceedings. 111. Restriction on power of court to grant damages or account of profits for infringement.—(1) In a suit for infringement of a patent, damages or an account of profits shall not be granted against the defendant who proves that at the date of the infringement he was not aware and had no reasonable grounds for believing that the patent existed.
Explanation.—A person shall not be deemed to have been aware or to have had reasonable grounds for believing that a patent exists by reason only of the application to an article of the word "patent", "patented" or any word or words expressing or implying that a patent has been obtained for the article, unless the number of the patent accompanies the word or words in question.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the defendant from such acts as are prejudicial to the rights conferred by this Act. The applicant shall furnish proof of registration and demonstrate substantial similarity between the registered layout-design and that which is alleged to be infringing, subject to considerations regarding permissible variations inherent in integrated circuit manufacturing processes. Should the respondent dispute the validity of the registration or assert a prior art defense establishing independent development of an identical or substantially similar integrated circuit, the Court may appoint a technical expert for assessment. Any decision rendered by the High Court shall be appealable to the Supreme Court on questions of law only, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days from the date of judgment and accompanied by certified copies of all pleadings. The aggrieved party may also seek damages commensurate with actual loss or reasonable royalty.

A Layout-Design is defined as the final three-dimensional arrangement of the electronic circuits wherein all layers of a semiconductor integrated circuit are included. Such a Layout-Design shall be eligible for registration under this Act provided it is original, and not previously published or exploited in any manner anywhere in India or elsewhere. The term ‘integrated circuit’ refers to those structures which are intended to perform an electronic function, capable of being mass produced, and having elements and interconnections essential for that function. Any Layout-Design substantially similar to a registered Layout-Design shall be considered infringing, subject to the provisions regarding permitted use as outlined herein. Registration confers upon the applicant exclusive rights in respect of the Layout-Design. The right extends to acts such as reproduction, communication to the public, sale and import.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that another has engaged in acts constituting passing off, and such allegation involves a comparison between goods or services offered by the defendant and those for which a trade mark is registered under this Act, the defendant may present evidence demonstrating due compliance with any registration notice published pursuant to the provisions herein. Such evidence shall be considered alongside all other submissions during proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority. The aggrieved party shall bear the onus of proving that the defendant’s actions create a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of the goods or services in question, subject to the defendant's right to challenge this finding on appeal.

(1) Where an application for the registration of a trade mark has been made under section 18 or a trade mark has been registered under section 23, the applicant or the registered proprietor may make an international application on the form prescribed by the Common Regulations for international registration of that trade mark.
(2) A person holding an international registration may make an international application on the form prescribed by the Common Regulations for extension of the protection resulting from such registration to any other Contracting Party.
(3) An international application under sub -section ( 1) or sub -section ( 2) shall designate the Contracting Parties where the protection resulting from the international registration is required.

(4) If the Registrar is satisfied after hearing the applicant and all the opponents, if desirous of being heard, that the certificate of registration may properly be surrendered, he may accept the offer and by order revoke the certificate of registration.

Any person who possesses confidential information relating to a design, and who, having obtained such information in the course of any proceedings under this Act, discloses it to any other person, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. However, such disclosure shall not be construed as an offence where it is made for the purpose of preventing serious injury to the public or to secure the safety of India. The Controller of Designs may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, require any applicant for a design to furnish a security deposit to ensure compliance with the provisions of this Act and to safeguard against frivolous or malicious applications. This security, if deemed necessary for the protection of national interests or to specify security india, may be increased at the discretion of the Controller. Any security so furnished shall be returned to the applicant upon satisfactory completion of the registration process or final determination of the application, less any costs or damages incurred by the Controller.

In any proceeding under this Act before the Registrar, evidence shall be given by affidavit: Provided that the Registrar may, if he thinks fit, take oral evidence in lieu of, or in addition to, such evidence by affidavit.

unregistered geographical indication.
(2) Nothing in this Act shall be deemed to affect rights of action against any person for passing off

Where an objection is taken under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark on the ground that it is likely to be confused with an earlier mark, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the proprietor use mark. The proprietor use mark may, within the time specified in such notice, file its response and evidence demonstrating the absence of likelihood of confusion. Such evidence may include data relating to actual consumer perception and sales figures for both marks. If the Registrar is satisfied, after considering the response and any counter-evidence filed by the objector, that there exists no reasonable possibility of confusion arising from the use of the proposed trade mark, registration shall proceed as provided herein. An appeal against this determination lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The functions conferred upon the Chairperson under this Act shall be exercised subject to the oversight and direction of the Governing Body, notwithstanding any challenge brought before the Intellectual Property Tribunal alleging undue influence from said body. Any decision made by the Chairperson concerning the registration of a layout-design, or relating to an interim injunction against infringement, may be appealed to the Tribunal within sixty days of communication thereof. The appeal shall not operate as a stay of the original order unless the Tribunal is satisfied that irreparable harm would result pending disposal of the appeal; provided that the applicant for such stay must demonstrate demonstrable prejudice. Further, any determination by the Chairperson regarding costs incurred in proceedings before them is open to review on grounds of manifest arbitrariness.

The Controller may, by an order, authorise an officer referred to in section 73, to be the adjudicating officer for holding an inquiry and imposing penalty under the provisions of this Act, in the manner as may be prescribed, after giving the person concerned a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

(1) Where an application for a patent has been published but a patent has not been granted, any person may, in writing, represent by way of opposition to the Controller against the grant of patent on the ground—
(a) that the applicant for the patent or the person under or through whom he claims, wrongfully obtained the invention or any part thereof from him or from a person under or through whom he claims;
(b) that the invention so far as claimed in any claim of the complete specification has been published before the priority date of the claim—
(i) in any specification filed in pursuance of an application for a patent made in India on or after the 1st day of January, 1912; or

Where any person is found to have infringed upon the exclusive right under this Act relating to an artistic work, such person shall be liable for damages sustained by the owner of the copyright. The amount of compensation may be determined by the High Court, taking into consideration the extent of the infringement and the loss suffered by the copyright holder. Provided that in cases where the alleged offence is committed without reasonable knowledge or belief that such act would constitute an infringement, the court may award a reduced sum as it deems just and equitable. Further, any person who reproduces, distributes, exhibits, or otherwise exploits an artistic work in violation of these provisions shall be subject to additional penalties as provided herein. The owner of copyright is entitled to seek injunctive relief to restrain further acts of infringement.

The Registrar may, by an order, authorise an officer referred to in section 3, to be adjudicating office r for holding an inquiry and imposing penalty under the provisions of this Act, in the manner as may be prescribed, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

(1) For the purposes of this Act, there shall be an office which shall be known as the patent office.
(2) The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify the name of the Patent Office.
(3) The head office of the patent office shall be at such place as the Central Government may specify, and for the purpose of facilitating, the registration of patents there may be established, at such other places as the Central Government may think fit, branch offices of the patent office.
(4) There shall be a seal of the patent office.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright shall subsist in a literary work for sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the author's death; provided that where the work is made under the direction or control of the trade mark proprietor, and the author is an employee, such copyright shall vest in the proprietor. Any person desiring to use a copyrighted work for commercial purposes other than private study, research, or criticism must obtain prior written permission from the owner of the copyright. Failure to comply with this requirement constitutes infringement under this Act. The Registrar may, upon application by any aggrieved party demonstrating substantial reliance and demonstrable financial loss, issue an order restraining further unauthorized reproduction if it is established that the infringing act has caused undue prejudice.

Registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to have been granted in error, and consequently, provided cancelling registration may occur, if it is established that the layout-design was substantially similar to an already registered design under this Act. The determination of substantial similarity shall consider the overall impression created by the designs, irrespective of minor variations. An application for cancellation must specify the grounds upon which it is based and identify the prior registered design. The Registrar may require further evidence supporting the claim of substantial similarity before proceeding with a hearing concerning the validity of the design registry registration.

An application for registration of a india trade mark shall be refused if it contains any matter which, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, is likely to deceive or confuse the public relating to the nature, quality or geographical origin of goods or services. Provided that, where a proposed trade mark includes only descriptive terms, such refusal may be waived if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through use subsequent to the date of application and furnishes evidence establishing widespread recognition of the mark as indicating the source of the goods or services. Further, any representation of a geographical indication shall not be registrable unless it is duly authorized by the proprietor of the geographical indication and complies with conditions prescribed under this Act regarding fair trade practices.

An applicant registration shall be deemed to have effect from the date of entry in the Register, subject to the provisions contained herein. The Trade Marks Registry may, upon satisfaction of all statutory requirements and payment of the prescribed fees, register a trade mark in the name of the applicant. A certificate of registration shall be issued to the registered proprietor as conclusive evidence of their ownership of the mark, unless and until such registration is revoked or cancelled in accordance with the procedures outlined in this Act. Provided that, the registration of a trade mark shall not confer any right to exclusive use of the mark in relation to goods or services not specified in the application. Any assignment or transmission of rights in a registered trade mark shall be subject to notification to the Registry and entry in the Register.

The registered trade mark ‘SecureFlow’ for software relating to data encryption shall permit use by Bharat Informatics Limited where such use is solely within the context of providing secure government services, and provided that any modification or adaptation of the computer programme incorporating the SecureFlow trade mark is undertaken only by employees of Bharat Informatics Limited possessing appropriate security clearances as determined under extant governmental regulations. Further, such use registered trade mark shall be subject to a periodic audit conducted by an independent auditor appointed by the Controller, confirming adherence to prescribed data handling protocols and non-commercial exploitation. Any distribution or licensing of the modified computer programme outside of government service provision will constitute infringement under this Act.

A performer shall be deemed to include an actor, singer, musician, dancer, lecturer, and any other person who makes a performance. Where a cinematograph film is made, the principal photographer shall be considered the author of such film as provided herein, but nothing contained in this Act shall prejudice the rights conferred upon a performer by virtue of their individual performance captured within said cinematograph film. Any adaptation or alteration of a recorded performance requiring significant creative input beyond mere reproduction may constitute an independent work subject to copyright, however, the original performer’s right to attribution and integrity remains unaffected. A performer who has consented to the recording of a live performance shall be entitled to a share in any royalties earned from the subsequent communication to the public of such recording, subject to agreements made between the performer and the producer or broadcasting entity. The duration of moral rights granted to a performer under this Act shall extend for a period of fifty years from the date of their last performance.

(1) The Authority may appoint such committees as may be necessary for the efficient discharge of its duties and performance of its functions under this Act. (2) The persons appointed as members of the committee under sub-section (1) shall be entitled to receive such allowances or fees for attending the meetings of the committee as may be fixed by the Central Government.

A patent shall be granted for an invention which is new, involves an inventive step, and is capable of industrial application as provided herein. Any translation work, being a literary or dramatic work, submitted as part of a patent application, shall be accompanied by a declaration of its accuracy and completeness, certified by a translator duly qualified in the relevant language pair. Where a copy translation work is presented, the original language version shall be considered the primary document for the purposes of determining novelty and inventive step. The Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require an applicant to furnish a certified copy of the original work if doubts arise regarding the fidelity of the translation. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the patent application liable to be refused. A patent shall vest in the applicant unless otherwise determined under this Act.

(1) No person shall publish a sound recording in respect of any work unless the following particulars are displayed on the sound recording and on any container thereof, namely:— (a) the name and address of the person who has made the record; (b) the name and address of the owner of the copyright in such work; and (c) the year of its first publication. (2) No person shall publish a video film in respe ct of any work unless the following particulars are displayed in the video film, when exhibited, and on the video cassette or other container thereof, namely:— (a) if such work is a cinematograph film required to be certified for exhibition unde r the provisions of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 (37 of 1952), a copy of the certificate granted by the Board of Film Certification under section 5A of that Act in respect of such work; (b) the name and address of the person who has made the video film and a declaration by him that he has obtained the necessary licence or consent from the owner of the copyright, in such work for making such video film; and (c) the name and address of the owner for the copyright in such work.

In all proceedings under this Act before the Authority or the Registrar,— (a) the Authority or the Registrar, as the case may be, shall have all the powers of a civil court for the purposes of receiving evidence, administering oaths, enforcing the attendance of witnesses, compelling the discovery and production of documents and issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses; (b) the Authority or the Registrar may, subject to any rule made in this behalf under this Act, make such orders as to cost as it considers reasonable and any such order shall be executable as a decree of a civil court. (4) A suit for a declaration may be brought by virtue of this section at any time 2after the publication of grant of a patent, and references in this section to the patentee shall be construed accordingly.

Any person who demonstrates a new invention, being a product or process, and seeks protection under this Act shall submit a complete specification detailing the manner in which the invention may be worked. An applicant claiming priority for a new invention shall, subject to the provisions herein, be entitled to a patent if the invention is not publicly known and possesses an inventive step. However, a patent shall not be granted for an invention that is an obvious variation of existing knowledge, or one lacking practical utility. Should a patent be wrongfully granted for an invention not truly new, any aggrieved party may petition the Controller for revocation of said patent, and upon sufficient evidence of prior art demonstrating lack of novelty, the Controller may order the patent cancelled. The rights conferred by a patent shall extend to preventing others from making, using, selling, or importing the new invention without the patent holder’s consent, subject to licensing provisions as provided herein.

An application for registration of a service shall be refused if the proposed marks are deemed descriptive of the nature of the service. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish such further information or documentary evidence as is necessary to ascertain the character, conditions, and extent of use of the services in relation to which the trade mark is sought to be registered. Where a geographical indication is included within the description of the service, the application shall specify the territory from which the goods or services originate, and the Registrar may direct that such geographical limitation be incorporated into the register. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The register said geographical indication shall be open for public inspection during normal business hours, subject to any conditions prescribed in regulations made under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the author of a work shall be the first owner of the copyright therein: Provided that— (a) in the case of a literary, dramatic or artistic work made by the author in the cou rse of his employment by the proprietor of a newspaper, magazine or similar periodical under a contract of service or apprentice ship, for the purpose of publication in a newspaper, magazine or similar periodical, the said proprietor shall, in the absence of any agreement to the contrary, be the first owner of the copyright in the work in so far as the copyright relates to the publication of the work in any news paper, magazine or similar periodical, or to the reproduction of the work for the purpose of its being so published, but in all other respects the author shall be the first owner of the copyright in the work; (b) subject to the provisions of clause ( a), in the case of a photograph taken, or a painting or portrait drawn, or an engraving or a cinemato graph film made, for valuable consideration at the instance of any person, such person shall, in the absence of any agreement to the contrary, be the first owner of the copyright therein; (c) in the case of a work made in the course of the author ’s employment under a contract of service or apprenticeship, to which clause ( a) or clause (b) does not apply, the employer shall, in the absence of any agreement to the contrary, be the first owner of the copyright therein;

(2) If, at any time after the granting of a licence to produce and publish the reproduction or translation of any work under section 32 A, the owner of the right of reproduction or any person authorised by him sells or distributes copies of such work or a translation thereof, as the case may be, in the same language and which is substantially the same in content at a price reasonably related to the price normally charged in India for works of the same standard on the same or similar subject, the licence so granted shall be terminated: Provided that no such termination shall take effect until after the expiry of a period of three months from the date of service of a notice in the pr escribed manner on the person holding the licence by the owner of the right of reproduc tion intimating the sale or distribution of the copies of th e editions of work as aforesaid: Provided further that any copies already reproduced by the licensee before such termination takes effect may continue to be sold or distributed until the copies already produced are exhausted.

Any person alleging infringement of copyright in a literary or dramatic work, including adaptations thereof, shall furnish to the High Court having jurisdiction proof of ownership of valid copyright and reasonable evidence suggesting substantial similarity between the protected work and the allegedly infringing material. However, such claim may be subject to scrutiny if the claimant fails to demonstrate prior publication or registration as provided herein, though lack of either shall not *ipso facto* invalidate a legitimate claim. Where a defendant successfully argues fair dealing for purposes of criticism or review, the Court may award costs against the plaintiff and stay further proceedings. An appeal from any decree passed by a High Court in respect of copyright infringement lies to the Supreme Court, provided that leave to appeal is obtained within sixty days from the date of the impugned order; furthermore, cross-objections shall be limited to matters already raised before the High Court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no india trade mark shall be deemed invalid solely on the grounds that its use by the proprietor following registration resulted in confusion amongst consumers with a prior unregistered mark employed within a geographically limited area. However, where such confusion is demonstrated to have caused demonstrable financial prejudice to the possessor of the prior mark, an appeal may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board asserting dilution of distinctiveness. The Board shall consider evidence pertaining to consumer perception and market share data; provided that the proprietor of the india trade mark demonstrates bona fide intention to use the mark throughout India. Any order issued by the Board is subject to further appeal before the High Court.

The Registrar shall maintain an entry register variety for each plant variety recorded under this Act, detailing essential characteristics and geographical provenance as declared by the applicant. Any person aggrieved by an entry made, or omitted to be made, in the entry register variety may within sixty days from the date such entry is published, file an appeal before the Appellate Board. The appellate board shall consider any evidence submitted by both the appellant and the Registrar, including expert testimony regarding varietal stability and distinctiveness. Provided that, the burden of demonstrating error or material misrepresentation in the entry register variety shall lie with the appellant. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final subject to further appeal under the appropriate provisions relating to judicial review.

(iii) services which are associated with those goods or goods of that description or goods which are associated with those services or services of that description, limited to use in relation to goods to be sold or otherwise traded in, or services for use, or available for acceptance, in any other place in India: Provided that in any such case, on application in the prescribed manner by the proprietor of a trade mark who proposes to assign it, or by a person who claims that a registered trade mark has been transmitted to him or to a predecessor in title of his since the commencement of this Act, the Registrar, if he is satisfied that in all the circumstances the use of the trade mark in exercise of the said rights would not be contrary to the public interest may approve the assignment or transmission, and an assignment or transmission so approved shall not, unless it is shown that the approval was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation, be deemed to be invalid under this section or section 40 if application for the registration under section 45 of the title of the person b ecoming entitled is made within six months from the date on which the approval is given or, in the case of a transmission, was made before that date.

A person entitled patent under this Act shall, upon filing an application with the Patents Office, disclose all information pertaining to the derivation of their right, including details of any prior assignments, transmissions, or testamentary distributions affecting the invention’s ownership. Such disclosure must be accompanied by certified copies of relevant documentation substantiating the transfer, provided that the Controller may require further evidence if deemed necessary for verification. The application shall specify the nature and extent of the claimant's interest in the patent, whether as sole proprietor, co-owner, or otherwise. Failure to provide complete and accurate information regarding entitlement may render the applicant’s claim vulnerable to challenge by third parties asserting conflicting rights, subject to due process considerations as provided herein.
For the purposes of this Act, a body corporate shall be deemed to be domiciled in India if it is incorporated under any law in force in India.

(1) On application ma de in the prescribed manner to the High Court or to the Registrar by any person aggrieved, the Register or the High Court, as the case may be, may make such order as it may think fit for cancelling or varying the registration of a trade mark on the g round of any contravention, or failure to observe a condition entered on the register in relation thereto.
(2) Any person aggrieved by the absence or omission from the register of any entry, or by any entry made in the register without sufficient cause, or by any entry wrongly remaining on the register, or by any error or defect in any entry in the register, may apply in the prescribed manner to the High Court or to the Registrar, and the Register or the High Court, as the case may be, may make such order for making, expunging or varying the entry as it may think fit.
(3) The Register or the High Court, as the case may be, may in any proceeding under this section decide any question that may be necessary or expedient to decide in connection with the rectification of the register.
(4) The Register or the High Court, as the case may be, of its own motion, may, after giving notice in the prescribed manner to the parties concerned and after giving them an opportunity of being heard, make any order referred to in sub-section
(1) or sub-section (2).

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if, following publication under this Act, an objection is raised by any person claiming such right or interest as is specified herein. Such objection must be communicated to the Registrar in writing within the prescribed period, and shall clearly state the grounds upon which it is based. The Registrar shall then serve notice of the objection on the applicant for registration, affording them an opportunity to file a counterstatement. A notice served under this Act shall include the date of service and details of the objecting party. Further, any subsequent communication relating to the application registration notice will be deemed valid if delivered electronically as per regulations.

A person making a request to the Controller in the prescribed manner for information relating to any such matters as may be prescribed as respects any patent specified in the request or as respects any application for a patent so specified shall be entitled, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee, to have information supplied to him accordingly.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a trade mark registered pursuant to an international registration shall provide evidence demonstrating misleading or deceptive use by another party within the territory of India. Failure to submit such compelling evidence, verified under oath and conforming to prescribed forms, will render the application for rectification void ab initio. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require further affidavits or expert testimony to ascertain the veracity of claims made regarding consumer confusion or dilution. Any person found deliberately submitting false information in support of a rectification proceeding relating to particulars international registration shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

Where any proceeding under this Act is pending before a competent authority and the applicant or patentee dies, the proceeding shall not abate but the legal representative of the deceased shall, subject to such directions as the competent authority may deem fit, have the right to prosecute or defend the same. If the legal representative fails to prosecute or defend the proceeding within a period of ninety days from the date of death of the applicant or patentee, the competent authority may, after giving reasonable opportunity of being heard, dismiss the proceeding. Any person claiming to be the legal representative shall submit an affidavit establishing their entitlement, and failure to do so may result in a penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees. Provided that, the competent authority may, in exceptional circumstances, extend the aforementioned ninety-day period. Any false claim made regarding legal representation shall be punishable as contempt of this authority.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving a request from an international trade mark proprietor seeking renewal of their international registration extending to India, examine whether the underlying national registrations remain valid and enforceable. Provided that, where any such national registration has expired, the renewal application may proceed only if the proprietor demonstrates diligent efforts were undertaken to reinstate said registration within a reasonable period following its expiry years internationally. Any party aggrieved by a decision refusing or granting such renewal may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of the order’s communication. The Tribunal shall consider whether the failure to maintain national registrations constitutes wilful neglect, impacting the integrity of international trade mark protection as provided herein.

A person shall not act as a practise patent agent within India unless that individual has been duly registered under this Act and possesses a certificate of registration issued by the Controller. For the purposes of this section, “practise patent agent” means a person who advises others on matters relating to patents, drafts patent applications, or represents clients before the Patent Office. An applicant seeking registration as a practise patent agent shall satisfy the Controller that he possesses the requisite technical and legal qualifications, as provided herein. Further, an individual registered as a practise patent agent may, subject to regulations framed under this Act, facilitate resulting international registrations based on Indian patents.

Where a patent has been granted for an invention, and subsequent modifications or improvements thereof are made which, while falling within the scope of the original claim, represent a significant advancement in functionality or utility, such advancements may be subject to a patent of addition. However, where infringement proceedings are initiated based on allegations that the patented invention incorporates elements derived from prior art not considered during the initial examination, the Controller shall investigate whether this constitutes a valid patent addition regard. Failure to disclose relevant prior art impacting the inventive step in the patent of addition will render the patent liable for revocation and subject the patentee to penalties as provided herein, including compensatory damages to aggrieved parties.

Any person dealing in goods with a geographical indication authorised under this Act, and falsely representing such goods as originating from a geographical area in respect of which a registered geographical indication exists, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Where the offence involves repeated contravention, the penalty may extend to ten lakh rupees. The Registrar, upon receiving credible evidence of such misrepresentation, may issue a cease and desist notice to the offending party, requiring immediate cessation of the unlawful activity. Failure to comply with such notice within thirty days shall constitute an aggravated offence, attracting enhanced penalties and potential criminal prosecution. Any goods found to be in violation of these provisions shall be liable to seizure and destruction, subject to the discretion of a designated officer. The burden of proof regarding the geographical origin of the goods shall lie with the defendant.

Where any party believes that a patent has been granted in contravention of, or otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of this Act, such party may, within six months from the date of publication of grant of the patent, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. The notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based and shall be accompanied by a statement of facts relied upon to support the objection. Subject to any procedural direction issued by the Controller, the patentee shall be afforded an opportunity to respond to the notice of opposition within a prescribed period. Any appeal against an order passed by the Controller in respect of such opposition lies to the Appellate Board, and is subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to revocation of a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider only questions of law arising out of the decision appealed against and may affirm, reverse, or modify the order appealed from, subject to such inquiry as it deems necessary. Where an infringement action is instituted following a patent having been granted new patent, any interlocutory orders passed by the trial court shall be appealable directly to the High Court. Failure to comply with an injunction issued under this Act shall render the defaulter liable for compensatory damages as determined by the Court and may also attract imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year.

Goods bearing counterfeit or otherwise infringing trademarks, whether found at the place where the offence was committed or elsewhere, are deemed contraband and subject to confiscation under this Act. Any person involved in the production, importation, distribution, sale, or exposure for sale of such goods shall be liable to prosecution and penalties as provided herein. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify categories of goods particularly vulnerable to trademark infringement and prescribe enhanced seizure procedures for these items. Upon conviction, courts shall order the destruction or disposal of confiscated infringing goods, ensuring that their subsequent re-entry into commerce is prevented. This confiscation goods clause applies irrespective of whether a civil suit for damages has been initiated.

Where an application filed patent relates to an invention for which patent rights are already held by another party, the Controller may, subject to conditions prescribed herein, grant permission for a limited license of the patented technology. Such permission shall not prejudice the validity of the existing patent but allows for specified use within India as determined by the Controller. The applicant seeking such licensing permission must demonstrate compelling reasons for its necessity and provide details regarding proposed royalty rates and duration of the license. Any assignment of rights arising from this permitted license shall be subject to prior approval from the Controller, ensuring equitable distribution of benefits derived from the technology. Further, any subsequent application filed patent based on improvements to the licensed invention requires notification to the original patent holder.

(1) All applications and communications to the Controller under this Act may be signed by, and all attendances upon the Controller may be made by or through a legal practitioner or by or through an agent whose name and address ha d been entered in the register of patent agents maintained under section 125 of the Patents Act, 1970 (39 of 1970).

Any person claiming an interest and alleging that a trade mark sought to be registered is likely to deceive or cause confusion, or is descriptive of the goods or services concerned, or is contrary to law, may file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry. Such notice shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by a statement of the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to respond. Where the trade mark incorporates a geographical indication identifying goods originating from a specific region, the Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require evidence establishing the lawful user of such geographical indication by the opponent. The notice opposition applicant bears the burden of proving the grounds for opposition, and failure to do so may result in dismissal of the opposition.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and it appears to the Registrar that the opponent has established a prima facie case of likelihood of confusion arising from the use by the applicant of a sign identical or similar to a previously described trade mark used in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those specified in the application, the Registrar may grant an ex parte injunction restraining the applicant from proceeding further with the registration application. Such injunction shall remain in force until the determination of the opposition proceedings, provided that the applicant shall be given reasonable opportunity to be heard and present evidence in rebuttal of the opponent’s claims. The Registrar may, at any time, modify or discharge such an order as deemed appropriate.

An application for registration of a layout design shall include a statement specifying whether the applicant claims the layout design as an original work, and if so, detailing the nature of their contribution to its creation. Where multiple entities have participated in the conception and execution of a layout design, the application must clearly identify all such participants and state their respective roles in establishing the layout design relation. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the extent of each participant’s involvement, particularly where disputes arise concerning ownership or authorship. Such information shall be deemed confidential and accessible only to parties directly involved under this Act. Failure to accurately disclose the details pertaining to the layout design relation will render the application liable for rejection.

Any person claiming to be interested in the registration of a geographical indication, and being the applicant, shall submit an application to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by a statement of proposed use of the geographical indication. The application shall clearly identify the goods to which the geographical indication relates, and shall delineate the geographical area within India constituting the region of origin. A register of all registered geographical indications shall be maintained by the Registry, open for inspection by the public subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Registration of a geographical indication shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered. However, such right shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, and shall not prevent other producers within the defined geographical area from using descriptive terms customary in their trade. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of a registered geographical indication may be adjudicated as provided herein.

Nothing in this Chapter shall affect any rights or liabilities in any work in connection wit h a copyright society which had accrued or were incurred on or before the day prior to the commencement of the Copyright (Amendment) Act, 2012, or any legal proceedings in respect of any such rights or liabilities pending on that day.

The Controller shall, upon receipt of a request for extension of time under this Act, require the applicant to submit a duly verified statement setting forth the grounds justifying such extension and supported by documentary evidence demonstrating due diligence on the part of the applicant. Any application so filed may be rejected if the Controller is satisfied that the delay in processing has been occasioned by willful default or negligence attributable to the applicant. The Controller shall provide an opportunity for the applicant to be heard, either in person or through a duly authorized representative, before passing any order refusing such extension. Decisions of the Controller regarding extensions are subject to appeal under this Act. Further, the Controller may, at his discretion, require submission of additional information or clarification from any party involved in proceedings concerning patent applications or opposition matters.

A mark, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be distinctive, and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. A mark consisting exclusively of descriptive character or characters which, in the language of the relevant trade, are commonly used to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, geographical origin or other characteristics of the goods or services, shall not be registered, unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use. However, a mark may be registered even if it is not inherently distinctive, provided that the applicant furnishes evidence of extensive and continuous use demonstrating acquired distinctiveness to the Registrar. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, require the applicant to submit statutory declarations and supporting documentation to substantiate such claims of acquired distinctiveness. A mark shall not be registered if it is likely to cause confusion among the public, considering the overall similarities and the nature of the goods or services.

The Registrar may require an applicant for registration of a proposed trade mark to furnish evidence demonstrating the extent and nature of the *mark use* undertaken prior to the date of application. Such evidence shall include, but not be limited to, invoices relating to sales, advertising materials distributed, and specimens illustrating the manner in which the mark is affixed to goods or packaging thereof. Where the applicant claims user as a potential trade mark, the period of such use shall be calculated from the earliest date of any such *mark use*. The Registrar may consider evidence submitted by third parties challenging the genuineness or extent of claimed *mark use*, provided that such challenges are filed within the prescribed timeframe and accompanied by supporting documentation. Any determination regarding the validity of *mark use* evidence is subject to appeal under this Act.

Any registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to any person or entity, specifying the scope, duration, and territorial extent of such license, and the royalties payable therefor, as mutually agreed upon in a written instrument. Such instrument shall clearly delineate the rights conferred, including but not limited to, the right to reproduce, exploit, and assign the licensed layout-design. Where a license is granted, the registered proprietor shall furnish a copy of the licensing agreement to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. Any assignment of the registered layout-design, whether partial or complete, shall be subject to similar requirements of written instrument and registration. The manner applying appellate review to disputes concerning the validity or scope of such licenses or assignments shall be governed by the provisions relating to rectification and revocation of registration, adapted accordingly. Provided that, the Registrar may, at their discretion, require further documentation to ensure clarity and enforceability of the licensing or assignment terms. All royalty payments shall be subject to applicable tax laws.

Where an objection is raised by any person under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark, such objector may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice of the Registrar’s decision. The appellant shall state the grounds of appeal and serve a copy thereof on the applicant. Provided that if the objection relates solely to the absolute ground under section 9 concerning deceptiveness, the applicant may, within thirty days of service of the copy of the grounds of appeal, file its written response. It is established that ‘carry business india’ constitutes a descriptive phrase used by the respondent, and any claim to exclusive right therein shall be subject to challenge based on demonstrable lack of acquired distinctiveness.

For the purposes of this Act, "international trademark" means a trade mark registered through an application based on an international registration granted under the Madrid Protocol. An applicant seeking to obtain protection for a trade mark in India by way of such an international registration shall be deemed to have made an application for registration under this Act. Such an application is subject to examination as if it were an initial application filed directly with the Trade Marks Registry, provided that the prescribed application fee accompanied by the requisite documentation relating to the international registration must be remitted at the time of filing. The Registrar may require further particulars or modifications to ensure compliance with Indian trade mark law.

The Trade Marks Act, 1999, provides that any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the approval or rejection of registered draft regulations submitted under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. Such an appeal shall be in respect of matters of law and fact pertaining to the compliance with prescribed procedures during the formulation and submission of the draft regulations, as well as concerning the interpretation of any provision relating to their content. The Board may, after affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against; provided that any order made by the Board shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions governing appeals to the Supreme Court.

An application for entry into the design register shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings or other representations of the integrated circuit layout-design sought to be registered, conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or clarification regarding the layout-design and its representation as deemed necessary for proper examination. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall assign it a serial number and intimate the same to the applicant by post or electronic means. Any alteration made to the drawings or representations after the assignment of the serial number shall be inadmissible unless sanctioned in writing by the Registrar. The design register shall be maintained electronically and shall be accessible for public inspection subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Information pertaining to pending applications shall not be disclosed, provided that this does not impede due process.

An application for registration of copyright shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the work where the work is published outside India, or if the applicant claims ownership based on assignment, a duly executed instrument evidencing such assignment. The Registrar may require the submission of further documentation to verify authenticity and compliance with prescribed formalities under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to registration, refusal, amendment or cancellation shall have the right to appeal to the Registrar Copyrights Appellate. Such appeals must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, accompanied by a fee as determined by notification issued by the government. The appellate authority may dismiss frivolous appeals and direct compliance with any deficiencies in the original application.

Any description which is made available to potential users and constitutes an unauthorized representation of a registered trade mark, shall be deemed a misrepresentation under this Act, notwithstanding any claim of artistic merit or novelty. However, a valid registered proprietor, seeking relief against such misrepresentation, shall first demonstrate actual confusion amongst a substantial segment of consumers, or a reasonable likelihood of such confusion. An appeal against a decision denying interim injunction based on insufficient evidence of consumer confusion may be made to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within thirty days of the order. The burden of proving lack of confusion, where the alleged misrepresentation closely resembles the registered trade mark, shall lie with the defendant. Any finding of misrepresentation shall be subject to review if new evidence of prior use or legitimate competitive activity is presented.

Where an appeal lies under this Act before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the Board shall consist of a Chairperson who is a Judge of a High Court or has held judicial office and at least two Technical Members. A person shall be appointed as a Technical Member only if he possesses specialized knowledge and experience in trade marks law, patents, designs, copyrights or geographical indications. The Chairperson may require any authority or officer to furnish such information as the Board deems necessary for the proper disposal of an appeal; provided that the presiding officer of the Board shall ensure confidentiality regarding sensitive commercial information submitted during proceedings. Technical Members shall exercise their powers and discharge their functions in accordance with principles of natural justice, subject to applicable rules of procedure.

Where a registered trade mark owner grants a license to use their trade mark, subject to conditions specified in the licensing agreement, such license may be assigned by the licensee to another party provided that the original licensor’s consent is obtained prior to the assignment. Failure to secure this consent shall render the assignee jointly and severally liable for any breach of contract arising from the licensed usage. Furthermore, where a trade mark owner seeks to prevent unauthorized use or dilution of their registered mark, they may apply to the court for an injunction sub section restricting such activities, even if no direct contractual relationship exists between the proprietor and the infringing party. The court shall consider the terms of any prior licensing agreements when determining the scope and validity of such injunctive relief.

If it appears to the Central Government that a foreign country does not give or has not undertaken to give ade quate protection to the works of Indian authors, the Central Government may, by order published in the Official Gazette, direct that such of the provisions of this Act as confer copyright on works first published in India shall not apply to works, publishe d after the date specified in the order, the authors whereof are subjects or citizens of such foreign country and are not domiciled in India, and thereupon those provisions shall not apply to such works.

Where a basic application relating to an invention has been made outside India, any person may file in India an application for a patent constituting a continuation thereof, provided that such application is filed within twelve months from the date of the first filing of the basic application. Subject to this, the applicant shall disclose all information known to him as to the state of progress of the invention and shall furnish particulars of the basic application. Any assignment or license granted prior to the institution of proceedings in India relating to the subject matter of the patent under this Act shall be recorded with the Controller, along with an affidavit verifying its authenticity. Failure to do so may render such assignment void. The Controller may require further documentation demonstrating the transferor’s entitlement as per the basic application.

An application for registration of an integrated circuits layout design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings or photolithographic masks representing the layout. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the creation of the integrated circuits layout, including details regarding the date of first manufacture and the place where such manufacture occurred. Provided that, if the applicant is unable to provide all requested information, an affidavit explaining the reasons for omission may be submitted under this Act. Any person claiming rights in a registered integrated circuits layout design shall notify the Registrar of any change in ownership or control affecting those rights, within thirty days of such alteration as provided herein.

Where an exclusive licensee is granted rights under this Act pertaining to copyright in any work, such license shall be deemed an assignment of those specified rights for the duration and geographical scope expressly defined within the licensing agreement. The licensor shall retain no further power to grant conflicting licenses or assignments concerning the same rights during that period, subject to any provisions allowing for sub-licensing as stipulated by contract. Any transfer of ownership in the copyright work subsequent to the granting of an exclusive license shall be void unless it expressly incorporates and affirms the terms of the original license agreement. The exclusive licensee may enforce all rights granted under this Act against infringers, and remedies available to the copyright owner are also available to them. Provided that, termination clauses within licensing agreements shall be governed by principles of fairness and equity as determined by appropriate judicial forums.

For the purposes of this Act, “use” of a trade mark involves the application of the mark to goods or their packaging with the consent of the proprietor, or in relation to any business, the use of the mark in advertising or otherwise to promote the goods or services. Such use shall be deemed to occur at the place where the goods are applied to, or the business is carried on, and may extend to use on imported goods. A trade mark shall be considered to be in use in India if it is lawfully used in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, and such use shall be continuous and genuine. However, mere display of the mark as stock in trade shall not constitute use as provided herein. Any mark use that is likely to cause confusion or deception is prohibited.

Where a registered Geographical Indication is utilized in connection with goods not conforming to the standards of quality, production or other characteristics as defined under this Act, an aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board seeking rectification of the register. Such application must specify the particulars of the non-conforming goods and demonstrate that the use constitutes a misrepresentation likely to mislead consumers regarding the origin of those goods. The registered proprietor shall be afforded an opportunity to present counterarguments; however, if it is established that the continued registration allows for such deceptive practices, the Board may order the Geographical Indication to be deemed falsify geographical in relation to the specific goods or classes of goods involved. This determination is subject to appeal before a High Court.

The Registrar shall maintain an inspection register at each Trade Marks Registry office, accessible during prescribed business hours to any person interested in trade mark matters. Any party seeking access to the inspection register may request a certified copy of entries relating to a specific trade mark application or registered trade mark, subject to payment of applicable fees as determined by notification issued under this Act. The Registrar is empowered to refuse access to the inspection register if satisfied that such access would likely prejudice ongoing proceedings or compromise confidential information pertaining to an applicant or proprietor. Upon registration, details regarding the expiry date of a trade mark shall be prominently recorded in the inspection register and publicly available. Notice of published expiry will be disseminated through the Trade Marks Registry website for a period not less than thirty days prior to the effective date of cessation.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a trade mark to goods or services in the manner likely to be mistaken for those of another, shall be deemed to have engaged in the purpose of falsifying used goods, notwithstanding any prior use or lack of registration of said trade mark. Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, evidence of such registration shall be admissible, but not conclusive, in determining the intent to deceive. However, registration does not preclude a finding of purpose falsifying used if the application is demonstrably intended to mislead consumers regarding the source or quality of the goods or services. A claimant alleging such falsification may, subject to the provisions herein, seek an injunction restraining further application of the mark. Provided that, the court may consider the extent of actual confusion caused, if any, in determining appropriate relief. Any instrument used in the commission of this offence shall be liable to seizure.

Further, any transfer of ownership impacting the control and management of production within the defined geographical area shall be reported to Parliament year by year for review.
