For the purposes of this Act, "producer" with respect to a cinematographic work shall mean the individual or corporate body which has arranged for the making of the film and bears ultimate responsibility for its production. The producer shall be deemed the owner of all copyrights therein, subject to any agreements made with authors, composers, lyricists, photographers, or other individuals contributing to the creation of the work. Provided that where a work is produced jointly by two or more producers, they shall be deemed joint owners of copyright and shall hold such rights as tenants in common. The term "producer" does not include those engaged solely for technical assistance under contract.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by or on behalf of both the assignor and the assignee, and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, is granted to a person to use a registered trade mark, the licensor may, subject to any contract to the contrary, initiate infringement proceedings against any third party not bound by the license. However, any fraudulent or malicious use of a trade mark by a licensee, despite a clear stipulation against such use in the licensing agreement, shall constitute grounds for immediate revocation of the license and may, as provided herein, attract a sentence imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Failure to register an assignment within the prescribed period shall render the assignment void, and the original proprietor shall retain all rights to the trade mark. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, require further evidence of valid consideration for any assignment or license.

For the purpose of this Act, a ‘layout design’ includes features relating to the arrangement or interconnection of elements which define an integrated circuit. The term 'element' shall encompass any circuitry, semiconductor material, or other component incorporated within the layout design. Where an application for registration is received, and the Controller determines that the layout design incorporates original features not previously disclosed, the registry shall place the application on record pending examination as to novelty and inventive step. Provided that such placement does not constitute a grant of exclusive rights under this Act, and subject to any objections raised by third parties within the prescribed period.

Where, by or under this Act, any act, other than the making of an affidavit, is required to be done before the Registrar by any person, the act may, subject to the rules made in this behalf, be done instead of by that person himself, by a person duly authorised in the prescribed manner, who is—
(a) a legal practitioner, or

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that it designates India and any application for extension of such registration under this Act shall be made within a period of six months from the date of expiration of the initial term of the international registration. Where an international registration designating India is opposed, the Registrar may require the deposit of a sum not exceeding fifty thousand rupees as security for costs; failure to comply with such requirement within thirty days shall render the international registration liable to be refused. Any person aggrieved by a decision under this Act relating to services trade mark protection afforded through an international registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days, subject to a penalty of ten thousand rupees for each day of delay.

For the purposes of this Act, a “person” shall include any natural person, artificial person, legal entity, or body, whether incorporated or unincorporated. Where a person claims rights as an inventor, that person shall be deemed to have full capacity to exercise such rights, subject to the provisions relating to assignment and transmission as provided herein. Any application submitted under this Act on behalf of a minor or a person of unsound mind shall require the consent of a legally appointed guardian, and such guardian shall be responsible for all communications and undertakings made in connection with the application. A person who knowingly provides false information in any document filed under this Act may be subject to penalties, including revocation of any patent granted based on such information. Provided that, a nominee or legal representative acting on behalf of a deceased person shall be considered a person entitled to pursue proceedings under this Act.

(2) A copy of any entry in any register or of any document kept in the patent office or of any patent, or an extract from any such register or document, purporting to be certified by the Controller and sealed with the seal of the patent office shall be admitted in evidence in all courts, and in all proceedings, without further proof or production of the original.
(3) The Controller or any other officer of the patent office shall not, in any legal proceedings to which he is not a party, be compellable to produce the register or any other document in his custody, the contents of which can be proved by the production of a certified copy issued under this Act or to appear as a witness to prove the matters therein recorded unless by order of the court made for special causes.

The owner of copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work may grant licenses granting rights to reproduce, distribute, perform, or communicate the work to the public, subject to the terms and conditions specified therein. Such licenses shall be assignable by way of written agreement, and registration of such assignment with the Registrar of Copyrights is deemed conclusive evidence thereof against third parties. Where a copyright owner desires to register copyrights in multiple works simultaneously, a single application may be submitted, provided that each work is clearly identified and accompanied by the requisite fee for each individual registration. Any person acquiring an interest in a copyrighted work through such assignment or license shall be entitled to enforce the terms of the agreement as if they were the original copyright owner, subject to any limitations expressly stated within the licensing documentation. The Registrar may require further declarations regarding ownership and chain of title during the process of registering copyrights.

Where any work has been infringed by the unauthorized reproduction or distribution thereof, the owner of copyright in such work shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of infringement. For the purposes of determining ownership under this Act, a *recording means person* who undertakes the technical direction and control of the sound recording process shall be deemed the primary author, unless evidence demonstrates otherwise through contractual agreements or demonstrable creative contribution beyond mere technical execution. Any individual participating in the creation of a sound recording, but not fulfilling the criteria for authorship as defined herein, may claim rights incidental to their participation, subject to limitations imposed by this Act regarding remedies available. Provided that such claims must be substantiated with documentary evidence establishing the nature and extent of said participation. The right to claim damages shall remain solely with the primary author or duly authorized assignee.

Where an applicant submits a corrected application following notice under this Act regarding deficiencies identified by the Registrar, such correction shall not constitute a new application but shall be treated as a continuation of the original submission; however, if the alterations introduced render the initial claim substantially different from that originally presented, the Registrar may deem it to represent a fresh application and require payment of the prescribed fee anew. Any party aggrieved by this determination concerning an *application corrected* may within sixty days of publication of the Registrar’s order file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appellate board shall consider any evidence submitted by both the applicant and any interested parties, provided that such evidence relates directly to the scope of the alteration and its impact on distinctiveness as defined herein.

Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the application for rectification is based and provide a period of sixty days within which the registered proprietor may submit his response. Failure by the registered proprietor, or any person acting as the registered proprietor proposed, to adequately demonstrate continued use or adherence to stipulated conditions will render him liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt.

(2) Copyright shall not subsist in any work specified in sub -section ( 1), other than a work to which the provisions of section 40 or section 41 apply, unless— (i) in the case of a published work, the work is first published in India, or where the work is first published outside India, the auth or is at the date of such publication, or in a case where the author was dead at that date, was at the time of his death, a citizen of India; (ii) in the case of an unpublished work other than a work of architecture, the author is at the date of making of the work a citizen of India or domiciled in India; and (iii) in the case of a work of architecture, the work is located in India. Explanation.—In th e case of a work of joint authorship, the conditions conferring copyright specified in this sub-section shall be satisfied by all the authors of the work. (3) Copyright shall not subsist— (a) in any cinematograph film if a substantial part of the film is an infringement of the copyright in any other work; (b) in any sound recording made in respect of a literary, dramatic or musical work, if in making the sound recording, copyright in such work has been infringed. (4) The copyright in a cinematograph film or a record shall not affect the separate copyright in any work in respect of which or a substantial part of which, the film, or, as the case may be, the sound recording is made.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish to the Registrar, along with the application, a clear representation of the marks as applied for, conforming to prescribed guidelines regarding colouration or stylization. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, issue a notice to any persons claiming rights in relation to similar trademarks already registered under this Act. Such notice applicant registration must specify the grounds on which objection is raised and shall be accompanied by supporting documentation demonstrating prior use or established reputation. Failure of the applicant to respond adequately within the stipulated period, as provided herein, may result in the application being deemed abandoned. The Registrar shall consider any representations made by interested parties before proceeding with examination.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal and must specify the grounds upon which the appellant considers the decision to be erroneous. The appellate board shall give notice to the Registrar and any other party who appeared in opposition proceedings, affording them an opportunity to present arguments against the appeal. A registered act relating to a trade mark shall remain valid subject to compliance with all relevant provisions concerning renewal fees and prescribed forms. Failure to adhere to these requirements may result in removal from the register as provided herein.

Any person who falsifies any entry in a register maintained by the Trade Marks Registry, or knowingly makes a false representation to an officer of the said registry, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, direct rectification of any incorrect entry discovered upon inspection of its records. Any application for registration found to contain deliberately misleading information, and submitted despite knowledge of its falsity, shall be deemed void ab initio, and the applicant barred from submitting further applications for a period of two years. Provided that, an honest mistake regarding a material fact may be rectified by amendment within one month of discovery, subject to payment of a prescribed fee. All records maintained by the Trade Marks Registry are open to inspection during office hours by any person paying the specified fees, but sensitive information relating to applicant addresses shall remain confidential.

The Central government may, after due appropriation made by Parliament by law in this behalf, make to the Authority grants and loans of such sums of money as the Central Government may think fit for being utilised for the purposes of this Act.

Where the owner of a registered trade mark grants a license permitting the use of their mark, such license may be assigned to any person, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the original agreement. Provided that, where a licensed user subsequently seeks to register a trade mark identical to the registered mark for goods or services similar to those for which the registration is already subsisting, the application shall be refused if it is established that such registration would likely cause confusion amongst consumers. Further, any assignment of a license under this Act shall require notification to the Registrar within thirty days of the transfer, detailing both the assignor and assignee. The Registrar may request further documentation as deemed necessary to verify the validity of the assignment. This provision applies irrespective of whether the original trade mark registration was obtained prior to or subsequent to the granting of the initial license.

The Controller may, upon receiving a request from any interested party alleging that a granted means patent does not satisfy the requirements of this Act, initiate proceedings for revocation. Such request shall be accompanied by a statement specifying the grounds on which the revocation is sought and supported by such evidence as the requester deems appropriate. The Controller shall serve notice of the request upon the patentee, affording them an opportunity to file a counter-statement addressing the allegations made. Following consideration of both the request and the counter-statement, along with any further submissions from interested parties, the Controller may direct the Registrar to hold a hearing. At such hearing, all parties shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present oral arguments and additional evidence. The decision of the Controller regarding revocation shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon application by any proprietor of a registered trade mark, extend the period of registration thereof for further periods of ten years each, subject to payment of the prescribed fees. Such extension shall be granted only if the applicant demonstrates continued use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the register during the immediately preceding five-year period. However, this requirement is not applicable where the non-use can be attributed directly to actions taken by a third party without the proprietor’s consent. The limitations on extending registration apply equally if the applicant has entered into a licensing agreement affecting the mark's use, as provided herein.

The registrar semiconductor shall maintain a comprehensive register of all layout-designs, and any person aggrieved by an act of the registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, appeal to the Chairperson, who shall constitute a single-person bench for expeditious resolution of such disputes. Failure to accurately record a layout-design in the register, or any wilful omission thereof, shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Any false representation made to the registrar semiconductor, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The registrar may, with prior approval of the Central Government, prescribe fees for all applications, registrations, and inspections conducted as provided herein. Any officer of the registrar found to be in collusion with an infringer shall be summarily dismissed from service and subject to prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall include, as essential particulars, a map of the delimited area of production or origin, clearly delineating its boundaries; details regarding the qualities, reputation or other characteristics which are attributable to the applicant’s geographical origin; and evidence demonstrating that the said qualities, reputation or characteristics originate in the defined geographical area. The Registrar may require further information pertaining to traditional knowledge associated with the goods, provided such request is made within sixty days of receipt of the application. Any alteration to the particulars relating registration after initial publication shall be subject to a period of objection by interested parties, as determined under this Act. Failure to provide adequate documentation regarding the geographical area’s distinctiveness may result in rejection of the application. The Registrar shall maintain records of all objections and responses received concerning these particulars.

An application for registration of an integrated circuit layout design shall include particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, whether the applicant is the first maker of the layout-design or has derived title thereto, and a statement indicating whether any prior publication or exploitation of the layout-design has occurred. Where the applicant claims derivation of title, the application must clearly identify the original registrant and provide documentary evidence substantiating such claim under this Act. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify the validity of the law registration referred to in the application, including assignments or licenses relating to the design.

A certificate of registration, issued for a new plant variety as provided herein, shall be prima facie evidence of a validly protected right in respect of said variety, subject to subsequent proof of essential characteristics and distinctiveness. The certificate shall specify the designated name of the variety, the applicant’s details, the date of registration, and the period of validity, which period may be extended in accordance with the provisions relating to renewal. Where a variety is declared essentially derived from an existing registered variety, a separate certificate shall be issued denoting such derivation and identifying the initial variety from which it originates, and the holder of the certificate for the initial variety shall have rights over the essentially derived variety. Any transfer of the certificate registration shall be subject to notification to the Authority and recorded accordingly.

Where any proprietor or registered licensee contravenes any provision of this Act or the regulations made thereunder, or fails to comply with any direction issued by the Controller, an inquiry imposing penalty shall be initiated against such proprietor or registered licensee. The Controller may, subject to due process and affording a reasonable opportunity for representation, direct that such inquiry be conducted by an officer designated by him. Upon conclusion of the inquiry, if it is established that a contravention has occurred, the Controller may impose a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Further, where a mark separately registered under this Act is involved in the contravention, the penalty shall be doubled. The Controller’s order imposing penalty shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of its communication.

Any person aggrieved by an entry in the Designs Register, or by a refusal to enter a design, may apply to the Controller for rectification of register. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The Controller shall give notice of the application to the concerned party and afford them an opportunity of being heard, subject to just cause shown. Failure to comply with a direction issued under this Act concerning rectification proceedings constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment or fine, or both. Any order made by the Controller regarding rectification register is final, provided that an appeal lies to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

Where any act relating to the registration of a layout-design is performed by a design agent person, the liability for any errors or omissions committed in such performance shall be borne solely by the said design agent person, subject to the provisions regarding vicarious liability under this Act. An aggrieved party may appeal against any decision concerning the actions of a design agent person to the relevant Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. Provided that, if the act was performed pursuant to express instructions received in writing from the applicant or registered proprietor, the responsibility for such errors shall be jointly borne by both parties unless it is demonstrated that the design agent person acted fraudulently or negligently beyond the scope of their mandate.

An application patent period shall extend to twenty years from the date of filing, subject to any adjustments arising from post-grant opposition proceedings as provided herein. Where an applicant has failed to comply with requirements regarding the furnishing of information under this Act, the Controller may, after giving the applicant an opportunity of being heard, extend the application patent period by a duration not exceeding six months. Such extension shall only be granted if the failure to furnish the requisite information was demonstrably unintentional and did not prejudice the interests of any other party. Furthermore, where a request for examination is delayed due to circumstances beyond the applicant’s control, the Controller may, upon satisfactory demonstration of such circumstances, grant an appropriate extension; however, this shall not extend the overall application patent period beyond twenty-four months from the original filing date.

Where an international registration is made under this Act, the proprietor shall have the option to extend the protection conferred thereby to any country designated in such registration where India maintains reciprocal trade relations with that designated state. Such extension may be effected by way of a license granted to another party, provided that the terms of said license are filed with the Registrar within three months of the grant thereof and specify the scope of permitted use relating to the registered trademark. Further, any assignment of rights pertaining to an international registration shall require prior notification to the Controller, detailing the assignor and assignee, along with a declaration confirming adherence to all conditions stipulated under this Act regarding fair competition and consumer protection. The Registrar may request further documentation as deemed necessary to ascertain compliance.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall apply geographical names that conform to the prescribed format and contain an exhaustive index of all registered names pertaining to similar goods or services. Where any objection is raised by a prior registrant alleging likelihood of confusion with existing index names registered under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written arguments rebutting such objections within sixty days from the date of receipt of notice. The Registrar may, after considering the submissions and representations made by both parties, either reject the application or direct modification of the proposed geographical indication to mitigate any potential conflict. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of three months from the date of such order.

An exclusive licensee under this Act shall register with the Controller within thirty days from the date on which the license agreement comes into effect, providing a certified copy of the said agreement and details of the licensed territory. Such registration is subject to verification by the Controller regarding the terms granting rights as an invention exclusive licensee. The Controller may require further documentation demonstrating the validity of the license and its compliance with provisions relating to patentability. Failure to register shall render the exclusive licensee unable to enforce certain remedies under this Act pertaining to infringement, provided that a grace period of fifteen days is allowed for rectifying any clerical errors in the submitted documents. Any alteration to the terms of the license agreement must also be reported to and re-registered with the Controller.

Any person claiming utilisation of a registered variety, whether through commercial sale, propagation, distribution or any other method, shall furnish a statement of account to the breeder or his successor, as provided herein, detailing the extent of such utilisation and the remuneration derived therefrom. The breeder may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign or license the right to utilise the variety to any other person, and such assignment or license shall be in writing and registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Where a farmer is engaged in the utilisation of a variety for the purpose of research or for saving, selling, sharing or distributing seeds of such variety, such utilisation shall be exempt from the requirement of a statement of account, provided that such farmer is not engaged in commercial production. Any dispute regarding claims utilisation or the appropriate remuneration shall be adjudicated by the designated authority, and decisions shall be binding on all parties concerned, unless appealed to a higher court. Failure to comply with the provisions relating to statements of account may result in penalties as prescribed.

A certification trade mark shall be registrable if its use by any party conforms strictly to the prescribed standards and regulations detailed within the relevant quality control guidelines, as notified under this Act. Application for registration must include a comprehensive specification outlining the characteristics of goods or services eligible to bear the mark, alongside a precise definition of the certification process. The applicant shall demonstrate to the Registrar that they possess the requisite authority to ensure compliance with these standards and have established an effective mechanism for monitoring adherence by certified users. Provided that such mechanism is independently verifiable, the Registrar may grant registration; however, this remains subject to periodic review to confirm continued suitability.

Any person who contravenes any provision of this Act relating to the unauthorized propagation or sale of plant varieties shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each instance. Repeated offences may attract penalties escalating up to ten thousand rupees per instance, as determined by an adjudicating officer appointed under this Act. Furthermore, any entity found guilty of misleadingly representing a variety's characteristics or origin in commercial transactions will face additional fines and potential prohibition from propagating material for a period not less than one year. The Central Government shall establish a mechanism to ensure that funds recovered through penalties are deposited into the gene fund shall be utilized exclusively for supporting research and development activities related to plant breeding, particularly benefiting smallholder farmers and public institutions.

Any person alleging an infringement of a registered geographical indication may file a suit in the competent civil court seeking remedies including, but not limited to, injunctions restraining the use of the geographical indication or any confusingly similar indicator, and damages for losses suffered by the registrant as a consequence of such infringement. Subject to appeal under this Act, the court shall determine whether the defendant’s use constitutes an unfair advantage or misappropria­tion, considering factors such as consumer deception and dilution of the distinctive character of the registered geographical indication. Where a suit is filed alleging infringement of a reference geographical indication, the court may order the destruction of goods bearing the infringing indicator. The remedies available under this Act shall be without prejudice to any other rights or remedies available to the registrant under general principles of law.

A mark registered proprietor shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses relating to the use of the trade mark for specific goods or services as defined within the license agreement. Such licenses may be granted on a sole, exclusive basis or in a non-exclusive manner, subject to conditions stipulated by the proprietor and recorded with the Registrar. Any assignment of the registered trademark, whether partial or complete, shall include provisions regarding any existing licenses; these provisions must ensure that the rights of licensees are not prejudiced without their express written consent. Further, where a mark registered proprietor intends to sub-license usage rights, they must provide prior notification to all current licensees, detailing the scope and terms of the proposed sub-licensing arrangement. This requirement is provided that it does not unduly restrict the proprietary’s ability to commercialize its intellectual property.

Any user party proceeding initiated under this Act relating to a registered trade mark shall require prior notice to be served upon all registered users of that trade mark, detailing the grounds for the proceeding and the relief sought. Such notice shall be served via registered post and electronic mail, with proof of delivery maintained by the initiating party. A registered user may, subject to the discretion of the adjudicating authority, participate fully in the proceeding, including presenting evidence and cross-examining witnesses. Provided that a registered user failing to respond to the notice within thirty days of service may be deemed to have waived their right to participate, unless sufficient cause is demonstrated. The adjudicating authority may, as provided herein, direct costs against a user party demonstrating frivolous or vexatious conduct during the proceeding. Any decision rendered shall be binding on all registered users, unless successfully challenged through established appellate mechanisms.

An application to a High Court under this Act shall be deemed to be a court application where such application seeks redressal for alleged infringement of patent rights, or challenges the validity of a granted patent. A court application must specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to allegations of novelty lacking in an invention, obviousness of the claimed subject matter, or insufficiency of disclosure. The applicant shall further provide particulars of the patent in question and demonstrate standing to bring such a court application. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application as provided herein.

A mark shall not be registrable as a certification trade mark in the name of a person who carries on a trade in goods of the kind certified or a trade of the provision of services of the kind certified.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an application for rectification of a registered trademark may be made by any person claiming interest alleging that such registration is invalid or ought to be amended or expunged. Such applications shall be filed in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The Registrar shall serve notice on the registered proprietor, affording them an opportunity to file their counterstatement within a stipulated period as provided herein. Upon receipt of the counterstatement, the Registrar may direct the presentation of such evidence as they deem necessary for determining the dispute. Where the application relates to newly acquired distinctiveness, the applicant must demonstrate use consistent with building consumer recognition. The registered proprietors trade shall be considered in light of all submitted documentation and arguments.

(2) Where, in the case of a literary, dramatic, musical or artist ic work, or, subject to the provisions of sub-section (3) of section 13, a cinematograph film or sound recording, a name purporting to be that of the author, or the publisher, as the case may be, of that work, appears on copies of the work as published, or, in the case of an artistic work, appeared on the work when it was made, the person whose name so appears or appeared shall, in any proceeding in respect of infringement of copyright in such work, be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, to be the author or the publisher of the work, as the case may be. (3) The costs of all parties in any proceedings in respect of the infringement of copyright shall be in the discretion of the court.

Where an appeal under this Act is preferred against any decision or order made by the controller, the Appellate Board may, after giving notice to the appellant and the respondent, hear the appeal at such time and place as it thinks fit. The Board shall follow the procedure specified herein for hearing appeals, subject to such modifications as it deems necessary for ensuring fairness and expeditious disposal of the matter. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, provided that the grounds of appeal shall be limited to questions of law arising out of the decision or order of the Appellate Board. The controller shall furnish all relevant records pertaining to the case to the Appellate Board and the High Court as required.

Where an infringement of copyright has occurred and it is established that a company proved offence by means of acts carried out by its employees or agents, the prosecution may proceed against both the company and any director, manager, secretary, or other officer thereof who was directly involved in the decision-making process relating to the infringing activity. Such officers shall be deemed guilty participants unless they demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the court, that they took all reasonable steps to prevent the infringement from occurring. The burden of proving such due diligence rests upon the accused officer. Further proceedings against any individual shall not preclude concurrent prosecution of the company under this Act, subject to principles of fairness and proportionality as determined by the adjudicating authority.

Where a registered Geographical Indication has been infringed and the infringer is not a registered proprietor, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings seeking damages proportionate to the loss suffered, subject to demonstrating reasonable diligence in discovering the infringing activity. Provided that, if the alleged infringement occurs prior to registration but subsequent to public notice under this Act, the assessment of damages shall consider any reliance placed by consumers upon the indication as signifying origin and quality attributable to the registered geographical area. The Registrar may, at the request of an interested party, investigate complaints regarding such unregistered use and issue directions for its cessation; however, these directions do not confer a right to claim damages infringement unregistered under this Act independently. Appeals against any order made by the Registrar concerning such investigations shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An integrated circuit, for the purposes of this Act, shall be construed as a three dimensional microelectronic structure including all layers and interconnections therein, which is designed for the performance of electronic functions. Any person exploiting such an integrated circuit commercially without due authorization from the proprietor of the layout-design registered under this Act, shall be liable to legal proceedings. The Registrar may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, maintain a public register of all registered layout-designs and associated proprietors. A layout-design is considered distinct if it demonstrates novelty and originality in its configuration; however, mere aesthetic variations are insufficient for establishing such distinction as provided herein. Where a dispute arises concerning ownership of a particular integrated circuit’s layout-design, the appropriate authority shall conduct an inquiry to determine rightful proprietorship based on evidence presented by all parties concerned. Any application for registration must include detailed technical drawings and specifications of the said layout-design. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application.

An applicant desiring to secure an international registration for a trade mark, in addition to fulfilling the requirements as provided herein relating to domestic applications, shall file with the Trade Marks Registry a statement indicating the countries or territories beyond India where protection is sought. The application for international registration shall be accompanied by a certified copy of any basic application or registration relied upon and shall conform to the provisions of the Madrid Protocol on International Registration of Marks. Where an applicant seeks to designate a country which is not a member of the said Protocol, such designation shall have no effect unless reciprocal arrangements exist between India and that country as determined by notification in the Official Gazette. The Registry may require translation of any document submitted which is not in English or Hindi, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any opposition to an international registration extending to India shall be governed by the provisions relating to domestic oppositions, with such modifications as the Central Government may deem necessary. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in refusal of the application for international registration or limitation of its effect.

A patent agent, if found to have acted with reasonable care and skill but nonetheless provided incorrect advice resulting in the rejection of a valid patent application, shall not be liable for any loss suffered by the applicant unless such loss arises from demonstrable fraud or wilful misrepresentation on the part of the agent. However, nothing contained herein shall preclude an action for professional negligence against a patent agent where it is established that the agent failed to conduct reasonable searches as provided within the prescribed rules, and this failure directly contributed to the invalidation of a subsequently granted patent. Any person aggrieved by the actions of a patent agent may lodge a complaint with the Controller of Patents, who shall investigate such complaints and may impose penalties including suspension or revocation of registration, subject to principles of natural justice. The Controller’s decision in any matter relating to disciplinary proceedings against a patent agent shall be final and binding, save for appeal to the High Court.

For the purposes of this Act, "attributable geographical area" means a defined and limited geographic region on the territory of India from which goods originate, where a particular quality, reputation or other characteristic of those goods is essentially attributable to its origin. This determination shall consider factors including natural conditions, traditional practices, and local expertise employed in production. Where such characteristics are widely advertised and accepted by consumers as indicative of origin, this advertised acceptance relates directly to the establishment of an attributable geographical area. Goods claiming protection under this Act must demonstrably derive these qualities from within the specified boundaries as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking to challenge the acceptance of an application for trade mark registration shall file a written notice of opposition with the Registry within three months of the date such acceptance is advertised under this Act. The notice must specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior use or registration of a similar mark in respect of identical or closely related goods or services. Failure to adequately articulate these grounds may result in the Registrar dismissing the opposition as frivolous.

The applicant for registration shall be afforded an opportunity to respond to the notice and submit counter-arguments within one month from receipt thereof. Provided that the Registrar deems the opposition to have merit, a hearing shall be convened wherein both parties may present evidence and arguments. The Registrar’s decision on the validity of the application registration notice shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act.

Where an appeal arises from any decision or order made by the Controller relating to the registration of a layout-design, or concerning the validity of a registered layout-design, such appeal shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appellant may seek review of findings pertaining to novelty and originality under this Act, particularly where evidence presented contradicts the initial assessment. It is provided that any party aggrieved by an order affirming the rights of a “registered proprietor”, in relation to a layout-design, may petition the Appellate Board demonstrating substantial prior use or publication undermining the claim of exclusive right. The Controller shall provide detailed reasoning for all decisions regarding registration and validity, which reasoning shall be accessible to all parties involved subject to confidentiality provisions as provided herein.

An invention, subject to the provisions of this Act, shall be considered novel only if it does not form part of the state of the art prior to the date of the complete specification. Any allegation of prior art, submitted by a party opposing the grant of a patent, shall be accompanied by demonstrably authentic evidence establishing the date and source of such prior art, failing which the Controller may dismiss the opposition. Where a claimed invention is a modification or combination of existing processes, it shall be deemed to involve an inventive step only if such modification or combination results in a non-obvious improvement in functionality or efficiency. An appeal against the Controller’s decision regarding novelty or inventive step may be preferred to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the Controller’s order and accompanied by a prescribed fee. The burden of proving lack of inventive step shall lie upon the party alleging it.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to traditional dwellings, including but not limited to structures commonly known as placed houses parliament, shall require submission of detailed architectural plans demonstrating adherence to established regional construction techniques and materials. Such applications must further include documented evidence confirming continuous use of the indicated methods within the defined geographical area for a minimum period of thirty years preceding the date of application. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the proposed geographical indication lacks distinctiveness or falsely suggests a connection with the identified traditional dwelling practices. Any alteration to the architectural design or construction methodology, subsequent to registration, shall be subject to approval by the Geographical Indications Registry and may invalidate the registered status as provided herein.

(2) Notice of the acquisition shall be given to the applicant, and, where a patent has been granted, to the patentee and other persons, if any, appearing in the register as having an interest in the patent.

Any application for registration of a trade mark shall be subject to a search conducted by the Trade Marks Registry to ascertain whether the mark is the subject of an existing patent, privilege or copyright, and whether its registration would be detrimental to the rights of any other person. The Registry may, as provided herein, require the applicant to furnish a no-objection certificate from the holder of any such existing right, failing which the application shall be deemed to be abandoned. Where an application concerns a mark identical or deceptively similar to a mark already registered for identical or similar goods or services, the applicant shall notify the existing right holder of the pending application and provide proof of such notification to the Registry. Failure to adequately notify the existing right holder may result in the rejection of the application or the revocation of any registration obtained improperly. The Registry reserves the right to request further information or clarification from either party to ensure a fair and just determination.

A work shall be considered to be published when copies thereof are made available to the public, whether by sale, distribution, public exhibition, or otherwise. For the purposes of this Act, the publish translation of a work, whether literary, dramatic, musical or artistic, requires the prior authorization of the copyright holder, except as otherwise provided herein. However, a translation may be published without such authorization if it is intended solely for internal study or research, and is not disseminated further. Subject to the provisions relating to fair dealing, any unauthorized publish translation constitutes an infringement of copyright and is actionable under this Act. Provided that, the translation accurately reflects the original work and does not introduce any substantial alterations or distortions.

Where a registered layout design is infringed, the owner shall be entitled to seek remedies as provided herein. The injured party may institute civil proceedings for damages, which shall include compensation for loss of profits and any measure of the damage suffered by the owner attributable to the infringement. Further, subject to demonstrating reasonable efforts to mitigate losses, exemplary damages may be awarded at the discretion of the court. A request for an injunction restraining further acts of infringement is also permissible under this Act. The procedure for determining the extent of damages shall follow principles of fairness and proportionality, considering factors such as the duration of the infringing activity and the willful nature thereof. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding remedies may appeal to the relevant appellate forum as prescribed.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent in India shall submit an application demonstrating novelty and non-obviousness, as provided herein, and fulfilling all requirements relating to patent india as stipulated within this Act. The application shall disclose the invention in a clear and complete manner sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. Subject to the provisions concerning priority dates, an applicant claiming convention priority under the Paris Convention shall file the necessary documents within the prescribed timeframe. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application. Furthermore, any subsequent amendment to the application shall not extend beyond the scope of the original disclosure. A patent granted under this Act shall be subject to revocation on grounds of lack of novelty, obviousness, or insufficient disclosure, as determined by due process.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration india of a trade mark, or requiring the limitation of a trade mark, or dismissing an application for revival of a trade mark, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such terms and conditions as the Appellate Board may deem fit. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, either confirm the decision of the Registrar, or reverse it, or vary it in such manner as it thinks fit. An application for registration of a trade mark shall not be refused solely on the ground that it is identical with a trade mark already registered in India for different goods or services, provided that such trade marks are not likely to cause confusion. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding on all parties, except where a substantial question of law arises for determination by the High Court.

Where any patent has been amended subsequent to its grant, the Controller shall ensure that a record of such amendment is maintained in the public register. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the amendment relates to the scope of protection claimed, the description of the invention, or the claims appended thereto. Any party aggrieved by an amendment may, subject to provisions under this Act concerning appeals, petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for review if it is demonstrated that the amendment materially alters the originally granted patent and prejudices the interests of third parties. The Controller shall not register any amendment unless satisfied that it complies with prescribed formalities and does not extend the term of protection beyond what is permissible under these patents amendments.

For the purposes of this Act, “audiovisual work” means a compilation comprising cinematographic films and literary works, including musical scores, lyrics, and dramatic elements, fixed in any medium; provided that such compilation shall be considered an audiovisual work only if it constitutes an original work of authorship. The right to reproduce an audiovisual work under this Act extends only to the entire work as presented, and not to individual components unless expressly authorized by the copyright owner of each component element. A certificate purporting to be issued by an authorized officer under this Act, and bearing the official seal of that office, shall be admissible as evidence in any proceeding before a court or tribunal. Such certificate shall be deemed prima facie proof of the facts stated therein, relating to the grant, modification, or revocation of patents, subject to the provisions allowing for rebuttal by presentation of contrary evidence. The validity of such a certificate may only be challenged upon establishing demonstrable fraud or fabrication affecting its issuance. A provisional specification, submitted under this Act, shall be treated as a document establishing an early filing date for an invention, subject to the subsequent filing of a complete specification as provided herein. The provisional specification need not contain claims, but must adequately describe the invention to allow a person skilled in the relevant art to understand its nature. An applicant may, at the time of filing the complete specification, amend the provisional specification to correct any obvious errors or omissions, provided that such amendment does not introduce matter extending beyond the content initially disclosed. Where a complete specification is filed claiming priority from a provisional specification, the Controller shall examine whether the complete specification adequately supports the claims made and is based upon the disclosure contained within the provisional specification. Failure to demonstrate such support may result in objections being raised during the examination process. The provisional specification shall be maintained confidentially until the complete specification is filed or until fifteen months have elapsed from the date of filing, whichever occurs first.

Furthermore, any unauthorized reproduction or adaptation of a work displayed publicly via digital means, accessible to the general public, may be considered equivalent to publication, subject to verification by the Controller.

A patent shall vest in the legal person who first lawfully acquires ownership of the invention, subject to the provisions contained herein regarding prior claims and public knowledge. Any assignment of a patent, or an interest therein, shall be in writing and registered with the Controller of Patents as provided herein, failing which such assignment shall be void as between the parties. Where a patent is jointly held, no co-owner may grant a license or assign their interest without the consent of all other co-owners, unless otherwise agreed in a written co-ownership agreement filed with the Controller. In cases involving complex technical subject matter, the Controller may, at any stage of the application or opposition proceedings, seek the advice of a judicial member technical possessing requisite expertise. The patentee shall maintain accurate records of all licenses granted and assignments made, and these shall be open to inspection upon reasonable notice. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the patent vulnerable to revocation.

Any person claiming damages for the use of a registered trademark without consent shall be entitled to recover from the defendant such sum as the Court deems fit, having regard to the loss suffered by the claimant, but not exceeding five times the value of the goods or services in relation to which the infringement occurred. The Court may also award interest on such sum at such rate as it considers appropriate. Where the infringing use is found to have been made for the purpose of securing an unfair advantage or to deceive or confuse the public, the Court shall grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts. It is provided that this remedy shall be available only to citizens India and those registered in India under this Act. Further, any order granted under these provisions may be enforced as if it were a decree of the High Court.

A patent of addition may be granted for any invention which is a modification or improvement relating to an invention for which a patent has been granted, or for which an application for a patent is pending, provided that the invention involving the modification or improvement is not separately patentable. An application for a patent of addition shall be filed in the prescribed manner and shall include a declaration stating that the invention is a modification or improvement of the invention claimed in the existing patent or pending application. The application shall be examined as if it were an application for a separate patent, subject to the condition that the patent of addition shall not be granted unless the main invention is also protected by a patent. The patent of addition shall be granted for the unexpired term of the main patent, and the patentee of the main patent shall also be the patentee of the patent of addition. Where a patent of addition is granted, the main patent and the patent of addition shall be treated as a single patent for the purposes of renewal fees and other administrative matters, as provided herein.

Where infringement of a patent has occurred, the right to damages shall accrue to the patentee or, where applicable, the author of the invention as recognized under this Act. Such damages shall be calculated based on the loss suffered by the patentee as a result of the infringing activity, taking into account any profits made by the infringer attributable to the use of the patented article. The Controller may order an infringer found guilty of infringement to cease the manufacture, sale, or importation of the includes article patented and to provide accounts of sales for assessment of damages. Further, the Controller may impose a penalty not exceeding three times the amount of damages awarded, provided that the infringing activity was undertaken knowingly and with intent to deceive. The patentee shall be entitled to recover costs incurred in establishing infringement, subject to limitations as determined by the Controller.

A patentee desiring registration of a process for the production of novel food items utilising genetically modified organisms shall submit an application to the Controller as provided herein. The application shall include a detailed description of the biological material employed and demonstrate substantial differentiation from previously known varieties, alongside evidence of nutritional value or improved shelf life. Any claim relating to traditional Indian foods or processes must be accompanied by documented proof of indigenous knowledge and benefit-sharing arrangements with relevant communities. Failure to disclose such information may invalidate the patent. The Controller may require a sample of the food item for independent verification. A patentee shall maintain accurate records concerning the origin, modification, and production scale of any patented food product subject to inspection under this Act. Provided that, registration does not confer immunity from regulations governing food safety and standards established by other competent authorities.

Any assignment of a patent application or a patent, whether wholly or partially, shall be evidenced by an instrument in writing, and such instrument shall be registered with the appropriate district court having jurisdiction over the matter. The district court, upon registration of the assignment, shall issue a certificate of registration to the assignee, confirming the transfer of rights, title, and interest in the patent or patent application. Subject to the provisions contained herein, a licensee of a patent may, with the consent of the patent holder, further assign their rights to a third party, and such subsequent assignment shall also require registration with the district court. Where a patent is jointly held, any assignment requires the written consent of all co-owners, unless otherwise agreed in a prior agreement filed with the district court. Failure to register an assignment shall not invalidate the assignment itself, but may affect its enforceability against third parties unaware of the transfer. The district court may prescribe fees for registration and maintain a public register of all assignments.

Any person exploiting a registered semiconductor layout-design without the authorization of the proprietor shall be liable for infringement as provided herein. A registered proprietor may, subject to conditions prescribed by regulations, grant licenses authorizing others to exploit their layout-design. Any dispute regarding the validity of registration or infringement shall be adjudicated by the designated Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal following a summary procedure established for expeditious resolution. The Tribunal may issue injunctions restraining further exploitation and award damages commensurate with actual loss suffered or reasonable royalty, whichever is higher. Evidence presented before the Tribunal relating to manufacturing costs must include detailed breakdowns of semiconductor fabrication expenses. Any appeal from decisions of the Tribunal shall lie directly to the Supreme Court.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered Semiconductor Integrated Circuit layout-design shall, prior to initiating proceedings before the High Court, furnish to the alleged infringer a notice of such claim, detailing the specific layout-design infringed and the nature of the infringement, subject to the provisions contained herein. An assignment of a registered layout-design shall be in writing and signed by the assignor or duly authorized agent. The form issuing for such assignment shall clearly state the particulars of the layout-design, including the registration number, the date of registration, and the name and address of the assignee. 

Where a layout-design is jointly held, no joint owner shall assign their share without the consent of all other joint owners, and any such assignment not complying with this requirement shall be void. Any application for the registration of a geographical indication shall be examined by the Registrar, and such examination shall be conducted as expeditiously as possible, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. The Registrar may, before refusing an application, require the applicant to furnish further information or evidence, or to limit the scope of the geographical indication sought to be registered. Where a geographical indication is registered, the register shall contain the particulars of the goods in respect of which the geographical indication is registered, the area of origin, and the name and address of the applicant. A registration referred fact establishing the link between the goods and their geographical origin is a prerequisite for the grant of protection as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all registered geographical indications, which shall be open to inspection by the public, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may, within a period of ninety days from the date of such decision, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board.

Any person who applies for the registration of a trade mark under this Act, knowing it to be false, or who knowingly uses a trade mark registered by another, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services for which it was not registered, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, order the rectification of the register and require the removal of the offending mark from all goods and promotional materials. Any false representation concerning the nature, manufacturing process, characteristics, or suitability for purpose of goods bearing registered trade marks shall constitute an unfair trade practice. Provided that, a bona fide industrial or commercial use of a descriptive term shall not be deemed a violation of rights in the trade marks registered. The Registrar shall have the power to impose monetary penalties not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each such violation, as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking to license the use of a certification trade mark under this Act shall execute an agreement specifying the terms and conditions governing such licensing, including but not limited to the scope of permitted activities, quality control measures, and royalty payments. Such agreements may be assigned or sub-licensed subject to prior written approval from the Registrar, provided that the assignee undertakes to abide by all obligations imposed upon the original proprietor as stipulated herein. The Registrar shall have the power to reject any proposed assignment or sub-licence if it deems such transfer detrimental to the integrity of the certification trade mark or likely to mislead consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods or services bearing the mark. Further, any alteration to a licensing agreement requires notification and approval from the Registrar before its effective date.

Where a patent has been granted in respect of an invention which is subsequently found to relate to a substance or process already available as prior art, the Controller may, upon application by any interested party and after due inquiry and opportunity afforded to the patentee for representation, issue an order declaring that the said patent shall cease to have effect. Such cessation patent shall be deemed to have been invalid from its grant date; however, any acts done lawfully before the declaration of cessation shall not be treated as infringements under this Act. The Controller may require the applicant seeking such a declaration to furnish evidence demonstrating the availability of the prior art and its impact on the novelty of the invention.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute civil proceedings in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurred, and may seek an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement, as well as damages for loss suffered due to such infringement. However, a defendant may, in any such proceeding, file a counter-claim asserting the invalidity of the registration of the layout-design, or alleging that the acts complained of do not constitute commercial exploitation as defined herein. Should the Court find in favour of the defendant on such a counter-claim, the plaintiff’s claim for injunction and damages shall stand dismissed. An appeal from any decree or order of the District Court in such proceedings shall lie to the High Court, and further to the Supreme Court, subject to the usual terms and conditions. The burden of proving due diligence in preventing the infringement shall, in all cases, lie with the registered proprietor.

Where a registered trade mark is affixed to goods in such a manner as to create a likelihood of confusion amongst the public regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of those goods, and it is established that such affixation constitutes a falsifies trade mark, the proprietor of the trade mark shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief. This entitlement subsists provided that the defendant has acted with knowledge, or ought reasonably to have had knowledge, that the registered trade mark was being so affixed. Further, where the falsification involves the use of a colour scheme substantially similar to that associated with the registered trade mark, demonstrating intent to deceive, damages may be awarded to compensate for loss of reputation and goodwill suffered by the proprietor. The Registrar may also order the destruction of goods bearing the falsified mark.

For the purposes of this Act, “registered proprietor”, in relation to a layout-design, means the person whose name is entered as such in the Register of Layout-Designs, and includes any person deriving title from such person, subject to the provisions of this Act concerning assignment and transmission. A person shall be deemed to derive title from the registered proprietor where such transfer of rights has been duly recorded with the Intellectual Property Office. Provided that, where a layout-design is created pursuant to a contract for services or apprenticeship, the registered proprietor shall be the person agreed upon in such contract or, failing such agreement, the person under whose direction the layout-design was so created. Any rights vested in a legal representative as provided herein shall be subject to the terms of this Act.

An application for registration, once duly filed and examined in accordance with the rules prescribed under this Act, may be permitted to be amended by the applicant subject to such conditions as the Controller deems fit, provided that such amendment shall not result in the trade mark differing substantially from that in the original application. Any amendment seeking to expand the scope of goods or services covered by the application shall require a further examination fee as specified in the Schedule. The Controller may, at their discretion, require evidence of use relating to the amended specification, should it be deemed necessary to ascertain the genuine intention to use the trade mark for those goods or services. Where an application permitted amended relates to a collective or certification mark, the amendment shall not alter the fundamental characteristics of the collective or certification mark as defined in the application. Any third party adversely affected by such amendment may file a notice of opposition within the prescribed time limit.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the agricultural product or good indicating its origin, along with a map of the area where the good is produced or processed. The applicant must demonstrate that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods are essentially attributable to their geographical origin as provided herein. Prior use of the proposed indication by others shall not disqualify an application, subject to demonstrating continued adherence to established production standards and practices within the defined geographical area. Any alteration in these standards requires prior notification to the Registrar and approval based on a determination that such changes do not compromise the distinctiveness linked to the registration geographical indication.

Any person claiming priority under the Budapest Treaty for the filing of a patent application shall, within the period prescribed, furnish a certified copy of the international deposit receipt issued by the competent International Depositary Authority, as provided herein. Should the Controller, upon examination, find the deposit receipt to be incomplete or lacking requisite details confirming the date of deposit, they may issue a notice requiring the applicant to rectify the deficiency within a period not exceeding three months. Failure to comply with such notice shall be deemed a waiver of the priority claim, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of the deposit receipt or the interpretation of the Treaty itself, may be referred to the Appellate Board for adjudication, provided that such referral occurs no later than six months from the date of the Controller’s initial decision. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except on grounds of legal error established before a court of competent jurisdiction.

The owner of a registration mark certified under this Act may grant licenses conferring the right to use such certification mark upon goods or services meeting specified standards. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution, detailing the scope of permitted usage, duration, and any associated royalties payable to the registration mark proprietor. Assignment of a registration mark certification, whether partial or complete, requires prior written consent from the Registrar, ensuring continued adherence to the quality control protocols outlined during initial application. Any alteration to these protocols following assignment shall be subject to review and approval by the Registrar before the revised standards may be applied to goods bearing the certification mark. Further, sub-licensing of a registration mark certification is permitted only with express authorization from the original licensor, as provided herein.

Any order made under this provision may be appealed before the appellate forum as provided herein.

Any application for registration of a geographical indication shall be examined by the Registrar as provided herein, and such examination shall be completed within a period of eighteen months from the date of the application, subject to the applicant fulfilling all requirements regarding documentation and fees. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the application meets the criteria for registration, a notice of acceptance shall be published in the Journal. Any person may, within a period of four months from such publication, file a notice of opposition to the registration, detailing the grounds upon which the application is contested. The Registrar shall consider any opposition filed and may, after giving the applicant an opportunity to be heard, either reject the application or direct that the geographical indication be registered. A registration referred fact, once established and recorded in the Register, shall be prima facie evidence of the validity of the right to the geographical indication. However, such registration may be subject to revocation on grounds of non-use or misleading representation, as detailed in this Act. The Register maintained under this Act shall be open to inspection by any member of the public, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

Where any application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design is presented to the Registrar, it shall be accompanied by a verification in the form specified in Schedule A, signed by the applicant or an authorized signatory thereof, including a legal practitioner acting on behalf of the applicant. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the identity and authority of any such legal practitioner. An application filed without proper verification, or with a verification containing material misstatements, is liable to be rejected under this Act.

The Registrar shall serve notice of the receipt of an application upon all persons appearing from the records maintained by the office to be interested in the layout design, providing them opportunity for objection as provided herein. Any objections received must be accompanied by an affidavit verifying their factual basis and signed by a legal practitioner representing the objector. Furthermore, where an applicant seeks protection under the Patent Cooperation Treaty concerning a layout design, they shall submit a certificate of compliance confirming adherence to treaty requirements.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade mark” shall mean a mark capable of being represented graphically and which is used or proposed to be used, in relation to goods or services, including sounds, smells, tastes or any combination thereof, for the purpose of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others. Such marks may include words, names, symbols, devices, letters, numerals, shapes, configurations, patterns, or combinations thereof. The owner of a registered trade mark shall be liable to pay a copyright society fee as determined by the central government, provided that such fee is proportionate to the usage and commercial exploitation of the mark under this Act.

The owner of a registered trademark shall have the right to grant licenses conferring specific rights to use the mark in relation to particular goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms stipulated within the license agreement. Assignment of such licensing rights is permissible, subject to adherence to procedures prescribed under this Act and notification to the Trade Marks Registry. Where a licensee engages in activities exceeding the scope of granted rights, or where unauthorized use occurs through an assignee, the trademark owner shall be entitled to initiate a proceeding infringement trade action against the infringing party. Further, any agreement transferring licensing rights must clearly delineate the duration and geographical extent of such transfer, preventing ambiguity and ensuring clarity for all stakeholders involved.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation pertaining to the method of its derivation, including specifics regarding any genetic modification undertaken and the lineage tracing back to original parent material. The Registrar may require submission of additional data demonstrating stability and uniformity of characteristics across successive generations, particularly where the claimed novelty arises from hybridization techniques. Any applicant seeking registration as a *registration variety* must provide evidence substantiating that the distinctiveness criteria outlined in Schedule B have been met; failure to do so shall render the application liable for rejection. Further, documentation relating to geographical location and cultivation practices employed during evaluation periods must be included, provided that such information does not compromise trade secrets.

An erasure order injunction shall be granted by a competent court where a registered trade mark is found to have been obtained through fraudulent means, including but not limited to misrepresentation concerning the use or reputation of the mark, or suppression of material facts during registration proceedings. Such an injunction may restrain any person from using, advertising, or otherwise exploiting the infringing trade mark and shall include provisions for the erasure of all representations of the mark from public display, subject to a reasoned order specifying the duration and scope of such erasure. The court may also award compensation to aggrieved parties as provided herein.

The registrar shall maintain a register of trade marks in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Any person desiring to inspect the said register shall apply to the registrar in writing and may, upon payment of the prescribed fee, inspect the same subject to such conditions as the registrar may deem fit. The registrar may require any applicant for registration to furnish a statement of use showing how the trade mark has been used within the period specified herein. Provided that the registrar may, if satisfied with sufficient cause, extend the time for furnishing such a statement. All decisions made by the registrar shall be communicated in writing and are subject to appeal as provided under this Act. The registrar’s functions include the examination of applications and the determination of registrability.
