The registration of a trademark, as provided herein, may be subject to review and subsequent modification if it transpires that the use thereof has been discontinued for a continuous period exceeding five years. Furthermore, any person demonstrating substantial prejudice arising from the continued registration shall have standing to petition the Registrar for its cancellation. Such petitions must specify with particularity the grounds upon which they are founded and provide verifiable evidence supporting the claim of prejudice. The Registrar shall consider limitations on remedies where the trademark owner can demonstrate a reasonable explanation for cessation of use, such as temporary export restrictions or unavoidable operational disruptions. Cancelling registration shall not be ordered unless the Registrar is satisfied that the conditions precedent have been fully met.

Any person who, having benefited directly or indirectly from the use of plant genetic resources for the development of a new variety, fails to contribute an equitable share of the profits derived therefrom to the National Gene Fund shall be liable to pay a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Contributions to the National Gene Fund are deemed public money and any willful default in making such contributions constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The Authority may, subject to due process, seize assets derived from the infringing activity to recover unpaid sums owed to the Fund. Further, repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the Appellate Board.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, falsely represents a registered design as being his own, or sells, offers for sale, or distributes any article incorporating such falsely represented design, shall commit an offence under this Act. Where a design is registered in the name of a person other than the true creator, subject to the provisions herein, the true creator may apply to the Controller for rectification of the register. The Controller, upon being satisfied that the registered proprietor is not the true creator, may direct that the register be amended accordingly. A commission offence shall be cognizable by any Magistrate and shall be triable by any competent court. Provided that no prosecution for a commission offence shall be instituted except with the prior written consent of the Controller, unless such offence is committed by a repeat offender as determined by the Controller. Any evidence admitted in a court relating to a design registration shall be considered prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein.

(4) Any police officer not below the rank of deputy superintendent of police or equivalent, may, if he is satisfied that any of the offences referred to in sub -section ( 3) has been, is being, or is likely to be, committed, search and seize without warrant th e goods, die, block, machine, plate, other instruments or things involved in committing the offence, wherever found, and all the articles so seized shall, as soon as practicable, be produced before a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or Metropolitan M agistrate, as the case may be: Provided that the police officer, before making any search and seizure, shall obtain the opinion of the Registrar on facts involved in the offence relating to trade mark and shall abide by the opinion so obtained.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars relating to the name, address, and nationality of the applicant, whether individual or association, and a map of the territory constituting the geographical indication. The Registrar may require such further information as is necessary for proper examination of the application. Where an objection is raised by any interested party against the registration of a geographical indication under this Act, the plaintiff forthwith shall be notified of the grounds of objection and afforded an opportunity to submit its response within a period specified by the Registrar. A registered practitioner may represent the applicant in proceedings before the Registrar or any other authority constituted under this Act. The Registrar’s decision on such objections shall be final, subject to appeal as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions contained in this Act and in any rules made thereunder, every patent agent whose name is entered in the register shall be entitled:—
(a) to practice before the Controller; and
(b) to prepare all documents, transact all business and discharge such other functions as may be prescribed in connection with any proceeding before the Controller under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the proprietor of a registered design shall be entitled to grant licenses for the exploitation of their design rights, specifying the geographical area and duration of such license. Any assignment of a design or any interest therein shall include all rights pertaining to security india action relating to that design, as determined by the Controller. A licensee may sub-license their rights under this Act with the prior written consent of the proprietor, provided that such sub-licensing does not contravene the terms and conditions stipulated in the original license agreement. The Central Government may, upon application by any interested party, investigate instances where a design license appears to be unreasonably restrictive or discriminatory, impacting national economic interests. Such investigations shall be conducted with due regard for confidentiality and intellectual property rights as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Tribunal. The Tribunal shall consider such appeals expeditiously and may, while hearing any appeal, require the Chairperson of the relevant authority to appear and produce records pertaining to the original decision. Failure to comply with such a requirement shall render the erring officer liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable from their salary. Further, where an appeal is filed alleging improper influence exerted upon the original adjudicating officer, the Tribunal may initiate inquiries into administrative misconduct, subject to applicable service rules and disciplinary proceedings. The Chairperson’s testimony before the Tribunal shall be deemed admissible as evidence.

Where an application for a patent is filed in India claiming priority from an application filed outside India, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the earlier application as evidence. Such certification shall be obtained under the procedures prescribed by the relevant national authority or, where applicable, pursuant to the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposits for Industrial Designs. The applicant shall provide this documentation within the time specified in the notice issued by the Controller; failure to do so may result in the application being deemed withdrawn. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the acceptance or rejection of such certified copies may appeal under this Act, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Costs incurred in relation to these proceedings shall be determined by the Appellate Board and are liable costs unless the appellant demonstrates reasonable grounds for the appeal were absent.

The registered proprietor of any layout-design shall have the exclusive right to exploit the layout-design in any manner, including reproduction, modification, or commercial exploitation, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any assignment of the registered proprietor’s rights in a layout-design shall be in writing and registered with the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry to be effective against third parties. A license, whether sole or non-exclusive, granted by the registered proprietor shall similarly be documented in writing and registered as provided herein, detailing the scope of permitted exploitation and any applicable royalty or consideration. Where a layout-design is jointly held by multiple registered proprietors, each shall have an equal right to grant licenses, unless otherwise agreed in a written agreement amongst them. Failure to register an assignment or license does not invalidate the transfer of rights between the parties, but may affect its enforceability against subsequent purchasers or licensees acting in good faith. The registered proprietor layout remains subject to the limitations on rights as stipulated elsewhere in this Act.

An officer or employee in the patent office shall not, except when required or authorised by this Act or under a direction in writing of the 2Central Government or the Controller or by order of a court,—
(a) furnish information on a matter which is being, or has been, or dealt with under this Act ; or
(b) prepare or assist in the preparation of a document required or permitted by or under this Act to be lodged in the patent office; or
(c) conduct a search in the records of the patent office. POWERS OF CONTROLLER GENERALLY

Where an applicant has filed a patent application outside India, a subsequent convention application shall be deemed to include any rights or obligations arising from prior assignments or licenses granted in relation to the invention. Such assignments and licenses are subject to registration under this Act within six months of the filing of the convention application, provided that failure to register does not invalidate the assignment or license itself but may affect its priority. Any licensee permitted to exploit a patented invention shall be bound by the terms of the underlying patent and any conditions attached thereto as stipulated in the original grant. The Controller may require disclosure of all such assignments and licenses during examination proceedings. Further, an applicant seeking to enforce rights under this Act must provide evidence of valid assignment or license documentation relating to the convention application.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be examined in relation to their distinctiveness, considering whether, through use prior to the date of application, the mark has become reasonably associated with a particular service. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating such acquired distinctiveness, and the form and manner of presentation of this evidence shall be as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall record particulars thereof in a register maintained for that purpose, noting the filing date and any priority claims asserted. Objections raised by third parties to the acceptance of an application must be addressed according to procedures outlined herein; the applicant shall have opportunity to respond to such objections in writing. The decision of the Registrar concerning the registrability of a mark is final, subject to appeal under this Act. Decisions made by the registrar accordance with established practice are binding on all parties involved.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be deemed to possess exclusive rights pertaining to the use of the said mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any prior usage or registrations. Any party desiring to utilize a registered trade mark for commercial purposes beyond the scope of a permitted activity as defined under this Act may apply to the proprietor for a license. Such application shall specify the intended use and duration of the proposed utilization. The proprietor may grant such license on terms and conditions, including royalty payments, as they deem fit, provided that any assignment or sub-licensing of rights granted under this clause requires prior written consent from the registered proprietor. This provision concerning registration mentioned clause applies equally to assignments made before or after the date of registration.

(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in section 3 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (4 of 1963), any person may institute a suit for a declaration that the use by him of any process, or the making, use or sale of any article by him does not, or would not, constitute an infringement of a claim of a patent against the patentee or the holder of an exclusive licence under the patent, notwithstanding that no assertion to the contrary has been made by the patentee or the licensee, if it is shown—
(a) that the plaintiff has applied in writing to the patentee or exclusive licensee for a written acknowledgment to the effect of the declaration claimed and has furnished him with full particulars in writing of the process or article in question; and
(b) that the patentee or licensee has refused or neglected to give such an acknowledgment.
(2) The costs of all parties in a suit for a declaration brought by virtue of this section shall, unless for special reasons the court thinks fit to order otherwise, be paid by the plaintiff.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall include a representation of the integrated circuit in a form specified by the regulations. The Registrar shall examine each application to ascertain whether the layout-design is original and not contrary to public order or morality. Where an applicant has failed to comply with any requirement under this Act, the Registrar may afford him an opportunity to remedy such failure within a prescribed time. If the layout-design incorporates elements already registered, the design registry shall record that fact in the register. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the fees for various proceedings before the design registry and specify conditions relating to the examination of applications.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the variety, including its botanical name, origin, method of reproduction, and any distinctive features readily discernible by experts. Upon receipt of an application, the Plant Varieties Registry shall publish a notification inviting objections from interested parties within a period specified under this Act. Where no valid objection is received, or where such objections are withdrawn or dismissed, patents shall entered in the Register of Plant Varieties. The Registrar may require applicants to submit additional data relating to the stability and uniformity of the variety. Patents shall entered subject to the provisions regarding compulsory licensing as provided herein.

For the purposes of registration, an agricultural good claiming protection as a Geographical Indication shall demonstrate, through verifiable documentation, that the applicant is demonstrably engaged in the production of such goods within the defined geographical area. Such documentation must include records confirming adherence to prescribed cultivation practices and quality control measures, as stipulated by relevant governmental authorities. Furthermore, the application shall specify the precise boundaries of the geographical unit claiming origin, supported by detailed maps and historical data establishing a long-standing association between the agricultural good and that territory. If such goods are agricultural goods, produces the goods and possesses exclusive rights to utilize traditional knowledge pertaining to their production, as evidenced by community consensus resolutions duly authenticated under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to constitute a business basic application where the applicant demonstrates continuous and verifiable engagement with the goods or services specified in the application for a period not less than six months immediately preceding the date of filing. Such engagement must manifest through documented commercial activities, including but not limited to sales records, advertising expenditures, and contractual agreements relating directly to those goods or services. Provided that, where the applicant is a start-up entity as defined under applicable government regulations, this requirement may be relaxed subject to submission of an incubation certificate from a recognized body. The Registrar may require further evidence substantiating the claimed commercial activities at any stage during examination and opposition proceedings; failure to provide such evidence shall render the application liable for rejection.

(2) The provisions of this section shall be without prejudice to any right of determining a contract exercisable apart from this section.

(1) Any person aggrieved by an order or decision of the Registrar under this Act, or the rules made t hereunder may prefer an appeal to the High Court within three months from the date on which the order or decision sought to be appealed against is communicated to such person preferring the appeal.
(2) No appeal shall be admitted if it is preferred aft er the expiry of the period specified under sub-section (1): Provided that an appeal may be admitted after the expiry of the period specified therefor, if the appellant satisfies the High Court that he had sufficient cause for not preferring th e appeal within the specified period.
(3) An appeal to the High Court shall be in the prescribed form and shall be verified in the prescribed manner and shall be accompanied by a copy of the order or decision appealed against and by such fees as may be prescribed.

An application for registration as a geographical indication shall contain particulars specifying the name of the agricultural product or good, its essential qualities and characteristics derived from its origin, the defined geographical area constituting such origin, the production methods employed, and the history and traditions relating to its establishment. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information deemed necessary for assessing compliance with these provisions. Any association representing producers of goods conforming to the standards specified in the application shall be eligible to file on behalf of its members, provided that a majority of such producers consent in writing. Further, any alteration to production methods or quality characteristics after registration will require prior approval from the Registrar, subject to guidelines issued under this Act concerning continued adherence to established norms.

Where a patent application is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal before the Appellate Board. The Board shall consider all evidence presented by the applicant and the Controller, and may direct that further information be furnished or an inquiry held. If the Board allows the appeal, it shall direct the Controller to proceed with the examination of the patent application as if the refusal had not been made. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may prefer an appeal from such order to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of that order. The applicant’s remedies are subject to any conditions imposed by the Board regarding costs and timelines for compliance with directions issued under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Copyright Society, registered as provided herein, may prefer an appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, either confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed from and shall pass such orders as it deems fit. Failure to file an appeal within the stipulated period shall not be excused, save upon demonstration of sufficient cause. Any wilful misrepresentation before the Copyrights Appellate Board, or the submission of falsified evidence, shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, and may additionally render the appellant liable for prosecution under the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The decision of the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to any remedies available under the writ jurisdiction of the High Court.

(d) “design” means only the features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines or colours applied to any article whether in two dimensional or three dimensional or in both forms, by any industrial process or means, whether manual, mechanical or chemical, separate or combined, which in the finished article appeal to and are judged solely by the eye; but does not include any mode or principle of construction or anything which is in substance a mere mechanical device, and does not include any trade mark as defined in clause (v) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 (43 of 1958) or property mark as defined in section 479 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) or any artistic work as defined in clause (c) of section 2 of the Copyright Act, 1957 (14 of 1957).

The Registrar of Copyrights and the Appellate Board shall have the powers of a civil court when trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908), in respect of the following matters, namely, — (a) summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath; (b) requiring the discovery and production of any document; (c) receiving evidence on affidavits; (d) issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses or documents; (e) requisitioning any public record or copy thereof from any court or office; (f) any other matter which may be prescribed. Explanation.—For the purpose of enforcing the attendance of witnesses, the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Registrar of Copyrights or the Appellate Board, as the case may be, shall be the limits of the territory of India.

Where an action alleging court suit infringement of a registered trademark is brought before a High Court, the plaint shall specify the details of the infringing use, including but not limited to the goods or services involved and the geographical area where such infringement occurs. The defendant may, within thirty days from the date of service of summons, file with the High Court a counter-claim asserting validity of their own mark or challenging the plaintiff’s registered trademark. Should the defendant claim entitlement to use a similar mark based on an entitled assignment transmission from a prior rights holder, they must produce documentary evidence substantiating such transfer and its effective date. The High Court shall afford both parties reasonable opportunity for argument and presentation of evidence as provided herein. Any order restraining or preventing infringement shall be subject to conditions regarding damages and costs determined by the court.

An invention claimed in a complete specification shall not be deemed to have been anticipated by reason only that at any time within one year before the priority date of the relevant claim of the specification, the invention was publicly worked in India—
(a) by the patentee or applicant for the patent or any person from whom he derives title; or
(b) by any other person with the consent of the patentee or applicant for the patent or any person from whom he derives title, if the working was effected for the purpose of reasonable trial only and if it was reasonably necessary, having regard to the nature of the invention, that the working for that purpose should be effected in public.

(5) While disposing of the claim under sub-section (4), the Authority shall explicitly indicate in its order the amount of the benefit sharing, if any, for which the claimant shall be entitled and shall take into consideration the following matters, namely:— (a) the extent and nature of the use of genetic material of the claimant in the development of the variety relating to which the benefit sharing has been claimed; (b) the commercial utility and demand in the market of the variety relating to which the benefit sharing has been claimed. (6) The amount of benefit sharing to a variety determined under this section shall be deposited by the breeder of such variety in the manner referred to in clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 45 in the National Gene Fund.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration, or concerning any matter arising during the consideration thereof, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant. The appellate board may allow the appeal and direct the registry to proceed with the application as if it had been originally accepted, or may dismiss the appeal. Where an applicant has failed to pay a prescribed registry fee paid for renewal of registration within the time allowed under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a notice of intention to remove the trade mark from the register. The removal shall not take effect until six months from the date of such notice.

Where the copyright in a literary or artistic work incorporates a denomination variety which is itself subject to registration under the Designs Act, 2000, the owner of such copyright shall be deemed to hold an exclusive license to reproduce and communicate that portion of the work embodying the registered design variety. This license may be assigned by the copyright holder, provided that any subsequent assignee undertakes to respect the terms of the original design registration. The right to grant this license is prescribed by regulations framed under this Act, detailing procedures for notification and valuation of such assignments. Further, where a work utilizes a denomination variety without prior authorization from the registered proprietor, the copyright holder shall be liable to account for royalties as determined by the Controller. This provision applies irrespective of whether the use constitutes infringement under the Designs Act.

(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, the following acts do not constitute an infringement of the right to the use of a registered certification trade mark—
(c) the use of a certification trade mark in relation to goods or services adapted to form part of, or to be accessory to, other goods in relation to which the mark has been used without infringement of the right given as aforesaid or might for the time being be so used, if the use of the mark is reasonably necessary in order to indicate that the goods or services are so adapted and neither the purpose nor the effect of the use of the mark is to indicate otherwise than in accordance with the fact that the goods or services are certified by the proprietor. (2) Clause ( b) of sub -section (1) shall n ot apply to the case of use consisting of the application of a certification trade mark to goods or services, notwithstanding that they are such goods or services as are mentioned in that clause if such application is contrary to the regulations referred to in that clause. (3) Where a certification trade mark is one of two or more trade marks registered under this Act, which are identical or nearly resemble each other, the use of any of those trade marks in exercise of the right to the use of that trade mar k given by registration, shall not be deemed to be an infringement of the right so given to the use of any other of those trade marks.

Where an application for compulsory license is made, the Controller shall inquire into whether the patentee has been approached by the applicant regarding a license and if so, under what terms. The applicant shall demonstrate that negotiations were undertaken in good faith with the intention of securing access to the patented invention. Further, it shall be established that the proposed royalty or other consideration offered by the applicant did not meet the criteria for patentee reasonable terms as determined by prevailing industry standards and market conditions. The Controller may require both parties to submit detailed financial analyses substantiating their positions regarding appropriate compensation. Subject to this, the application will proceed under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "Bench" shall mean a constituted panel of judicial officers established under this Act for adjudicating disputes and exercising powers as provided herein. A Bench shall be comprised of such number of persons as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify; subject to the condition that at least one member of each Bench shall possess qualifications relevant to intellectual property law or a technical background related to semiconductor technology. The composition of a Bench may vary depending upon the nature and complexity of the matter before it, as determined by the presiding officer. Decisions of a Bench shall be made by a majority vote of the members present.

Where a photograph is made as a result of a performance, the performer shall have an exclusive right to authorize or prohibit the making of such photograph. This authorization extends to all subsequent reproductions, communications to the public, and any other acts restricted under this Act. Provided that, where the photograph is made incidentally during a performance intended primarily for another purpose, such as news reporting or artistic documentation, the performer’s rights shall be limited to preventing commercial exploitation without explicit consent. Further, if the making of the photograph constitutes fair dealing with the original performance, as determined by considerations of public interest and originality, this restriction may not apply. The right conferred herein is subject to any contractual agreements entered into prior to the creation of the makes performance photograph.

(1) The register referred to in section 6 shall be divided into
two Parts called respectively Part A and Part B.
(2) The particulars relating to the registration of the geographical indications shall be incorporated and
form Part A of the register in the prescribed manner.
(3) The particulars relating to the registration of the authorised users shall be incorporated and form
part of Part B of the register in the prescribed manner.

(1) When an application for registration of a variety (other than an essentially derived variety) has been accepted and either— (a) the application has not been opposed and the time of notice of opposition has expired; or (b) the application has been opposed and the opposition has been rejected, the Registrar shall register the variety. (2) On the registration of the variety (other than an essentially derived variety), the Registrar shall issue to the applicant a certificate of registration in the prescribed form and sealed with the seal of the Registry and send a copy thereof to the Authority for determination of benefit sharing and to such other authority, as may be prescribed, for information. The maximum time required by the Registrar for issuing the certificate of registration from the date of filing of the application for registration of a variety shall be such as may be prescribed.

An aggrieved party seeking remedies under this Act may apply to the relevant High Court demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising from an entry appearing in the Entry Register. Such application shall be accompanied by a sworn statement detailing the nature of the misleading impression created by the erroneous or incomplete information contained within the Entry Register document, and quantifying the resultant damages suffered. The court may order the rectification of any inaccurate entries upon being satisfied that such inaccuracies have caused, or are likely to cause, confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or character of goods or services. Further, the court shall possess jurisdiction to award compensation for losses incurred as a direct consequence of reliance placed on information presented in the Entry Register document, provided that the applicant proves reasonable diligence in verifying the accuracy of such information was not exercised.

(1) Where it appears to the Controller that the invention so far as claimed in any claim of the complete specification has been anticipated in the manner referred to in clause (a) of sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) of section 13, he may refuse to 5the application unless the applicant—
(a) shows to the satisfaction of the Controller that the priority date of the claim of his complete specification is not later than the date on which the relevant document was published; or
(b) amends his complete specification to the satisfaction of the Controller.
(2) If it appears to the Controller that the invention is claimed in a claim of any other complete specification referred to in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 13, he may, subject to the provisions hereinafter contained, direct that a reference to that other specification shall be inserted by way of notice to the public in the applicant's complete specification unless within such time as may be prescribed,—

If any party by whom notice of any opposition is given under this Act or by whom application is made to the Controller for the grant of a licence under a patent neither resides nor carries on business in India, the Controller may require him to give security for the costs of the proceedings, and in default of such security being given may treat the opposition or application as abandoned.

Any unauthorized transmission of a registered trade mark, or a substantial reproduction thereof, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, shall be deemed an infringement under this Act. Such transmission, whether by electronic means, telecommunication, or any other mode of conveyance, is strictly prohibited, subject to the provisions relating to fair use as determined by the Registrar. Any person found engaging in the transmission of counterfeit goods bearing a registered trade mark, or facilitating such transmission, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Furthermore, all infringing materials used in the transmission, including any apparatus employed, shall be subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. The burden of proving legitimate transmission rests with the accused. A second or subsequent offence shall attract enhanced penalties, including a minimum imprisonment term of one year.

A trade mark may be registered as a promotion trade mark subject to compliance with the conditions hereinafter prescribed. An application for registration as a promotion trade mark shall specify the goods or services in relation to which the promotion is conducted and the period during which such promotion is intended to operate, provided that this period shall not exceed one year from the date of registration. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the genuineness of the promotional activity and its connection with the underlying trade mark. Further, the applicant must satisfy the Registrar that the use of the trade mark as a promotion trade mark does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services. Any alteration to the promotional scheme requires prior approval from the Registrar.

Every person appointed under this Act shall be deemed
to be a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860).

Any person who, not being a registered proprietor of a registered trade mark or a duly licensed user thereof, uses in the course of trade, or for the purpose of any business, any colourable variation of the registered trade mark, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for each such infringement, and the goods bearing such mark shall be deemed to be counterfeit goods as provided herein. Where the infringement involves goods of a dangerous or counterfeit nature, the penalty shall not be less than one lakh rupees. The Court may, subject to the provisions of this Act, also grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further use of the mark and order the destruction of all infringing goods and materials used in the manufacture thereof. Any appeal against an order of penalty shall lie before the High Court, and shall be subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

For the purposes of this Act, an affidavit registered proprietor is defined as the individual or entity whose name appears on the Register of Trade Marks as the current and lawful owner of a trade mark, subject to any rights or interests recorded against it. Such proprietor shall be deemed to possess exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services specified in the registration, provided that this exclusivity is not affected by prior usage or other registered rights under this Act. An affidavit from the registered proprietor verifying the accuracy of information submitted relating to ownership transfer or alteration may be required as evidence for any application processed under this Act.

Any person alleging an offence relating to the use of a registered trade mark, or a mark deceptively similar thereto, shall submit a detailed statement of facts to the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of becoming aware of the alleged offence. The statement shall clearly identify the registered trade mark, the alleged infringing mark, and the nature of the unlawful activity. The Registry may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require the complainant to furnish further evidence or clarification. Where the Registry is satisfied that a prima facie case exists, it may initiate an inquiry and direct the alleged offender to submit a response. Failure to respond to such a direction, or to provide satisfactory evidence, may be considered an admission of the alleged offence and shall be recorded accordingly in the records of the Trade Marks Registry. Any order issued by the Registry shall be without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act.

(1) The Central Government shall establish, for the purposes of this Act, a Registry which shall be known as the Plant Varieties Registry. (2) The head office of the Plant Varieties Registry shall be located in the head office of the Authority, and for the purpose of facilitating the registration of varieties, there may be established, at such places, as the Authority may think fit, branch offices of the Registry.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, any person desiring to oppose such application may file a Notice of Opposition with the Registrar within the time period as prescribed. The Notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and shall be accompanied by the requisite fee. Upon receipt of a Notice of Opposition, the Registrar shall promptly serve a copy thereof on the applicant for registration.

The applicant for registration may, subject to any conditions specified by the Registrar, file a counterstatement in response to the Notice of Opposition within a period determined by regulations. The Registrar may, after giving both parties an opportunity of being heard, determine whether the grounds for opposition are sufficient to warrant the rejection or modification of the application. A notice opposition applicant shall be afforded due process as per rules framed under this Act.

Applications for registration of geographical indications shall be made to the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed, including detailed information regarding the quality, reputation or other characteristics of the goods which are claimed to derive their origin from the territory specified in the application. The central government shall, upon receiving an application, direct the Registrar to issue a public notice inviting objections within three months from the date of publication. Any objection received shall be considered by the Registrar and forwarded to the central government for determination. The specification accompanying the application shall clearly define the geographical boundaries and production methods relevant to the indication, as determined appropriate by the examining officer.

Any person aggrieved by an entry in the Designs Register, or by a failure to make an entry, may apply to the Controller for rectification of register. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The Controller shall afford the applicant and any other interested party an opportunity of being heard under this Act. Where the rectification sought involves a matter relating to priority established under the Budapest Treaty, the Controller shall consider evidence pertaining to international design applications and registrations. Failure to comply with procedural requirements regarding service of notice or representation may result in dismissal of the application. The Controller’s order concerning rectification register is final subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for registration of a trade mark relating to semiconductor integrated circuits shall be examined to ascertain whether the proposed marks are distinctive in their class and as between such circuits. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness where the initial assessment indicates a lack thereof, provided that such evidence satisfies the criteria established under this Act concerning reputation and consumer recognition. An application registered proprieto shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the register, subject to any limitations imposed during registration relating to specific functionalities of the integrated circuit. Any challenge to the validity of such a registration must be brought within the prescribed timeframe and adhere to procedural requirements as provided herein.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall be subject to renewal upon expiry of the initial registration period of ten years, and such renewal may be effected by application to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. The applicant shall demonstrate continued bona fide use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, failing which the renewal request may be disallowed. Safeguards prescribed register relating to associated rights, including but not limited to licensing agreements and assignments, must accompany any application for renewal where such arrangements are extant. Provided that, if a valid objection is raised concerning potential conflict with prior rights, the Registry may suspend processing of the renewal until resolution of said dispute as provided herein. Any alteration to the registered trade mark during renewal shall be treated as a separate registration process and subject to examination anew. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in cancellation of the trade mark.

(1) Where an application for registration of a variety has been accepted absolutely or subject to conditions or limitations under sub-section (1) of section 20, the Registrar shall, as soon as after its acceptance, cause such application together with the conditions or limitations, if any, subject to which it has been accepted and the specifications of the variety for registration of which such application is made including its photographs or drawings, to be advertised in the prescribed manner calling objections from the persons interested in the matter. (2) Any person may, within three months from the date of the advertisement of an application for registration on payment of the prescribed fees, give notice in writing in the prescribed manner, to the Registrar of his opposition to the registration.

(1) Any person aggrieved by the absence or omission from the register of any entry, or by any entry made in the register without sufficient cause, or by any entry wrongly remaining on the register, or by any error or defect in any entry in the register, may apply in the prescribed manner to the Appellate Board or to the Registrar, and the Appellate Board or the Registrar, as the case may be, may make such order for making, expunging or varying the entry as it may think it. (2) The Appellate Board or the Registrar may in any proceedings under this section decide any question that may be necessary or expedient to decide in connection with the rectification of the register. (3) The Appellate Board or the Registrar, of its own motion, may, after giving notice in the prescribed manner to the parties concerned and after giving them an opportunity of being heard, make any order referred to in sub-section (1). (4) Any order of the Appellate Board rectifying the register shall direct that notice of the rectification shall be served upon the Registrar in the prescribed manner who shall upon receipt of such notice, rectify the register accordingly.

Where a Trade Mark owner desires to grant a license for use of their registered trade mark, such license shall be documented in writing and executed by both the Trade Mark owner and the proposed Contracting Party. The license agreement must clearly specify the goods or services relating to which the right to use is granted, the geographical territory covered by the license, and the duration of the license period. Further, it shall detail any restrictions imposed on the manner of use, including quality control measures that the Contracting Party must adhere to, as provided herein. Assignment of a trade mark license requires prior written consent from the Trade Mark owner unless the original agreement expressly permits assignment without such consent. Any subsequent transfer or encumbrance affecting the rights granted under this license shall be void unless approved by the Trade Mark owner in writing.

Where an application for grant of Plant Variety Rights is rejected by the Registrar under this Act, and the applicant claims that the rejection is based on a determination that the variety is an essentially derived variety from another variety, the applicant may appeal to the Authority Appellate Board. The Appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of rejection. Upon receipt of such an appeal, the Authority Appellate Board shall give notice to the Registrar and any other party directly affected by the decision appealed against, affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard. The Board may, after considering all evidence presented, confirm, vary or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Any determination regarding whether a variety is an essentially derived variety shall be based on the criteria as provided herein, taking into account traits and characteristics demonstrably attributable to the original variety.

If any person contravenes the provisions of section 129, 4he shall be liable to penalty, which may extend to five lakh rupees, and in case of the continuing default, a further penalty of one thousand rupees for every day after the first during which such default continues.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall, prior to acceptance of the application, cause a notice of the application to be published in the Trade Marks Journal, as prescribed under the rules made by the Controller. The Controller may, however, require the applicant to additionally notify any relevant trade association or industry body, if deemed necessary for ascertaining potential conflicts with existing marks or to facilitate opposition proceedings. Such notification shall be conducted in a manner specified by the Controller and shall include details of the mark, goods or services covered, and the applicant’s particulars. Failure to comply with the requirements to notify, where mandated, may render the application liable to be rejected, subject to a reasonable opportunity being granted to remedy the deficiency. Provided that, the Controller shall not impose a notification requirement where the mark is clearly devoid of any distinguishing character.

An application for registration of a registered layout design shall be deemed to satisfy the requirements of this Act if it contains a clear and accurate representation of the integrated circuit layout-design, accompanied by a declaration verifying its originality and absence of prior publication. The Controller may reject an application if he is satisfied that the layout-design lacks sufficient novelty or infringes upon any existing right under this Act or any other law for the time being in force. Furthermore, where a layout-design incorporates elements already registered as a separate registered layout design, the applicant shall provide explicit details of such incorporation and demonstrate compliance with the provisions regarding derivative works as provided herein. The Registrar may require additional documentation to ascertain these conditions are met before proceeding with examination.

(2) The Appellate Board shall, on receipt of an application under sub-section (1), give notice to the opposite parties in the prescribed manner and after giving them an opportunity of being heard, make such order as it may deem fit regarding cancellation of registration: Provided that where the ground of cancellation has been established with respect only to a part of a layout-design, the Board shall cancel only such part and the remaining part of the layout-design if capable of performing as a semiconductor integrated circuit shall be retained as registered on the register in the name of the registered proprietor of such layout-design.

For the purposes of this Act, "imported goods" shall mean any goods brought into India from outside India by sea, land or air, and includes goods which have been unloaded from a vessel or aircraft at an Indian port or aerodrome but are still under customs control as provided under the Customs Act 1962. Goods so imported shall be deemed to bear the mark of the proprietor unless it is established that such goods were genuinely traded in their country of origin and not for the purpose of defrauding any person under this Act, or otherwise infringing rights vested herein. Any alteration made to imported goods after entry into India may render them liable to seizure as per regulations prescribed therein.

For the purposes of this Act, an “accused offence” shall mean any act or omission constituting a violation of section 27, section 29, section 30, or section 51, as provided herein. Where such an accused offence is alleged to have been committed by a corporate entity, the responsibility for the said offence shall be deemed to lie upon the directors, managers, and other officers of the corporation who were directly involved in the decision-making process leading to the infringement. Nothing in this definition shall preclude the imposition of liability on any individual or entity beyond those specifically identified as being part of that decision-making process, subject to demonstrating their direct participation in the accused offence.

Any order passed by the Tribunal affirming or reversing a decision of the Controller shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The aggrieved party shall have the right to present evidence and arguments before the member appointed bench as provided herein.

Where any person, without authorization from the copyright owner, undertakes reprography of works protected under this Act for commercial purposes, such person shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the extent of infringement. The amount of damages shall take into account not only the reasonable royalties that would have been paid had proper licenses been obtained but also any demonstrable loss suffered by the copyright holder as a direct consequence of the unauthorized reprography.  Further, where an infringing act is committed repeatedly or on a substantial scale, the court may award exemplary damages to deter future violations. Any individual found guilty of such infringement shall be subject to criminal proceedings and penalties as provided herein. The right to seek injunctive relief against further acts of reprography remains explicitly reserved to copyright owners.

Any person who, without the permission of the registered proprietor, manufactures, imports, sells, or distributes an Integrated Circuit, in whole or part, embodying a layout-design registered as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not less than ten lakh rupees but not exceeding five crore rupees, or imprisonment for a term not less than two years but not exceeding five years, or both. Where the violation relates to a layout-design registered for a semi-conductor chip intended for use in a national security application, the penalty shall not be less than twenty lakh rupees. Any material used in the manufacture of such infringing Integrated Circuit, and all articles incorporating the same, shall be deemed counterfeit goods and subject to seizure and destruction under the provisions of this Act. The proprietor of a registered layout-design may also seek an injunction restraining the infringer from further acts of infringement, and may recover damages for any loss suffered as a direct result of such infringement. Any appeal against an order of penalty shall lie before the designated court within thirty days of the order.

For the purposes of this Act, "patentee consideration royalties" means any sum or benefit granted by a patentee to another party in exchange for facilitating the manufacture, use, or sale of the patented invention within India, whether such grant is direct or indirect, and may include discounts, rebates, or other concessions offered as part of a commercial arrangement. An order adjudicating officer determining the reasonableness of patentee consideration royalties shall consider prevailing industry practices, the nature of the invention, and any agreements entered into between the parties concerned. Such determination shall be binding subject to appeal under this Act.

Where a copyright subsists in any work created by a company, the assignment or licensing of such copyright shall require certification from an approved proprietor certification body prior to its registration with the Copyright Office. Such certification shall attest to the authorization of the transfer by the requisite corporate governance structures and demonstrate adherence to internal policies regarding intellectual property management. A company may grant exclusive licenses under this Act, but any such license shall clearly define the scope of rights transferred and the duration of exclusivity, subject to a royalty obligation payable to the company proportionate to net revenue derived from the licensed work. Further, where a proprietor certification is required, failure to obtain it prior to assignment will render the assignee liable for damages as determined by a civil court.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be deceptively similar to another trade mark if, taking the whole mark as a whole, it is likely to cause confusion or deception as to the goods or services in relation to which the marks are used. In determining whether marks are deceptively similar, due regard shall be given to the overall impression created by the marks, including the visual, aural, and conceptual characteristics. Where a mark incorporates elements identical to a previously registered mark, but with minor variations, such variations shall not be considered sufficient to negate a finding of deceptive similarity, unless those variations are substantial and demonstrably alter the overall character of the mark. A mark shall not be considered deceptively similar if the prior mark is well-known and the subsequent mark is used on entirely dissimilar goods or services, provided that such use does not take unfair advantage of, or injure the reputation of, the prior mark as provided herein. Any party alleging deceptive similarity bears the onus of proving such similarity.

The design register shall be maintained at the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry and shall contain particulars of all registered layout-designs, including the name and address of the applicant, the title of the layout-design, the date of filing the application, and the date of registration. Any person may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, inspect the design register and obtain a certified copy of any entry therein. A layout-design, once registered, shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, or commercially use the layout-design. Provided that, the registration in the design register shall be subject to the provisions relating to revocation, and any rights conferred thereby may be subject to licensing arrangements as provided herein. The Registry may, at its discretion, refuse inspection in cases where it deems disclosure would be prejudicial to national security.

Where a notice of intended rectification of the Register of Patents is served upon any person claiming an interest in the patent, such person shall have a period of sixty days from the date of service within which to file objections. Any objection filed after the expiry of said period shall be deemed inadmissible and summarily dismissed by the Controller. Failure to comply with the requirements for serving a rectification register notice as provided herein shall render the application liable to rejection without further consideration. The Controller may, subject to due process, order the rectification of the Register if satisfied that an error or misstatement has occurred and that such correction is necessary to reflect the true status of the patent. Repeated frivolous objections may attract penalties under this Act.

An advertisement application registration shall be deemed invalid if the layout-design incorporated therein does not demonstrably exhibit originality, subject to the provisions regarding minor variations. The applicant shall furnish a detailed technical description accompanying the advertisement application, outlining the functionality and intended use of the integrated circuit layout-design. Further, the Registrar may require submission of additional documentation substantiating the claim of novelty, provided that such request is made within sixty days of receipt of the initial advertisement application. Any alteration to the layout-design subsequent to its initial advertisement shall necessitate a fresh advertisement application registration, as provided herein. The applicant must also declare compliance with all relevant export control regulations pertaining to the integrated circuit design.

A permitted register trade mark is defined as a trade mark that has been entered upon the Register under this Act and remains so until removed therefrom or subject to an order for rectification. For the purposes of determining entitlement to relief in proceedings concerning a permitted register trade mark, such registration shall be deemed to confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights within India relating to the goods or services specified in the register. A trade mark may be considered for inclusion on the permitted register if it is distinctive in its nature and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings as provided herein.
A certification trade mark shall not be assignable or transmissible otherwise than with the consent of the Registrar, for which application shall be made in writing in the prescribed manner.

A complete specification filed under this Act shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficient for a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect, and shall be accompanied by such drawings as are necessary for that purpose. Where an applicant claims priority from one or more earlier applications filed in a convention country, such claim shall be made in the complete specification and shall specify the priority date and the country in which the earlier application was filed. The applicant shall, within the prescribed period, furnish a certified copy of the earlier application, duly authenticated by the competent authority of the convention country, as evidence of the priority date claimed. Failure to furnish such certified copy may render the claim of priority ineffective, subject to the Controller granting an extension of time for sufficient cause. Any publication occurring after the priority date, but before the filing date in India, may be considered novelty-destroying, unless it relates to knowledge already in the public domain.

For the purposes of this Act, “industrial application” shall denote the use of a design in connection with articles manufactured by industrial processes, including any handcraft, but does not include methods or principles of construction or arrangement as well as any purely functional feature of an article necessary for its intended purpose. A design capable of industrial application must be new or original, and shall not be identical with any design which is, at the time of registration, known or has been previously published in India or elsewhere. Subject to the provisions herein, a registered design confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to apply that design to articles in the class of articles for which it is registered, and to manufacture, import, and sell articles bearing such design. Any act done without the consent of the proprietor shall constitute an infringement.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of trade marks, distinctly identifying each mark and its proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark used in India may apply for registration india in the prescribed manner, furnishing details of the mark, goods or services to which it relates, and the applicant’s particulars. The Registry may, prior to accepting an application, require clarification or amendment to ensure compliance with the requirements of this Act. Upon acceptance, the application shall be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal, allowing for opposition by any aggrieved party. Should an opposition be filed, the Registry shall conduct an inquiry, affording both the applicant and the opponent a reasonable opportunity to be heard. A trade mark, once registered, confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified, and shall be subject to renewal as provided herein, failing which it may be removed from the register. Where an application for compulsory licensing is filed under this Act, the Examining Authority shall determine whether the claimed use of the plant variety constitutes a substantial and necessary purpose. The applicant bears the burden of demonstrating that the asserted need aligns with the criteria as provided herein, particularly concerning public interest and equitable access to seeds. Any dispute regarding the validity of such claims purposes may be referred to an Appellate Board constituted under this Act. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to a further appeal to the High Court on grounds limited to questions of law pertaining to the interpretation of this Act or any rules made thereunder. The Authority may require additional evidence to substantiate the applicant's assertions and assess potential impacts on registered breeders.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark desiring to avail of the provisions for informing international organizations regarding a relevant licensing arrangement, or a change in ownership, shall submit a prescribed form to the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by the requisite fee as detailed in the Schedule. The Registry, upon verification of the submitted documentation, shall, within a period not exceeding thirty days, transmit the information to the designated international bodies, including the World Intellectual Property Organization. Should a dispute arise concerning the validity of the trade mark relation underpinning the licensing agreement, or ownership transfer, the aggrieved party may apply to the High Court for appropriate relief. Provided that, no such application shall be entertained unless the applicant demonstrates a prima facie case of irreparable harm. Failure to accurately inform these organizations, or providing misleading information, may render the proprietor liable to penalties as provided herein, including potential revocation of the trade mark registration. The Trade Marks Registry retains the right to request additional documentation to ensure compliance.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a person shall not manufacture, import, or sell any layout-design that infringes upon the exclusive right of another person in the design. An infringement occurs where a substantially similar layout-design is created, without authorization, and such creation constitutes an adaptation of the original work. The determination of substantial similarity shall consider the overall impression of the layout-design, taking into account its component elements and their arrangement. Where a licensee manufactures a layout-design in accordance with the terms of the license, such manufacture shall not constitute infringement under this Act. However, any subsequent assignment or modification of that licensed design requires explicit consent from the original registrant of the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act 2000.

Any assignment of patent rights arising from a licensing agreement shall vest in the assignee subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within such agreement, provided that any royalty payments due to the original patentee remain enforceable against both parties. Where claims relating to improvements on an already patented invention are assigned independently of the primary patent, the assignee of the improvement claims may exercise those rights only insofar as they do not infringe upon the existing patent held by another party, and shall be liable for any such infringement. A licensee acquiring exclusive rights to specific claims within a patent portfolio must demonstrate sufficient consideration has been exchanged, and evidence thereof maintained for a period of five years from the date of assignment. Failure to adequately document such consideration may render the assignment voidable under this Act. The scope of assigned claims shall be determined by their literal meaning as interpreted in light of the specification accompanying the original patent application.

Any person who falsely applies for the registration mentioned clause to a trade mark, or knowingly makes a false representation in an application, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a registered trade mark is used in a manner likely to deceive or cause confusion, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as he may deem fit, direct that the mark be altered or that its registration be suspended for a period not exceeding one year. Any aggrieved person may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the wrongful use of a registered trade mark, and the Court may grant such injunction, with or without conditions, as it thinks fit. Provided that no injunction shall be granted if the plaintiff has delayed unreasonably in seeking relief, and such delay has caused prejudice to the defendant. All fines collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

(1) A person shall be deemed to falsify a trade mark who, either,—
(a) without the assent of the proprietor of the trade mark makes that trade mark or a deceptively similar mark; or
(b) falsifies any genuine trade mark, whether by alteration, addition, effacement or otherwise. (2) A person shall be deemed to falsely apply to goods or services a trade mark who, without the assent of the proprietor of the trade mark,—

(b) uses any package bearing a mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to the trade mark of such proprietor, for the purpose of packing, filling or wrapping therein any goods o ther than the genuine goods of the proprietor of the trade mark. (3) Any trade mark falsified as mentioned in sub -section ( 1) or falsely applied as mentioned in sub-section (2), is in this Act referred to as a false trade mark. (4) In any prosecutio n for falsifying a trade mark or falsely applying a trade mark to goods or services, the burden of proving the assent of the proprietor shall lie on the accused.

(1) The registered proprietor of a trade mark may apply in the prescribed manner to the Registrar for leave to add to or alter the trade mark in any manner not substantially affecting the identity thereof, a nd the Registrar may refuse leave or may grant it on such terms and subject to such limitations as he may think fit.
(2) The Registrar may cause an application under this section to be advertised in the prescribed manner in any case where it appears to him that it is expedient so to do, and where he does so, if within the prescribed time from the date of the advertisement any person gives notice to the Registrar in the prescribed manner of opposition to the application, the Registrar shall, after hearing th e parties if so required, decide the matter.

Where an invention is disclosed as being derived from an earlier application filed in an invention convention country, and it appears to the Controller that the applicant has failed to comply with the requirements regarding the priority claim under this Act, the Controller may issue a notice of objection. Such notice shall specify the particulars of the non-compliance and afford the applicant an opportunity of being heard. If, after such hearing, the Controller is satisfied that the failure constitutes a material deficiency in the application, he may reject the patent application entirely or require amendment to ensure full compliance with the provisions relating to convention applications. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.
