CHAPTER II THE REGISTER AND CONDITIONS OF REGISTRATION

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to copyright ownership, licensing, or infringement, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board established for the purposes of this Act. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the impugned order, subject to condonation of delay upon sufficient cause being shown to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall have the power to call for the records pertaining to any case before it and may, if deemed necessary, direct a fresh examination of evidence or require additional submissions from the parties concerned. Provided that no appeal shall lie against an order relating to interim injunctions unless such injunction continues for a period exceeding six months. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for rights of review as provided herein, and may be enforced in the same manner as decrees of a civil court. The Appellate Board may also impose costs on parties appearing before it, subject to principles of fairness and equity.

Where any goods are seized by an officer authorized under the Customs Act, 1962, and it is determined that such seizure relates to a registered trade mark or a deceptively similar representation thereof, the owner of the trade mark shall be notified in writing within thirty days of the seizure. The proprietor may, subject to appeal before the Appellate Authority as provided herein, challenge the determination of infringement relating to imported goods. Any order made under this Act concerning seized goods is further subject to judicial review by a High Court if it appears that the Customs officer acted without due process or exceeded their authority in interpreting provisions pertaining to trade mark rights. The aggrieved party may petition for relief within ninety days of notification.

A patent, as provided herein, shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive right to make, use, sell and import the invention throughout India for a period specified under this Act. Such exclusivity is subject to diligent working of the patented invention within a reasonable time after sealing of the patent, failing which revocation proceedings may be initiated. A registered user trade, established through licensing agreements approved by the Controller, permits another party to utilize the patented invention in exchange for adequate remuneration determined as per regulations. The scope of any such license shall not extend beyond the terms and conditions explicitly outlined within the agreement and recorded with the Patent Office; provided that, the patentee retains ultimate authority over the quality of articles made under said license.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. The Appellate Board shall consider any objections raised by interested parties, provided that such objections are filed within thirty days of the publication of notice of the appeal. Further, a mark registered proprietor is obligated to maintain records pertaining to the use and exploitation of the registered trade mark, detailing geographical areas and goods or services in relation to which it is used. Failure to provide these records upon request by the Registrar shall render the mark liable for removal from the Register under provisions as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “proprietor certification” means the use of a mark by an individual or body who has been granted exclusive right to certify that goods or services meet specified standards, and who is registered as such under this Act. Such proprietor shall be entitled to prevent the use of their certification trade mark by any person not authorised by them in writing, provided that the use by the unauthorized party indicates a representation that the certified goods or services conform to the standards defined by the proprietor. The proprietor may specify conditions for continued certification and may revoke such right if those conditions are not met.

Any person possessing copyright in a work may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant an exclusive licence for the doing of any act which would otherwise constitute an infringement of that copyright. Such exclusive licence shall be construed as transferring to the licensee all rights necessary for exercising the licensed acts, save where expressly reserved by the licensor. Where an exclusive licence is granted, the licensor may not itself exploit the copyrighted work in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the license, provided that such inconsistency does not prejudice the licensee’s exercise of their rights. 

Any dispute concerning the scope or validity of an exclusive licence shall be determined by the appropriate High Court having jurisdiction over the matter. The grant of an exclusive licence may specify territorial limitations and duration; absent any such specification, it shall be deemed to extend throughout India for the remaining term of copyright subsisting in the work. A non-exclusive license does not confer these rights.

(1) Where the offence charged under section 56 is in relation to a registered layout-design and the accused pleads that the registration of the layout-design is invalid, the following procedure shall be followed:— (1)(a) if the court is satisfied that such defence is prima facie tenable, it shall not proceed with the charge but shall adjourn the proceeding for three months from the date on which the plea of accused is recorded to enable the accused to file an application before the Appellate Board under this Act, for the rectification of the register on the ground that the registration is invalid; (1)(b) if the accused proves to the court that he has made such application within the time so limited or within such further time as the time court may for sufficient cause may allow, the further proceedings in the prosecution shall stand stayed till the disposal of such application for rectification; (1)(c) if within a period of three months or within such extended time as may be allowed by the court the accused fails to apply to the Appellate Board for rectification of the register, the court shall proceed with the case as if the registration were valid .

(1) In the case of resale for a price exceeding ten thousand rupees, of the original copy of a painting, sculpture or drawing, or of the original manuscript of a literary or dramatic work or musical work, the author of such work if he was the fir st owner of rights under section 17 or his legal heirs shall, notwithstanding any assignm ent of copyright in such work, have a right to share in the resale price of such original copy or manuscript in accordance with the provisions of this section: Provided that such right shall cease to exist on the expiration of the term of copyright in the work. (2) The share referred to in sub -section (1) shall be such as the Appellate Board may fix and the decision of the Appellate Board in this behalf shall be final: Provided that the Appellate Board may fix different shares for different classes of work: Provided further that in no case shall the share exceed ten percent, of the resale price. (3) If any dispute arises regarding the right conferred by this section, it shall be referred to the Appellate Board whose decision shall be final.

Any person claiming an invention far claimed under this Act shall furnish a detailed statement of the matter constituting the invention for which protection is sought, demonstrating a clear and concise disclosure of the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. The statement shall be accompanied by one or more claims defining the scope of the invention, and each claim shall be supported by matter in the description. Where an invention comprises a process, the description shall clearly explain the steps involved and the parameters necessary for its successful implementation. Provided that, if the invention relates to a microorganism, a deposit of the microorganism with a recognised depository institution shall be considered sufficient disclosure, subject to the provisions herein. Failure to adequately define the invention far claimed, or to provide sufficient supporting detail, may render the application liable to be refused. The Controller may require the applicant to amend the claims to accurately reflect the invention disclosed.

The Registrar shall maintain a public register of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs as provided herein and may prescribe such forms and procedures for registration as are necessary to ensure accurate record keeping. Any person desiring to obtain registration of a layout-design shall submit an application in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee, to the Registrar, demonstrating originality and applicability to manufacture. The manner applying registrar includes verification of the applicant’s claim of ownership and a technical examination to ascertain whether the submitted layout-design satisfies the criteria for registrability under this Act. Should the Registrar deem further clarification necessary, they may issue a notice requiring the applicant to provide additional information or evidence within a specified timeframe. Subject to satisfactory completion of these procedures, the Registrar shall register the layout-design and assign a registration number; however, refusal of registration will be communicated in writing with reasons stated. The Register shall be open for inspection by any member of the public upon payment of the prescribed fee, facilitating transparency and promoting innovation within the semiconductor industry.

(3) In case of an application filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty designating India and claiming priority from a previously filed application in India, the provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2) shall apply as if the previously filed application were the basic application:
Provided that a request for examination under section 11B shall be made only for one of the applications filed in India.

The proprietor of a trade mark registered under this Act shall have the right to maintain an action for infringement of such trade mark, notwithstanding any other right of action the proprietor may have independently of this Act. Where a registered trade mark is used by a person other than the registered proprietor, and such use constitutes an infringement as provided herein, the proprietor may, at his option, seek an injunction restraining such use. Any contract restraining the use of a trade mark shall be void, except where such restraint is reasonably necessary to protect the goodwill of the proprietor. A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the trade mark and the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark in part or whole. Assignment of a trade mark shall be subject to the conditions specified in the register and any applicable rules. Provided that, assignment of a trade mark shall not affect any existing rights or liabilities. The registrar may, upon application, record the assignment of a proprietor trade mark.

Any person desiring to commercially exploit a copyrighted work through licensing or other means, shall register the terms of such exploitation with the Registrar of Copyrights to ensure proper accounting of remuneration due to the owner. Registration of royalty rates is mandatory for all licenses exceeding a period of one year, and shall include details regarding the basis of calculation, frequency of payment, and any deductions permissible as provided herein. The copyright owner may, subject to mutual agreement, specify different royalty structures for various modes of exploitation including reproduction, distribution, public performance, or adaptation. Provided that where a license is terminated prematurely by either party, final accounting of all accrued royalties shall be completed within ninety days from the date of termination and any dispute regarding such accounting shall be resolved through arbitration. Failure to register the terms may result in penalties as determined by the Registrar.

A proprietor seeking to grant a license relating to a registered trade mark shall execute a written instrument specifying the scope and duration of such license, including particulars of the licensed goods or services. Such license may be granted exclusively or non-exclusively, as determined by the grantor. Any assignment of registration under this Act shall include all rights and privileges pertaining to the mark, subject to any limitations expressly stated in the assignment deed. Where a trade mark has been assigned, subsequent licenses granted by the assignee shall remain valid unless explicitly revoked through written notice served upon the licensee. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the validity of any such license or assignment, provided that this requirement shall not impede legitimate commercial transactions. Further, sub-licensing is permitted only with prior consent from the original proprietor and documented as part of the initial registration record.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars as may be prescribed and include a copy of the layout-design in a form specified by the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the layout-design, its functionality, or any related documentation deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall assign it a registration number and record the date of filing. Any modification to the layout-design after the initial filing must be disclosed to the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated prior to publication. Failure to do so may result in objections during examination. The applicant is responsible for ensuring accuracy of all submitted details; any discrepancies identified by the registrar shall necessitate correction as provided herein.

(1) Subject to the provisions of section 19, when an application for registration of a trade mark has been accepted and either— (a) the application has not been opposed and the time for notice of opposition has expired; or (b) the application has been opposed and the opposition has been deci ded in favour of the applicant, the Registrar shall, unless the Central Government otherwise directs, register the said trade mark within eighteen months of the filing of the application and the trade mark when registered shall be registered as of the date of the making of the said application and that date shall, subject to the provisions of section 154, be deemed to be the date of registration.
(2) On the registration of a trade mark, the Registrar shall issue to the applicant a certificate in the prescribed form of the registration thereof, sealed with the seal of the Trade Marks Registry.
(3) Where registration of a trade mark is not comple ted within twelve months from the date of the application by reason of default on the part of the applicant, the Registrar may, after giving notice to the applicant in the prescribed manner, treat the application as abandoned unless it is completed within the time specified in that behalf in the notice.
(4) The Registrar may amend the register or a certificate of registration for the purpose of correcting a clerical error or an obvious mistake.

Any person aggrieved by any act of the registrar copyrights inconsistent with the provisions of this Act may, within thirty days from the date of such act, prefer an appeal to the High Court. Such appeal shall be in the form of a petition and shall set forth the grounds upon which it is based, and shall be duly verified. The High Court may, after giving the registrar copyrights an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the act complained of, or may remit the case back to the registrar copyrights for further consideration. Where an appeal relates to a matter also concerning a registered trade mark, the Trade Marks Registry may be directed by the High Court to provide relevant records or expertise to assist in the proceedings, subject to appropriate confidentiality undertakings. Failure to prefer an appeal within the stipulated time shall not preclude a civil suit for the same cause of action, provided that the court finds sufficient cause for the delay. Any order of the High Court under this provision shall be final and binding.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, the proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement against any person who, without authorization, applies a manufactured notification specifying the trademark or a confusingly similar representation in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those in respect of which the trade mark is registered. Such manufactured notifications shall be deemed to be acts of false representation under this Act, and the proprietor may seek an injunction restraining the use of such notifications, together with damages for any loss suffered by reason of the infringement. Provided that a genuine user defense may be raised if the unauthorized application of the manufactured notification was made prior to the date of registration and constitutes honest descriptive use relating to the characteristics of the goods or services.

Any assignment of a patented invention, or any interest therein, shall be in writing and duly executed by or on behalf of the assignor and assignee. Such assignment shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall not operate to convey any right to exploit the invention in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the patent. Where a patented invention incorporates elements protected by copyright, the assignment of the patent does not automatically transfer copyright ownership; separate assignment of such copyright shall be necessary, and the terms governing the copyright may differ from those governing the patent. A licensee of a patented invention may, with the explicit consent of the patent holder, sub-license the invention, provided that such sub-license is recorded with the appropriate authority as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding assignment or licensing may render the transaction voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. The patent holder retains the right to seek equitable relief against any unauthorized exploitation of the patented invention, even after assignment.

(1) Any person who circumvents an effective technological measures applied for the purpose of protecting any of the rights conferred by this Ac t, with the intention of infringing such rights, shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years and shall also be liable to fine. (2) Nothing in sub-section (1) shall prevent any person from,— (a) doing anything referred to therein for a purpose not expressly prohibited by this Act: Provided that any person facilitating circumvention by another person of a technological measure for such a purpose shall maintain a complete record of such other person including his name, address and all r elevant particulars necessary to identify him and the purpose for which he has been facilitated; or (b) doing anything necessary to conduct encryption research using a lawfully obtained encrypted copy; or (c) conducting any lawful investigation; or (d) doing anything necessary for the purpose of testing the security of a computer system or a computer network with the authorisation of its owner; or (e) operator; or (f) doing anything necess ary to circumvent technological measures intended for identificatio n or surveillance of a user; or (g) taking measures necessary in the interest of national security.

An application for registration of a design may be filed by any person claiming to be the owner of the design or by any manufacturer authorized by the claimant. Where an application is presented by a person other than the true and first inventor, he shall provide satisfactory evidence to substantiate his claim under this Act. The Controller shall, upon receiving such an application, initiate proceedings prosecution in accordance with the prescribed procedures. Upon successful completion of these proceedings and satisfaction that the design is registrable, the registration proprietor shall be entered into the Register of Designs. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the relevant appellate authority as provided herein.

Where an applicant files a provisional specification disclosing the invention for which patent protection is sought, such specification may include a provisional specification claim relating to a particular aspect or feature of the invention. The acceptance of a provisional specification shall not be construed as an indication that the claimed subject matter is novel or non-obvious under this Act. Upon filing a complete specification within the prescribed time limit following the provisional application, the applicant shall clearly indicate the relationship between the claims in the complete specification and the disclosures made in the earlier provisional specification claim. Failure to do so may result in objections being raised during examination of the patent application. The Controller may require the applicant to amend or clarify any such indication if it is deemed insufficient for establishing a clear link as provided herein.

(2) In any suit for infringement of a patent the court may, if it thinks fit, refuse to grant any damages or an account of profits in respect of any infringement committed after a failure to pay any renewal fee within the prescribed period and before any extension of that period.
(3) Where an amendment of a specification by way of disclaimer, correction or explanation has been allowed under this Act after the publication of the specification, no damages or account of profits shall be granted in any proceedings in respect of the use of the invention before the date of the decision allowing the amendment, unless the court is satisfied that the specification as originally published was framed in good faith and with reasonable skill and knowledge.
(4) Nothing in this section shall affect the power of the court to grant an injunction in any suit for infringement of a patent.

Where an invention relating to pharmaceuticals is patented under this Act, the Central Government may, subject to conditions specified therein, require the patentee to grant a license to any interested party willing to manufacture and sell the pharmaceutical product within India. Such requirement shall be predicated upon a determination that the patented invention is not available to the public at affordable prices or in sufficient quantities. The terms of such compulsory license, including royalty payments to the patent holder, shall be determined by the Controller, taking into account factors such as the nature of the invention and the extent of exploitation thereof. A reasonable period shall be allowed for the patentee to comply with a licensing requirement before enforcement actions may be initiated. Provided that any assignment or sub-license granted subsequent to the initial patent grant shall remain subject to these provisions.

For the purposes of this Act, “notice” with reference to any communication required or permitted to be given by or to any party shall mean a written document delivered personally or sent by registered post or recorded delivery. The manner issuing notice shall conform to the forms prescribed by the Trade Marks Registry and published in the Official Gazette. Such notice is deemed received on the date of personal delivery, or, where dispatched by post, seven days from the date of posting. Provided that any notice required under this Act may be served electronically, subject to verification protocols as determined by the Central Government.

Any act concerning a registered trade mark, including assignment, transmission, mortgage, or licensing, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and must be registered with the Trade Marks Registry to be fully enforceable against third parties. A registered act, if not duly recorded, may be considered voidable at the discretion of the Registry. The Registry shall maintain a public index of all registered acts, accessible for inspection subject to prescribed fees. Any person intending to record a registered act shall submit the necessary documentation, including a certified copy of the instrument and a statement of consideration, if any. Provided that, failure to register a transmission of ownership within six months of the event may attract penalties as prescribed herein. The Registrar may require further evidence or clarification to ensure the validity of the registered act and compliance with this Act.

Where a work has been reproduced without authorization from the copyright holder, and such reproduction substantially replicates the original work’s protected elements, it shall be deemed an infringing copy. Provided that, where the alleged infringing copy incorporates only minor alterations to the original work's arrangement or presentation, and those alterations do not constitute transformative creativity as defined under this Act, a determination of infringement may require consideration of whether such alterations were undertaken in good faith for purposes of adaptation or improvement. Further, if the reproduction was made solely for private use and is not offered for commercial gain, it shall be subject to review regarding potential exemptions as provided herein. Any party claiming an infringing copy must demonstrate proof of copyright ownership and evidence of unauthorized reproduction.

An application for rectification register may be filed by any person claiming an interest in a registered design, or by the proprietor of a design that is substantially similar to a design already on record. Such applications shall specify the particulars of the entry sought to be rectified and the grounds upon which it is claimed that the entry is erroneous or otherwise requires amendment. Where the application relates to a package incorporating a registered design, the applicant must clearly delineate the elements constituting the design as applied to said package in the rectification request. The Controller may require further information or clarification regarding the proposed rectification. Provided that the application complies with all requirements under this Act and the rules made thereunder, it shall be processed according to established procedures.

(3) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint; and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Act, and any reference in any such provision to the commencement of this Act shall be construed as a reference to the coming into force of that provision.

The Court trying any offence under this Act may, whether the alleged offender is convicted or not, order that all copies of the work or all plates in the possession of the alleged offender, which appear to it to be infringing copies, or plates for the purpose of making infringing copies, be delivered up to the owner of the copyright or may make such order as it may deem fit regarding the disposal of such copies of plates.

All orders of the Controller giving directions as to secrecy as well as all orders of the Central Government under this Chapter shall be final and shall not be called in question in any court on any ground whatsoever.

An applicant seeking grant of an application patent shall, upon request by any third party demonstrating legitimate industrial interest, provide a reasoned explanation regarding the scope and terms proposed for compulsory licensing under this Act. Such request must specify the nature of the technological field involved and the potential public benefit to be derived from the license. The Controller may, after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, direct the applicant to negotiate in good faith with the requesting party concerning a non-exclusive license on patent protected terms. Any assignment or transmission of the application patent shall include a covenant binding the assignee to adhere to any existing compulsory licensing arrangements previously agreed upon by the original applicant. Failure to comply with such directions may render the patent liable for revocation as provided herein.

(1) Subject to such co nditions as may be prescribed,— (a) a copyright society may accept from an author and other owners of right exclusive authorisation to administer any right in any work by issue of licences or collection of licence fees or both; and (b) an author and other owners of right shall have the right to withdraw such authorisation without prejudice to the rights of the copyright society under any contract. (2) It shall be competent for a copyright society to enter into agreement with any foreign society or organisation administering rights corresponding to rights under this Act, to entrust to such foreign society or organisation the administration in any foreign country of rights administered by the said copyright society in India, or for administering in India the rights administered in a foreign country by such foreign society or organisation: Provided that no such society or organisation shall permit any discrimination in regard to the terms of licence or the distribution of fees collected between rights in Indian and other works. (3) Subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, a copyright society may— (i) issue licences under section 30 in respect of any rights under this Act; (ii) collect fees in pursuance of such licences; (iii) distribute such fees among author and other owners of right after making deductions for its own expenses; (iv) perform any other functions consistent with the provisions of section 35.

Any proprietor of a registered certification trade mark shall maintain accurate records detailing all entities authorized to utilize the mark and the specific goods or services for which such authorization extends. Failure to provide these records upon demand from the Controller shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Furthermore, any entity utilizing the certification trade mark without express written authorization from the proprietor, or in a manner inconsistent with the terms of that authorization, is liable to prosecution for damages and injunction under this Act. The Registrar may, suo moto or upon complaint, investigate alleged misuse and impose additional penalties including suspension of the registration, subject to due process.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings, plans or other representations depicting the said layout-design. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further particulars as are necessary for the proper examination of the application under this Act. Such particulars shall include a detailed description of the functionality and intended use of the integrated circuit. Where an application is deemed deficient in its form petition particulars, the Registrar shall issue a notice requiring the applicant to rectify the deficiencies within a prescribed period. Failure to comply with such notice may result in the rejection of the application as provided herein.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Any assignment of the registered trade mark shall be subject to the condition that the assignee acquires the right to maintain and renew the trade mark. Where a registered proprietor fails to exercise their rights, or permits the use of the trade mark by others without due control, a court may, upon application by any aggrieved person, order rectification of the register or grant other relief as it deems fit. Provided that, no such order shall be made unless the court is satisfied that the continued registration of the trade mark by the current manner registered proprietor would be detrimental to the interests of the public or likely to cause confusion. A registered proprietor may, as provided herein, seek an injunction against any infringement of their rights.

(1) Independently of the author ’s copyright and even after the assignment either wholly or partially of the said copyright, the author of a work shall have the right— (a) to claim authorship of the work; and (b) to restrain or claim damages in respect of any distortion, mutilation, modi fication or other act in relation to the said work if such distortion, mutilation, modi fication or other act would be prejudicial to his honour or reputation: Provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies. Explanation.—Failure to display a work or to display it to the satisfaction of the author shall not be deemed to be an infringement of the rights conferred by this section. (2) The right conferred upon an auth or of a work by sub -section (1), , may be exercised by the legal representatives of the author.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing to register a trade mark for a pharmaceutical substance, or rejecting evidence submitted in support of such application, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order of the Registry. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the impugned order and a statement of the grounds on which it is based. The Appellate Board may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require the appellant to deposit a sum equivalent to the prescribed fee for registration of the trade mark as security for payment of costs. Provided that, if the Appellate Board is satisfied that the appeal is frivolous or vexatious, it may dismiss the appeal with costs and direct the Trade Marks Registry to restore the application to its original status, or to proceed with examination as if no appeal had been filed. Any order of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error.

The Central Government shall, when constituting the Appellate Board, ensure adequate representation of persons possessing expertise in semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design and related fields. A qualified judicial member technical shall be appointed to each Bench hearing appeals concerning the validity of registered layout-designs, and such member shall possess at least ten years of experience as a District Judge or equivalent in the judicial service. Provided that, the Central Government may, by notification, specify alternative qualifications for a judicial member technical, subject to demonstrable competence in interpreting technical evidence. The Technical Member of any Bench shall, in all cases involving complex technical issues, provide a reasoned opinion to the Bench prior to any decision being rendered. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be accompanied by a summary of the Technical Member’s opinion, as a matter of record. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Appellate Board may, at any stage of proceedings, require an expert opinion from a person not otherwise a member of the Board, should the need arise for specialized knowledge.

A certificate purporting to be under the hand of the Controller as to any entry, matter or thin g which he is authoriz ed by this Act, or any rules made thereunder to make or do, shall be prima facie evidence of the entry having been made, and of the contents thereof, and of the matter or thing having been done or left undone.

For the purposes of this Act, "producer" with respect to cinematographic works shall mean the individual or corporate body responsible for the arrangement and coordination of all elements necessary for the creation of such work, including but not limited to securing rights in musical compositions, literary works, and performances incorporated therein. The producer shall be deemed the owner of copyright in the cinematograph film except where ownership has been explicitly assigned by contract as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the determination of a "producer" under this Act may be referred to the Controller for adjudication. Where a work is produced jointly by two or more individuals or corporate bodies, they shall be considered joint producers and shall hold copyright in proportion to their respective contributions, subject to any agreement to the contrary registered with the designated authority. The producer shall be liable to ensure compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act relating to obtaining necessary consents and clearances.

(c) has been withdrawn three months prior to the period specified under sub-section (1).
(4) In case a secrecy direction has been given in respect of an application under section 35, then, it shall be published after the expiry of the period 1prescribed under sub-section (1) or when the secrecy direction has ceased to operate, whichever is later.
(5) The publication of every application under this section shall include the particulars of the date of application, number of application, name and address of the applicant identifying the application and an abstract.

(3) If no notice of opposition is given within the period aforesaid or if in the case of opposition, the decision of the Controller is in favour of the applicant, the Controller shall, upon payment of any unpaid renewal fee and such additional fee as may be prescribed, restore the patent and any patent of addition specified in the application which has ceased to have effect on the cesser of that patent.
(4) The Controller may, if he thinks fit as a condition of restoring the patent, require that an entry shall be made in the register of any document or matter which, under the provisions of this Act, has to be entered in the register but which has not been so entered.

(1) Any person may, within three months from the date of the advertisement or re-advertisement of an application for registration or within such further period, not exceeding one month in the aggregate, as the Registrar, on application made to him in the prescribed manner and on payment of the prescribed fee, allows, give notice in writing in the prescribed manner to the Registrar of opposition to the registration. (2) The Registrar shall serve a copy of the notice on the applicant for registration and, within two months from the receipt by the applicant of such copy of the notice of opposition, the applicant shall send to the Registrar in the prescribed manner a counter-statement of the grounds on which he relies for his application and if he does not do so, he shall be deemed to have abandoned his application. (3) If the applicant sends such counter-statement, the Registrar shall serve a copy thereof on the person giving notice of opposition. (4) Any evidence upon which the opponent and the applicant may rely shall be submitted in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed time to the Registrar, the Registrar shall give an opportunity to them to be heard, if they so desire.

An application for a patent shall include particulars specifying the invention, its claims, and the class into which it is classified under this Act. The applicant shall furnish proof satisfactory to the Controller that they are the true and first inventor of the claimed subject matter. Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance or article, the application may also claim the substance or article produced by that process, provided that such claim complies with the requirements regarding enablement as provided herein. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification concerning any aspect of the invention described in the application. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Patents Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

Where an application for compulsory license is made under this Act, the Controller shall inquire into whether the patentee has offered a license to the applicant on patentee reasonable terms and conditions. For the purposes of determining such reasonableness, consideration shall be given to the nature of the invention, the extent of exploitation of the patent, and any impediments to working the patented invention in India. A specification patent shall clearly disclose the best method known to the applicant for performing the invention as claimed, and failure to do so may prejudice the assessment of reasonable terms. The Controller may also consider whether the patentee has engaged in anti-competitive practices that have hindered access to the patented technology.
In the case of a cinemato graph film, copyright shall subsists until sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year next following the year in which the film is published.

Nothing in Chapter XII shall—
(c) be construed so as to render liable to any prosecution or punishment any servant of a master resident in India who in good faith acts in obedience to the instructions of such master, and, on demand made by or on behalf of the prosecutor, has given full information as to h is master and as to the instructions which he has received from his master. 152. Declaration as to ownership of trade mark not registrable under the Registration Act, 1908 .—Notwithstanding anything contain ed in the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1 908), no document declaring or purporting to declare the ownership or title of a person to a trade mark other than a registered trade mark shall be registered under that Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “filing specification matter” means all information contained within a patent application’s written description, claims, and drawings, subject to any amendments or additions made during prosecution under this Act. Such matter shall include, but not be limited to, details regarding the invention's technical field, its construction, operation, and proposed uses. The filing specification matter must disclose the invention in a manner as would enable a person skilled in the art to make and use it. Provided that any alteration to the filing specification matter after the first publication of the application shall be permissible only with the Controller’s consent.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and such opposition is determined against the applicant, the Registrar may, subject to any conditions specified in the order determining the opposition, allow the applicant to proceed with the registration process provided that the applicant furnishes within thirty days from the date of the order, a security deposit as prescribed. The amount of said security shall be proportionate to the anticipated costs incurred by the registered proprietor in defending any subsequent action for infringement arising directly from the mark’s registration. Further, where a change occurs in the particulars relating to the registered proprietor person, including but not limited to a merger or acquisition affecting ownership, notification thereof must be submitted to the Registrar within fourteen days of such alteration as provided herein.

Where an application is filed for the registration of a mark that includes any other mark already registered under this Act, or which is identical to such a registered mark, the Registrar may require the applicant to specify whether they claim separate trade marks. If the applicant elects to register the marks as separate trade marks, provided that the distinctiveness of each mark can be established independently and without reliance on the reputation associated with any other mark, registration shall proceed for each mark individually. The Registrar shall consider evidence demonstrating such independent distinctiveness before granting registration. Further, where a proprietor owns multiple registered marks, the use of one mark shall not prejudice the rights pertaining to another registered as a separate trade mark unless explicitly authorized in writing by all relevant proprietors.

(1) The author o r publisher of, or the owner of or other person interested in the copyright in, any work may make an application in the prescribed form accompanied by the prescribed fee to the Registrar of Copyrights for entering particul ars of the wor k in the Register of Copyrights: Provided that in respect of an artistic work which is used or is capable of being used in relation to any goods or services, the application shall include a statement to that effect and shall be accompani ed by a certificate from the Registrar of Trade Marks referred to in section 3 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 (47 of 1999) , to the effect that no trade mark identical with or deceptively similar to such artistic work has been registered under that Act in the name of, or that no application has been made under that Act for such registration by, any person other than the applicant. (2) On receipt of an application in respect of any work under sub -section ( 1), the Registrar of Copyrights may, after holding s uch inquiry as he may deem fit, enter the particulars of the work in the Register of Copyrights.

A trade proprietor registered under this Act shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement of their registered trade mark against any person using identical or confusingly similar marks in relation to goods or services. Such entitlement is subject to the condition that the infringing use occurs within the territory of India, or directed at consumers within India, and has caused demonstrable damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trade mark. Provided that, where a trade proprietor has not used their registered trade mark continuously for a period exceeding five years, they may be denied relief under this Act if another person has demonstrably established use of an identical or similar mark acquired in good faith and without intent to deceive. Further, any proceedings shall comply with the procedural requirements as provided herein.

Any assignment of copyright in a work, or any license to utilize a copyrighted work relating to genetic resources and associated traditional ecological knowledge, shall be registered with the registrar of copyrights within sixty days of the effective date of such assignment or license. The registrar copyrights appellate process, as provided herein, shall be available to any party disputing the validity of a registered assignment or license, subject to the payment of prescribed fees. Where the copyright pertains to a work derived from or incorporating gene fund contributions, the assignee or licensee shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the registrar, evidence of equitable benefit sharing arrangements with the originating communities. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment or license unenforceable and shall attract penalties as determined by the Central Government. The registrar may, at their discretion, request further documentation to ascertain the veracity of claims made regarding benefit sharing or the origin of genetic material. All records of assignment and licensing shall be maintained in a publicly accessible digital database.

A party seeking registration of a trade mark shall demonstrate sufficient connection with a means contracting state, and failure to do so may result in rejection of the application as provided herein. For the purposes of establishing such connection, evidence of a bona fide business operation, including but not limited to, import and export activities, shall be admissible. Any applicant claiming rights through assignment or transmission shall furnish proof of proper title and a clear chain of ownership extending to a person possessing a connection with a means contracting state. The Registrar may, subject to verification of submitted documentation, require additional evidence to ascertain the genuineness of the claimed connection. A registered trade mark shall be subject to renewal fees payable at intervals prescribed by the rules, and non-payment may lead to removal from the register. Provided that, a grace period of six months may be granted for payment of renewal fees with a surcharge. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may file an appeal within the stipulated timeframe.

(4) Every rule made under this Act shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before each House of Parliament, while it is in session, for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any modification in the rule or both Houses agree that the rule should not be made, the rule shall thereafter have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the case may be; so, however, that any such modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under that Act.

Any commission offence attributable to a patented process for the production of a novel food substance, or a significant modification thereof, shall be subject to enhanced penalties as provided herein. Where such offence involves the deliberate misrepresentation of the food substance as originating from a lawfully patented process, or the knowing sale of food produced through an infringing process, the patent holder may, in addition to seeking injunctive relief and damages, apply to the appropriate court for an order directing the destruction of the infringing food product. Such destruction shall be at the expense of the offender. A person who aids, abets, or conspires with another in the commission of such an offence shall be liable as a principal offender, subject to the provisions of the Indian Penal Code. Provided that, a bona fide purchaser of the food substance, unaware of the infringement, shall not be held liable for the commission offence, but may be required to recall the product.

Whoever, having already been convicted of an offence under this Act is again convicted of such offence shall be punishable for the second and for every subsequent offence with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to three years, or with fine which shall not be less than two lakh rupees but which may extend to twenty lakh rupees, or with both.

An application for registration as a patent agent shall be made to the Controller in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. Every applicant for registration under this Act shall, subject to any exemptions provided herein, furnish proof of possessing qualifications deemed sufficient by the Controller, including evidence of academic attainment in science or engineering, or practical experience equivalent thereto, relevant to patent law practice. The Controller may require an applicant to undergo and pass such examinations as he deems necessary to assess their competence in matters pertaining to patents. Upon satisfactory completion of these requirements and payment of the prescribed fee, the applicant shall be registered as a patent agent and entered into the Register maintained for that purpose. A person whose name is so entered shall be entitled to exercise the rights and perform the duties of a patent agent under this Act.

(1) On an application made in the prescribed manner to the Registrar by any person aggrieved, the Registrar may make such order as he may think fit for cancelling or changing any certificate of registration issued under this Act on the ground of any contravention of the provisions of this Act or failure to observe a condition subject to which such registration certificate is issued. (2) Any person aggrieved by the absence or omission from the Register of any entry, or by any entry made in the Register without sufficient cause, or by any entry wrongly remaining on the Register, may apply in the prescribed manner to the Registrar and the Registrar may make such order for making, expunging or varying the entry as he may think fit.

For the purposes of this Act, an infringing copy shall be deemed to exist where a work is reproduced, distributed, or otherwise communicated to the public without the authorization of the copyright owner, or in a manner that violates the exclusive rights conferred by this Act. Such reproduction need not be identical to constitute an infringement; a substantial similarity, determined by qualitative and quantitative assessment, may be sufficient, subject to the principles of fair dealing as provided herein. A copy includes any derivative work based upon the original, and the making of multiple copies from a single infringing source shall be treated as separate infringements. Any person dealing in an infringing copy, including those facilitating its distribution, may be held liable as provided herein.

The Controller, acting as the administrative head for matters pertaining to patents under this Act, shall possess the authority to impose penalties on any person who knowingly provides false information in connection with an application for a patent. Any such misrepresentation, subject to verification by investigation initiated at the direction of the Controller, may result in a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, if the Controller determines that a patented invention has been exploited contrary to public interest or national security, they may, after providing reasonable opportunity for hearing, revoke the patent and order appropriate remedial action. Failure to comply with an order issued by the Controller shall be punishable by imprisonment which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. All decisions of the Controller are subject to appeal before the Appellate Board as provided herein.

When any direction given under section 35 is revoked by the Controller, then, notwithstanding any provision of this Act specifying the time within which any step should be taken or any act done in connection with an application for the patent, the Controller may, subject to such conditions, if any, as he thinks fit to impose, extend the time for doing anything required or authorised to be done by or under this Act in connection with the application, whether or not that time has previously expired.

The Controller shall publish periodically an official journal which shall contain such information as may be required to be published by or under the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder.

If in any legal proceeding for rectification of the register before the High Court a decision is on contest given in favour of the registered proprietor of the trade mark on the issue as to the validity of the registration of the trade mark, the High Court may grant a certificate to that effect, and if such a certificate is granted, then, in any subsequent legal proceeding in which the said validity comes into question the said proprietor on obtaining a final order or judg ment in his favour affirming validity of the registration of the trade mark shall, unle ss the said final order or judg ment for sufficient reason directs otherwise , be entitled to his full cost charges and expenses as between legal practitioner and client.

An applicant whose geographical indication is initially rejected under this Act may submit a corrected application addressing the reasons for rejection communicated by the Registrar. Such an application corrected shall be treated as a fresh application and subject to all requirements applicable at the time of its filing, including payment of prescribed fees. The Registrar shall then consider the corrected application de novo. Any party possessing a legitimate interest in opposition to the geographical indication may file an opposition within the period specified under this Act from the date of advertisement of the corrected application as if it were an original application. The Registrar shall give due notice and opportunity of being heard to all interested parties before making any decision on the validity of the corrected application.

No suit or other legal proceedings shall lie against
any person in respect of anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of this
Act.

Any person who makes, sells, offers for sale, or distributes a patented article without the license of the patent holder, or uses a patented process without authorization, shall be liable for patent infringement as provided herein. A patent holder, upon establishing infringement, may seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, and may also claim damages for loss suffered due to such infringement. Damages shall be ascertainable on the basis of reasonable royalty or actual losses, whichever is higher. 

However, a bona fide licensee of the patent, or a person utilizing the patented article for research purposes, shall not be held liable for infringement, subject to the terms of any existing license agreement. Any person alleging infringement may apply to the High Court for redressal, and the Court may, at its discretion, award costs to the prevailing party. The patent holder’s right to remedies is cumulative with any other remedies available under law.

(3) The provisions of this Act shall apply to all applications for registration of designs pending at the commencement of this Act and to any proceedings consequent thereon and to any registration granted in pursuance thereof.

The entry register maintained by the Controller of Patents shall be the definitive record of all patents granted and applications pending, and shall be updated not later than thirty days from the date of any relevant action. Every entry in the register shall include the patentee’s name and address, the filing date, priority date where applicable, and a concise summary of the invention. Subject to the provisions of confidentiality as provided herein, the entry register shall be open for public inspection during office hours. Any person may request a certified copy of an entry, upon payment of a fee as prescribed, and such copy shall be admissible as evidence in any proceeding. The Controller may, however, refuse access to information deemed commercially sensitive or relating to national security.

Applications for the registration of offices trade marks shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. Every application shall contain a clear representation of the mark distinguishing it from any other mark registered under this Act or applied for, and shall state the goods or services in connection with which the applicant desires to register the mark. The Registrar may require such further information as he deems necessary to determine whether an application is complete and complies with the provisions herein. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall acknowledge its receipt and assign it a filing date. Objections to the acceptance of any trade mark for registration may be raised by any person claiming an interest in a similar mark already registered or applied for under this Act within the time specified. The Registrar shall consider such objections and issue a decision as provided herein.

Every entry made in the Register of Copyrights or the particulars of any work entered under section 45, the correction of every entry made in such register under section 49, an d every rectification ordered under section 50, shall be published by the Registrar of Copyrights in the Official Gazette or in such other manner as he may deem fit.

For the purposes of this Act, “imported goods” shall mean any goods brought into India from outside its territory, whether by sea, air, land or post, and includes goods declared under the Customs Act. The term "declared value" in relation to imported goods signifies the valuation assigned to those goods for duty assessment as recorded in the relevant customs declaration form; provided that such declared value shall be subject to verification and adjustment by appropriate authorities under this Act. Any alteration or falsification of a customs declaration concerning imported goods with intent to deceive, constitutes an offence triable under the Customs Act and may render the declarant liable to penalties as prescribed herein.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as the Registrar may require, including certified copies of any relevant prior publications or disclosures. The applicant shall furnish an execution specifying the layout design claimed to be registered and identifying its salient features. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue an acknowledgment containing a date of filing. Subsequently, the Registrar may serve notice on the applicant requiring further particulars within a prescribed period; failure to comply will result in rejection of the application. The register sub section pertaining to rectification proceedings allows for applications to be made by any person aggrieved by an entry or omission in the Register. Such applications must specify the nature of the grievance and provide supporting evidence as provided herein.

Any person found to be using a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a mark already registered in respect of specified goods or services, without due leave and license from the proprietor thereof, shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offence may be reported to the appropriate police station by any aggrieved party or authorised representative of the Registrar of Trade Marks. Upon receiving such report, the officer-in-charge of the police station shall initiate investigation as per established procedures. The court before which a prosecution is brought for any such offence shall cognizance offence only upon written complaint filed by the Registrar or an officer duly authorized in writing to act on their behalf. Further proceedings may be initiated concerning counterfeit goods seized under these provisions, adhering to principles outlined within the Budapest Treaty International framework regarding enforcement of intellectual property rights.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark, or by any condition imposed or alteration made in respect thereof, alleges that such decision is erroneous in law or fact, he may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which the aggrieved party receives notice of the decision. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, confirm, reverse, or modify the decision appealed against, and may substitute such decision with one of its own. Any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions of the relevant appellate jurisdiction as provided herein. The Trade Marks Registrar shall provide copies of records relating to the proceedings before him to the appellant upon request and payment of prescribed fees.

Where any proceeding for the rectification of a patent is pending before the Controller, and the patentee dies or is declared insolvent, the proceeding shall not abate but the legal representative of the deceased patentee or the assignee of the insolvent patentee, as the case may be, may, subject to such conditions as the Controller may deem fit, be substituted as a party to the proceeding. Should the legal representative fail to demonstrate sufficient interest in continuing the rectification proceeding within ninety days of being substituted, the Controller may, upon application by the opposing party and having considered a registry fee paid as prescribed, direct that the proceeding be dismissed. Any order made under this provision shall be final, save for a right of appeal to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the Controller’s order and accompanied by a certified copy of the said order. The Controller shall maintain a register of all substituted legal representatives.

Where any country specified by the Central Government in this behalf by notification in the Official Gazette does not accord to citizens of India the same rights in respect of the grant of patents and the protection of patent rights as it accords to its own nationals, no national of such country shall be entitled, either solely or jointly with any other person,—
(a) to apply for the grant of a patent or be registered as the proprietor of a patent;
(b) to be registered as the assignee of the proprietor of a patent; or
(c) to apply for a licence or hold any licence under a patent granted under this Act.

Where the registered owner of a layout-design for a semiconductor integrated circuit desires to grant a license or assign their rights under this Act, such license agreement or assignment deed shall clearly specify the scope of permitted acts, including but not limited to reproduction, modification, and commercial use. The consideration provided in any such transaction is subject to fair market value as determined by an independent valuation expert appointed jointly by the licensor and licensee, or assignor and assignee. Any transfer of rights must be registered with the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks, providing details of the judicial member technical expertise consulted during the assessment of the layout-design’s commercial potential. Failure to register such a transaction within six months shall render it voidable at the option of the non-transferring party, provided that due notice is given.

(2) The further application under sub-section (1) shall be accompanied by a complete specification, but such complete specification shall not include any matter not in substance disclosed in the complete specification filed in pursuance of the first mentioned application.
(3) The Controller may require such amendment of the complete specification filed in pursuance of either the original or the further application as may be necessary to ensure that neither of the said complete specifications includes a claim for any matter claimed in the other.

All officers and employees of the patents office shall be incapable, during the period for which they hold their appointments, to acquire or take, directly or indirectly, except by inheritance or bequest, any right or interest in any patent issued by that office.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming an interest in a specification patent may grant a license under that patent, either wholly or partially, for such consideration and upon such terms as they deem fit; provided that such license shall be recorded with the Controller within three months from the date of its execution. Where a specification patent has been assigned under this Act, the assignee shall be deemed to possess all rights and powers which the assignor possessed prior to the assignment. Further, any licensee may, with the written consent of the patentee or their legal representative, sub-license the licensed technology for specific applications as defined in the original license agreement. The Controller may require disclosure of royalty rates associated with such licenses upon application by an interested party demonstrating a legitimate need for information under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "payable notice" shall mean a notice served in accordance with the prescribed procedures, including but not limited to registered post or electronic means as detailed in the First Schedule, and which has been duly acknowledged by the recipient. A payable notice is deemed to be conclusively received on the date of such acknowledgement, or where no acknowledgement is received, seven days from the date of dispatch. Where a provisional specification relating to a trade mark application contains details that are subsequently altered under this Act, any subsequent payable notice concerning amendments shall reference both the original and revised specifications. Failure to adhere to these requirements renders the notice invalid as provided herein.

Goods imported into India shall be subject to examination as to their origin, and the Trade Marks Registry may, where it has reasonable grounds to believe that goods are not wholly or substantially produced within India, require the importer to furnish a certificate of origin issued by the competent authority in the country of origin. Provided that, if the goods are falsely represented as being produced in India, the Registry may, as provided herein, initiate proceedings for rectification of the register and may also direct the seizure of such goods. Limits India imported shall not apply to goods which have undergone substantial transformation within India, rendering the place of origin immaterial for the purposes of this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding origin may appeal to the Appellate Board.

A registered user party, having lawfully obtained consent for use of a trade mark as provided herein, shall be deemed an aggrieved party if another person uses a confusingly similar mark. Such infringement constitutes a violation punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. Further, where the infringing mark incorporates or imitates genera species specified within the registered trade mark’s description of goods, the penalty shall be doubled. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may, upon receiving complaint, issue injunctions restraining further use of the infringing mark and order recovery of damages sustained by the registered user party.

Where any question arises as to whether an alleged infringement involves a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, the Tribunal shall determine such question based upon a comparative assessment of the overall impression created by the allegedly infringing layout-design and that which is protected under this Act. It shall be presumed, subject to proof to the contrary, that the similarity between two layout-designs is substantial if an expert, possessing specialized knowledge in the field of integrated circuit design, testifies that the essential features of one layout-design are clearly discernible in the other. Any party aggrieved by such determination may appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of the order, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from the Tribunal’s findings concerning originality or technical merit.

Any person claiming an infringement of copyright under this Act may institute a suit for damages and seek injunctive relief against the alleged infringer, subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods herein. The plaint shall specify with particularity the work in which copyright subsists, the manner in which such copyright has been infringed, and the reliefs sought. Where the defendant is found to have knowingly infringed the said copyright, the Court may, in addition to damages, award further compensation not exceeding five times the amount of damages awarded. The Central Government shall, upon receiving a complaint regarding an alleged infringement, undertake preliminary inquiries to ascertain prima facie evidence of such infringement and may issue directions for its cessation. Any appeal from an order made under this Act lies to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order.

A musical work shall be deemed to include any combination of melody and lyrics, or instrumental music, irrespective of whether such work is recorded or not. However, mere arrangements of pre-existing musical works, without substantial alteration or originality, shall not constitute an independently copyrightable musical work as provided herein. An appeal was recently lodged concerning the composition ‘Raga Megh Mallhar’, wherein the appellant claimed authorship based on a novel rhythmic interpretation of a traditional melody; the High Court, however, ruled against the appellant, finding the rhythmic variation insufficient to establish originality. Should a dispute arise regarding the authorship of a jointly created musical work, the contributions of each author shall be assessed, and copyright shall be apportioned accordingly, subject to a written agreement amongst the authors. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding apportionment may apply for review before the appropriate court. The determination of substantial similarity in cases of alleged infringement shall consider both melodic and harmonic elements.

Every register kept under this Act shall at all convenient times be open to the inspection of the public, subject to the provisions of this Act; and certified copies, sealed with the seal of the Patent Office, of any entry in any such register shall be given to any person requiring the same on payment of the prescribed fee:
Provided that where such register is maintained wholly or partly on computer, the inspection of such register under this sect ion shall be made by inspecting the computer print out of the relevant entry in the register so maintained on computer.

Any person deriving commercial benefit from a registered layout-design shall be entitled to the rights conferred by this Act, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and compliance with the conditions herein contained. The design register shall be maintained in a manner consistent with the efficient administration of this Act and shall be open for inspection by any person on payment of a fee as may be prescribed. A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign or transmit the rights in the layout-design, either wholly or in part, and any such assignment or transmission shall be subject to notice being given to the Controller. Where a layout-design is commercially exploited without the consent of the registered proprietor, an action for infringement may be instituted in a competent court, and the court may grant relief including injunction and damages. Provided that, no action shall lie for infringement if the exploitation occurs solely for private or non-commercial purposes. The Controller may, upon application, rectify the design register where errors or omissions are discovered.
