Where an application for registration of a trademark has been granted and the certificate of registration issued, any party claiming ownership rights in a mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement. Such proceedings may include claims for damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the unauthorized use of the trade mark. The Registrar shall have the power to issue interim injunctions restraining acts of proceeding infringement pending final determination of the matter before an appropriate judicial forum, provided that such action is demonstrably causing irreparable harm to the reputation and goodwill associated with the registered trademark. Further, any representation or false designation made in connection with goods or services utilizing a similar mark shall be considered actionable under this Act.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently extended through the mechanism of the Madrid Protocol International, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred by such registration against any person infringing the same within the territory of India. Any act constituting infringement under this Act shall render the infringer liable for damages, including but not limited to lost profits, reasonable royalties, and costs incurred in protecting the trade mark’s validity. Provided that, where an opposition is filed against an international registration extension, the rights afforded by the Indian registration shall remain subject to the outcome of such opposition proceedings. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the acceptance or rejection of an international registration extension may appeal to the relevant appellate authority as provided herein.

Any agreement whereby the entire copyright or exclusive rights pertaining thereto in respect of any cinematograph film are assigned to another party shall be deemed an assignment copyright under this Act, subject to the conditions stipulated herein. Such assignments may encompass the right to reproduce the work, include its adaptation, distribute prints, and exhibit publicly, as mutually agreed upon by the assignor and assignee through a written contract. Provided that, where the assignment relates to a work jointly authored, all co-owners of the copyright shall execute the agreement or their duly authorised representatives do so on their behalf. The duration of any such assignment shall not exceed seventy years from the year following the date of creation of the cinematograph film, unless explicitly stated otherwise in the written instrument. Further, an assignee may sub-license rights as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed admissible if it complies with all requirements as provided herein regarding form and representation, and further subject to the applicant demonstrating sufficient capacity to make use of the mark legitimately within the Indian territory. The Registrar may require submission of additional documentation substantiating such usage, including but not limited to sales figures and distribution agreements. Where an application relates to a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark, the applicant must provide a clear and reasoned explanation demonstrating absence of likelihood of confusion. It is further stipulated that registration ought effected only upon satisfaction that no prior conflicting rights exist which would prejudice another party’s interests.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark desires to grant a license relating thereto, such license may be granted either for the whole duration of the registration or for a specified period, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. The registered proprietor shall retain ultimate control over the use of the trade mark, even where a license has been issued, and may impose reasonable restrictions on the licensed activities as provided herein. Any assignment of the right to utilize the trade mark under such a license must be notified to the Registrar in writing, along with supporting documentation establishing the transferor’s authority. The registered proprietor proposed for licensing shall ensure that all licensees adhere strictly to the conditions outlined within the agreement and any subsequent amendments approved by the proprietor. Failure to comply may result in termination of the license as determined by the Registrar.

Any person who uses, in the course of trade, a mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark relating to goods or services in respect of which the mark is registered, and such use results in a likelihood of confusion, shall be liable to a penalty as provided herein. Where the mark in question is used in relation to integrated circuits, or semi-conductor chips incorporating such integrated circuits, the penalty shall be doubled, and the Controller may, in addition to monetary penalties, order the destruction of the infringing articles. However, no action shall lie if the use of the mark is demonstrably fair and does not create a demonstrable use mark relation with the registered trade mark owner. Any appeal against an order of penalty or destruction shall be made to the High Court within ninety days of the order’s issuance, subject to the deposit of a prescribed fee. Failure to comply with an order of the High Court shall constitute contempt of court.

Any person applying for a patent under this Act shall furnish a statement and undertaking regarding prior art known to them, detailing all information which could reasonably affect the assessment of novelty and inventive step as required by this Act. The application shall be deemed incomplete if such statement and undertaking are absent or found to be materially deficient. A patent applicant may request a hearing if objections are raised concerning the sufficiency of disclosure, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Where a patent is granted for a product or process involving a biological material, the patent specification shall disclose the origin and geographical source of said material. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the patent vulnerable to revocation proceedings, and any resulting damages shall be assessed according to the principles of equitable accounting as provided herein. The Controller of Patents shall maintain a publicly accessible register of all patents granted and applications pending, ensuring transparency in the patents act 1970 regime.

Where any goods are knowingly offered or exposed for sale, or deceptively represented as possessing particular qualities, such representation shall constitute a false trade description. Any person who makes use of a false trade description under this Act is liable to prosecution and may be subject to pecuniary penalties as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority. Further, where a trade mark has been registered, any subsequent use of a sign or words identical or confusingly similar thereto, which incorporates such false trade description, shall constitute an infringement actionable at the suit of the registered proprietor. Impliedly registration shall not preclude remedies available under this Act for misrepresentation relating to the nature of goods or services offered. The aggrieved party may seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein.

The Controller of Patents, acting through the Patent Office, shall furnish to the applicant a statement of grounds of rejection under this Act. Any party aggrieved by any decision or order made by the Patent Office relating to the grant, revocation, or sealing of a patent may, within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision or order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Provided that the Appellant shall deposit with the Registry such fee as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Any question of law arising for determination in connection with any appeal under this Act shall be determined by the High Court.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused, and the applicant appeals such refusal under this Act, the appellate authority shall consider whether the grounds presented demonstrate a likelihood of confusion arising amongst consumers. It is provided that if the appellant establishes, to the satisfaction of the appellate authority, that the mark sought to be registered possesses distinctive character acquired through use subsequent to its initial application, notwithstanding any prior conflicting registration, the trademark may be granted new patent protection subject to conditions as deemed appropriate. For purposes of this appeal, "registered" means registered under this Act and shall include trademarks previously considered but ultimately rejected due to similarity with existing marks. The decision of the appellate authority is final, subject to further appeal to the High Court.

Any person desiring to register a work under this Act shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Registrar of Copyrights, accompanied by the requisite fee and a copy of the work claiming copyright. The application shall clearly state the title of the work, the author’s name and address, and the particulars relating to publication, if any. Where the applicant is not the author, proof of assignment or legal entitlement to make the application shall be furnished subject to verification by the Registrar. Failure to provide complete and accurate information in the application may render it liable for rejection, and a false declaration therein shall attract penalties including imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may require further evidence or clarification regarding any aspect of the application as deemed necessary before proceeding with registration.

Where a proprietor seeks to register a trade mark in India based on an earlier trade mark registered or applied for in respect of identical or similar goods or services, and such registration or application is founded upon an *agreement means madrid*, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant for the conflicting mark. Such notice shall specify the grounds relied upon by the proprietor, detailing any likelihood of confusion arising from the similarity between the marks and the identity or resemblance of the goods or services. The recipient of such notice may file a counter-statement within the prescribed period, disputing the claim and presenting evidence to demonstrate absence of deception or misrepresentation. Any dispute concerning the validity of the *agreement means madrid* itself shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, as provided herein.

The patent office register shall comprise a publicly accessible record maintained by the Controller General, detailing all applications for patents filed under this Act. This register shall include, but not be limited to, information pertaining to the applicant’s name and address, the title of the invention, the date of filing, and the status of examination as provided herein. Any modification to an application's claims or specifications shall also be recorded within the patent office register. Further, details concerning any opposition proceedings initiated against a granted patent, including the identity of the opponent and the grounds for objection, must be meticulously documented subject to rules framed by the Central Government.

(1) If the person committing an offence under this Act is a company, the company as well as every person in charge of, and responsible to, the company for the conduct of its business at the time of the commission of the offence shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any such person liable to any punishment, if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he had exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where an offence under this Act has been committed by a company and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance of, or that the commission of the offence is attributable to any neglect on the part of any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. Explanation.—For the purposes of this section,— (a) "company" means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals; and (b) "director", in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm.

A pharmaceutical substance, for the purposes of this Act, shall be considered novel subject to demonstration of inherent efficacy and a clear departure from prior art as established through diligent searching of both Indian and international patent literature. Any application claiming a pharmaceutical substance shall include comprehensive data regarding its chemical characterization, including structural elucidation and spectral analysis, and shall further detail the method of manufacture, ensuring reproducibility and scalability. Provided that, a substance previously known for a different therapeutic application may be patented if a new and non-obvious medical use is demonstrated, subject to rigorous clinical trial evidence. The applicant may also submit comparative data establishing improved bioavailability or reduced toxicity relative to existing treatments. Compliance with Good Manufacturing Practice guidelines is mandatory for all patented pharmaceutical substances intended for commercial production, as provided herein. Failure to adhere to these requirements may invalidate the patent.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act is dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar, such person may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall consist of a Technical Member and a Judicial Member, appointed in accordance with the provisions outlined herein. Appeals shall be finally decided within six months from the date of their receipt by the Tribunal, subject to unavoidable delays. Any order passed by the Tribunal shall be binding on all parties involved and may direct remedies including injunctions preventing further infringing acts or orders for account of profits derived from unauthorized use of a layout-design. The aggrieved party may also seek compensation for damages suffered as a consequence of such infringement, provided that the amount is determined reasonably and fairly, considering the circumstances of the case.

(2) The registration of a design shall not be invalidated by reason only of the exhibition or use of or the publication of a description or representation of the design in India during the period specified in this section as that within which the application may be made.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to use the trade mark in relation to specified goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms of the agreement between the proprietor and the licensee. Assignment of a trade mark, or any license granted thereunder, requires registration with the Trade Marks Registry, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Where an assignment or license involves a party located outside India, the manner informing international authorities shall be conducted in accordance with the procedures outlined by the International Bureau. The Registrar may require submission of documentation verifying the legal standing and address of foreign assignees or licensees. Any alteration to the terms of a registered license must also be notified to the Registry for record.

A trademark shall be deemed deceptively similar to another if, considering the impressions created in the minds of the average consumer, it is likely to cause mistaken identity. This assessment shall take into account the visual appearance, phonetic composition, and ideational significance of the marks, as well as the nature of the goods or services with which they are associated. The determination of similarity is a question of fact dependent on the overall impression created without undue emphasis on any single element. Crucially, there exists a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, which may arise even where the marks possess some distinguishing features.

(2) Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (1), an application for the registration of the title of any person becoming entitled by assignment to a patent or a share in a patent or becoming entitled by virtue of a mortgage, licence or other instrument to any other interest in a patent may be made in the prescribed manner by the assignor, mortgagor, licensor or other party to that instrument, as the case may be.

The Registrar may, upon receiving a notice of opposition to an application for registration of a trade mark, direct that the hearing be conducted before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board or, in its absence, designate an officer of the Trade Marks Registry to preside over such proceedings. Any party aggrieved by any order made under this Act relating to the refusal of registration, acceptance of a disclaimer, or the rectification of the register purposes legal shall have the right to appeal from that order to the Appellate Board, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and within the time stipulated herein. The Appellate Board may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against, and may substitute its own order in place thereof. Further appeals concerning decisions of the Appellate Board are permissible before the Supreme Court on grounds specified under this Act.

The right to exploit a registered design shall vest initially with the registrant, who may grant non-exclusive licenses conferring specific rights relating to manufacture, import, sale, or distribution of articles incorporating that design. Such licenses may be assigned freely, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the license agreement itself; however, any assignment shall not prejudice existing rights held by third parties under prior valid licenses granted by the original registrant. Where a design is jointly registered, all registrants are deemed joint owners and must consent in writing for any licensing or assignment of the design as a whole. The Central Government may, upon application from an aggrieved party demonstrating substantial reliance on a design previously licensed without proper authorization, issue directives compelling disclosure of license terms. This power shall be exercised cautiously to avoid undue interference with contractual arrangements concerning designs.

(1) The Controller may, at any time during the continuance of the patent, by notice in writing, require a patentee or a licensee, exclusive or otherwise, to furnish to him within two months from the date of such notice or within such further time as the Controller may allow, such information or such periodical statements as to the extent to which the patented invention has been commercially worked in India as may be specified in the notice.
(2) Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (1), every patentee and every licensee (whether exclusive or otherwise) shall furnish in such manner and form and at such intervals (not being less than six months) as may be prescribed statements as to the extent to which the patented invention has been worked on a commercial scale in India.
(3) The Controller may publish the information received by him under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) in such manner as may be prescribed.

The Registrar of Copyrights may, in the prescribed cases and subject to the prescribed conditions, amend or alter the Register of Copyrights by— (a) correcting any error in any name, address or particulars; or (b) correcting any other error which may have arisen therein by accidental slip or omission.

A denomination variety shall be distinguished by a unique and readily identifiable name assigned to the plant variety for the purposes of registration under this Act, and such denomination must conform to the requirements as prescribed. The denomination shall be clearly distinguishable from all other denominations of varieties of the same kind, or of closely related kinds, whose existence is a matter of common knowledge to persons dealing with such varieties. Provided that a denomination which is likely to cause confusion with a variety already protected, or which is contrary to public order or morality, shall not be accepted. A variety essentially derived from a registered denomination variety may, subject to the provisions herein, retain a denomination incorporating the original variety’s name, with appropriate modification to indicate its derivation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences for the use of such trade goods and services relating to that trade mark. Such licence may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the grantor in the terms thereof. Assignment of rights pertaining to a trade mark, including all associated goodwill and reputation, may occur through a written instrument executed by the proprietor, provided that any subsequent licensee shall retain rights granted prior to notification of such assignment under this Act. The assignee shall be bound by any existing licence agreements relating to the trade goods services unless expressly modified or terminated in writing with the consent of all parties involved. Further, any sub-licensing of a registered trade mark is permissible only with the express written authorization of the original proprietor.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act is dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar, such person may prefer an appeal to the prescribed proceeding appellate authority within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate authority shall give notice to all parties concerned and opportunity for them to be heard. Any party intending to support or oppose the appeal shall file a written submission along with relevant documents; it shall given affidavit verifying the truthfulness of contents thereof. Subject to this, the appellate authority may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. The decision of the appellate authority shall be final and binding. Provided that an appeal from the order of the appellate authority lies to the High Court within a further period of sixty days, on any ground of law.

(2) The Gene Fund shall, in the prescribed manner, be applied for meeting— (a) any amount to be paid by way of benefit sharing under sub-section (5) of section 26; (b) the compensation payable under sub-section (3) of section 41; (c) the expenditure for supporting the conservation and sustainable use of genetic resources including in-situ and ex-situ collections and for strengthening the capability of the Panchayat in carrying out such conservation and sustainable use; (d) the expenditure of the schemes relating to benefit sharing framed under section 46.

Where an applicant seeks to obtain a patent for an invention already described in a publication before the date of filing of the application, or where the invention was otherwise made available to the public before such date, the Controller may require the applicant to satisfy him that the invention did not at the time fall within the scope of any prior art. In determining whether an invention is obvious or anticipated under this Act, the publication shall be deemed to have been published on its advertised date, if any; otherwise, on the date it first became available to the public. For the purposes of assessing novelty and inventive step, the applicant shall priority date shall be taken into account in relation to such prior publications. Any person aggrieved by a decision under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Copyright Society, or by any decision of the Licensing Board established under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be preferred within ninety days from the date of the order or decision, and shall be filed in the manner prescribed. The Copyrights Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, reverse or vary the order or decision appealed from. The Board may, while considering an appeal relating to royalty rates, consult with experts possessing knowledge in the relevant field, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit. Provided that no appeal shall lie from any order relating to the registration of copyright. All orders of the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be final and binding, and no further appeal shall lie to any court. The Board shall be empowered to impose costs as it thinks appropriate.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, and subsequent circumstances arise wherein an advertisement relating to the goods or services for which registration subsists is employed by the proprietor in a manner calculated to mislead consumers regarding the nature, quality, or geographical origin of those goods or services, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Such proceedings shall be predicated on demonstrable evidence that the advertised representation creates confusion amongst potential purchasers. The proprietor shall be afforded an opportunity to present counter-evidence demonstrating a lack of such misleading effect. If the tribunal finds that the circumstances application advertised has indeed caused or is likely to cause deception, it may order injunctive relief restricting the continued use of the advertisement and award damages commensurate with the harm suffered by the aggrieved party.

An applicant patent, if contested under this Act, shall be subject to a notice of opposition filed by any person alleging prior art or lack of inventive step, provided that such notice is served within four months from the date of publication of the application. The Controller, upon receipt of a valid opposition, shall communicate it to the applicant, who may file a counter-statement within three months. Failure to submit a counter-statement may result in the applicant patent being deemed withdrawn. Where the Controller, after examining the evidence presented by both parties, is satisfied that the applicant patent does not meet the requirements of novelty or involves an obvious variation of existing knowledge, it may reject the application. Any aggrieved party may appeal such rejection to the Appellate Board established for the purposes of this Act, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and adherence to the procedural timelines as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, unless a substantial question of law is involved, warranting review by a higher court.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark contains a reference trade mark, the Registrar shall consider whether the applicant has demonstrated reasonable grounds for believing that the use of the proposed trade mark is unlikely to cause confusion amongst consumers. Such demonstration must include evidence establishing consumer familiarity with both marks and their respective goods or services. The Registrar may require further information from the applicant concerning the nature and extent of such familiarity, including market surveys conducted in accordance with prescribed guidelines. Provided that the reference trade mark is registered under this Act, the Registrar shall not refuse registration solely on the basis of similarity between the two marks unless it is satisfied that there exists a likelihood of dilution or unfair appropriation.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, no person shall be found to have made unlawful uses registered trade marks unless it is demonstrated that the defendant’s adoption of a sign creates a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public to the detriment of the proprietor. Provided that such demonstration considers not only the similarity of the signs themselves but also factors including the nature of the goods or services, the channels of trade and the state of information of the relevant consumers. It shall be a defence for the defendant to prove prior honest concurrent use of an identical mark in relation to similar goods, provided that such use did not create confusion at the time of registration. The Tribunal may order damages as appropriate.

An application for certificate registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation specifying the denomination proposed for the variety, along with justification demonstrating its distinctiveness relative to existing varieties as recorded in the Register. The Authority may require submission of additional data pertaining to the genetic composition and stability of the variety’s traits. Upon receiving an application, the Authority shall publish a notice inviting objections from any person or organization claiming rights relating to the plant variety. Objections received must be substantiated with evidence demonstrating prior knowledge or use of the proposed denomination or similar varieties. The applicant shall have opportunity to respond to such objections in writing. Following consideration of all submissions, the Authority may grant certificate registration if satisfied that the requirements under this Act are fulfilled and that the proposed denomination does not conflict with existing registrations.

The proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to injunctive relief restraining the use by any person of a sign identical or confusingly similar to the said trade mark in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those for which the trade mark is registered, provided that such use constitutes an infringement under this Act. Further remedies available to the proprietor include damages sustained directly and proximately caused by the infringing activity, as well as delivery up or destruction of any goods bearing the infringing sign. Where a dispute arises concerning the interpretation or application of these provisions, either party may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of order; such appeal shall be subject to review under established procedures as provided herein and binding on all parties involved in the original proceeding. The Board’s decision regarding trade goods services is final.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing to grant a layout-design right, or varying the terms of registration, or revoking a registration, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order and the prescribed fee. The Appellate Board may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the appellant to deposit with it such sum as it deems fit, not exceeding the amount of the registration fee and any costs awarded by the Registrar. Where an appeal relates to a layout-design right that is also the subject matter of a patent application, the Appellate Board shall consider the potential for concurrent rights and ensure no undue prejudice arises to either the layout-design right holder or the patent applicant. The manner applying appellate procedures shall be in accordance with rules framed by the Central Government, and all decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding.

An application for a patent of addition may be filed by any person who is entitled to apply for and obtain a patent under this Act, provided that the invention claimed in such application relates to the subject matter of an existing patent granted to him or her. The applicant shall disclose the connection between the new invention and the invention disclosed in the parent patent, demonstrating how the former builds upon or improves the latter. Further, the claims of the patent of addition must clearly define the inventive step that distinguishes it from the parent patent; otherwise, the application may be rejected. Subject to fulfilling these requirements, a patent of addition shall confer all rights and privileges as are granted under this Act for patents generally.

The Register shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all processes submitted for registration as patented processes, detailing the applicant’s name, address for service, and the nature of the claimed invention. Any person aggrieved by the acceptance of a registered patented process may file an appeal with the Controller within sixty days from the date of publication of the acceptance in the Patent Journal. Such appeals shall be accompanied by a statement of grounds and any supporting documentation deemed relevant to the assessment of novelty and inventive step as provided herein. The Register may, subject to due process, refuse registration if it determines that the claimed patented process is contrary to public order or morality. An applicant seeking registration of a patented process must disclose all prior art known to them at the time of filing.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Patents, or any decision refusing an application for a patent, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The Appellate Board shall, following a review of the record and consideration of submissions, issue an order appellate affirming, modifying, or reversing the Controller’s decision within ninety days of the filing of the appeal. Failure to issue such order within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed a contravention of this Act and attract a penalty of five thousand rupees per day of delay, payable to the aggrieved party. Any wilful misrepresentation of facts before the Appellate Board shall render the appellant liable to a fine not exceeding twenty thousand rupees, and may further disqualify them from filing future appeals. The decision of the Appellate Board constitutes a final order subject to judicial review only on grounds of jurisdictional error.

An applicant seeking registration of a layout design shall furnish with the application, a detailed technical description outlining the functionality and intended purpose of the integrated circuit. The Registrar may require further clarification or supplementary documentation deemed necessary for assessing novelty and originality under this Act. Where an applicant has previously published the layout design prior to filing the application, such publication shall not preclude registration provided that the applicant demonstrates due diligence in safeguarding confidentiality before the disclosure. Any subsequent modification to a registered layout design which substantially alters its characteristics may necessitate a fresh application for registration as a new layout design. The right of layout design providing is conferred upon the registered proprietor for the duration specified herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person who, prior to the registration of a trademark, has used such mark in India for bona fide purposes may apply to the Registrar for an assignment or license of that unregistered trade mark. Such application shall specify the territory within India where the use occurred and provide evidence thereof satisfactory to the Registrar. The Registrar may grant the application if satisfied that the applicant’s use was continuous and not merely sporadic, and that no other person has a superior right to the mark. Any assignment or license granted under this Act shall be recorded in the Register of Trade Marks and shall confer upon the assignee or licensee the rights as if it were a registered trademark for the duration specified within the agreement, provided that such use does not infringe upon any existing registered trade marks.

The applicant for registration of a trade mark shall submit the prescribed registry fee alongside the application for registration, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be rejected as provided herein. The amount of the registry fee shall vary according to the class of goods or services for which the trade mark is sought to be registered, and a schedule of such fees shall be publicly available on the official website of the Trade Marks Office. Any application for amendment of the register, or for renewal of registration, shall also attract a separate registry fee, the amount of which shall be determined based on the nature of the amendment or the remaining period of registration. Provided that, in cases where the applicant is a small enterprise or a start-up, as defined by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, a reduced registry fee may be applicable subject to fulfilling the conditions stipulated in the relevant notification. All fees paid under this Act shall be non-refundable except in cases of demonstrable clerical error by the Trade Marks Office.

Where, following the grant of a patent under this Act, it is demonstrated to the Controller, through presentation of verifiable *ii india document* and supporting affidavits, that the patented invention was commercially exploited by an unauthorized party within India without the consent of the patentee, the Controller may order such infringing entity to pay damages proportionate to the profits derived from said exploitation. Such damages shall be calculated considering the reasonable royalty which would have been payable had a license been granted to the patentee. Further, the Controller may, subject to due process and opportunity for both parties to present their case, issue an injunction restraining the infringer from further commercialization of the invention. The patentee shall bear the burden of proving unauthorized exploitation and resultant profits; provided that the Controller may consider evidence demonstrating a pattern of similar activity in determining reasonable royalty.

Any person who engages in the application of a deceptive trade mark, or a falsely applied trade description, with intent to defraud, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act, and shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed. However, a defendant alleging lack of knowledge of the deceptive nature of the mark or description may, subject to verification by the investigating officer, mitigate the penalty. The burden of proving reasonable care taken to ascertain the genuineness of the mark or description shall lie with the accused. 

Where the alleged offence reason stems from the sale of goods bearing such deceptive mark or description, the proprietor of the trade mark, or the person lawfully using the trade description, may initiate proceedings for recovery of damages and an injunction restraining further sale. Provided that, such proceedings shall not preclude any criminal prosecution initiated by the appropriate authority. Any evidence of prior complaints regarding similar infringements by the accused shall be admissible as an aggravating factor.

Any person claiming rights in an unregistered trade mark, and alleging that another person is using a deceptively similar mark, may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining such use, subject to proof of prior use and goodwill attached thereto. However, such injunction shall not be granted unless the applicant demonstrates a continuous and uninterrupted use of the unregistered trade mark for a period of not less than five years immediately preceding the date of the application. Any order granting such injunction may also direct an account of profits derived by the defendant from the unlawful use of the mark, provided that the plaintiff establishes a clear nexus between the defendant’s use and the profits claimed. An appeal from any order of the High Court in this regard shall lie to the Supreme Court, subject to the provisions of this Act and any other relevant law. The Court may, at its discretion, require the applicant to furnish security for costs.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any licensee granted under a patent may assign such license, either wholly or partially, to any person, provided that such assignment is made by instrument in writing and registered with the Controller. The assignee shall be subject to all the terms and conditions applicable to the original license agreement as recorded in the Register of Patents. Where an india patented invention has been assigned under this Act, notice of such assignment shall be given to the Controller within thirty days of the date of execution of the instrument effecting the assignment. Failure to provide such notice may render the assignor liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Controller may, upon application by any interested party, inquire into the terms and conditions of any license or assignment and determine whether they are prejudicial to public interest.

Any person applying for advertising international registration of a trade mark under this Act shall furnish a representation of the mark as it is to be advertised, along with a statement of the goods or services for which registration is sought, and a clear indication of the country of origin. The application shall be subject to verification by the Trade Marks Registry to ensure compliance with the provisions of the Protocol Relating to the Madrid Agreement Concerning the International Registration of Marks. Where the advertising international registration relates to goods or services falling within a class prohibited under the law prevailing in the designated country, the Registry may, after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, refuse the registration in respect of that country. Provided that, such refusal shall not affect the validity of the registration in other designated countries. The applicant may, within a prescribed period, appeal any decision of the Registry concerning the advertising international registration to the High Court. All fees associated with the processing of such applications shall be as prescribed by rules made by the Central Government.

The assignment of a registered trade mark shall require execution of a formal instrument in the prescribed form, attesting to the transferor’s complete relinquishment of all rights and title pertaining to the mark. Such instruments must be presented to the Registrar for registration within thirty days of the date of assignment; failure to do so renders the assignment voidable at the assignee's option. Where an agreement purports to grant a license to use a registered trade mark, such license may be assigned subject to conditions stipulated in the original agreement and as provided herein. The Registrar shall appear before any court or tribunal claiming jurisdiction over disputes arising from assignments or licenses under this Act, upon request by either party involved, to provide clarification regarding registration details and procedural compliance. Any alteration of terms within a licensed trade mark usage requires prior written consent from both licensor and the registered proprietor, duly acknowledged by the Registrar.

Any assignment of the right to an accompanied provisional specification, or of a patent obtained pursuant thereto, shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions governing such assignment, including but not limited to the territory, duration, and scope of the assigned rights. An assignee of such a right may, subject to the provisions of this Act, further assign the same to another person. Where an accompanied provisional specification relates to a patentable subject matter but lacks clarity regarding the inventive step, the Controller may, prior to acceptance, require the applicant to amend the specification to adequately demonstrate such step. Failure to comply with this requirement within a period of sixty days from the date of such requirement shall render the application liable to be refused. Any licensing agreement pertaining to rights derived from an accompanied provisional specification shall be registered with the appropriate authority as provided herein, and failure to do so may invalidate the license.

(1) Subject to the provisions of section 49, a person o ther than the registered proprietor of a trade mark may be registered as a registered user thereof in respect of any or all of the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is registered.
(2) The permitted use of a trade mark shall be deemed to be used by the proprietor thereof, and shall be deemed not to be used by a person other than the proprietor, for the purposes of section 47 or for any other purpose for which such use is material under this Act or any other law.

The Controller may, upon receipt of an application for registration of a biological material, require the applicant to submit a detailed specification outlining the method of isolation, cultivation, or generation of said material. This specification shall include comprehensive information regarding the genetic characteristics, phenotypic traits, and stability data demonstrating consistent performance over successive generations. Furthermore, the applicant must provide evidence confirming adherence to established bio-containment protocols during handling and storage procedures. A certificate from a recognized national repository verifying the authenticity and preservation status of the biological material may be submitted as supplementary documentation. The Controller shall consider this specification alongside other application details when determining eligibility for registration under this Act, provided that all requirements are met.

The Plant Variety Protection Authority shall administer a dedicated fund, known as the Gene Fund, for the purpose of incentivizing the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources for crop improvement. Contributions to the Gene Fund shall include a percentage of the sales value of seeds of protected varieties, as determined by the Authority in consultation with the Central Government, and any royalties received from the commercial exploitation of registered plant varieties, subject to a minimum contribution rate established through regulations. The Authority may also accept grants, donations, and other contributions from national and international organizations dedicated to plant genetic resource conservation. 

Disbursements from the Gene Fund shall be utilized to support the maintenance of national, state, and local gene banks, to reward farmers and local communities for conserving on-farm genetic diversity, and to fund research and development activities aimed at enhancing crop resilience and productivity. Provided that, twenty percent of the annual disbursements shall be allocated specifically to benefit marginal and small farmers engaged in the conservation of traditional varieties. Any unutilized funds shall not lapse and shall be available for utilization in subsequent financial years.

For the purposes of this Act, a “person interested” shall be deemed to include any individual or body corporate who has directly or indirectly acquired rights pertaining to the patent, or who is engaged in the manufacture, use, or sale of an article embodying the invention claimed in the patent application. Such person shall also encompass any legal entity that has provided substantial financial support towards the research and development leading to the invention, provided that such contribution is documented through a formal agreement executed prior to the filing date of the patent application. A person interested may file applications for rectification under this Act concerning the validity or scope of the patent, subject to demonstrating a material interest adversely affected by the patent’s existence or interpretation. The Controller shall consider any objections raised by a person interested with due regard to the principles of natural justice.

(1) Without prejudice to the provisions contained in sections 5 and 5 as regards amendment of applications for patents or complete specifications 1or other documents relating thereto and subject to the provisions of section 44, the Controller may, in accordance with the provisions of this section, correct any clerical error in any patent or in any specification or other document filed in pursuance of such application or in any application for a patent or any clerical error in any matter which is entered in the register.
(2) A correction may be made in pursuance of this section either upon a request in writing made by any person interested and accompanied by the prescribed fee, or without such a request.
(3) Where the Controller proposes to make any such correction as aforesaid otherwise than in pursuance of a request made under this section, he shall give notice of the proposal to the patentee or the applicant for the patent, as the case may be, and to any other person who appears to him to be concerned, and shall give them an opportunity to be heard before making the correction.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the respect registered trade mark in relation to specified goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof shall be determined at the discretion of the grantor, subject to any conditions stipulated under this Act regarding fair competition. Any assignment of a registered trade mark, whether partial or complete, including assignments relating to licensed use, requires registration with the Trade Marks Registry, and such registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the transfer of rights as provided herein. Further, where a license is assigned, the assignee shall possess all the same rights and obligations pertaining to the original licensee, subject to any limitations expressly stated in the original licensing agreement. The Registrar may require submission of detailed documentation substantiating the scope and duration of such licenses or assignments.
The Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament once a year a report respecting the execution of this Act by or under the Controller.

(2) Subject to the provisions contained in section 10, a complete specification filed with a convention application may include claims in respect of developments of, or additions to, the invention in respect of which the application for protection was made in a convention country, being developments or additions in respect of which the applicant would be entitled under the provisions of section 6 to make a separate application for a patent.
(3) A convention application shall not be post-dated under sub-section (1) of section 1 to a date later than the date on which under the provisions of this Act the application could have been made.

Any person importing into India any product manufactured using a patented invention, where such patent is a patent outside India, shall be subject to penalties as prescribed herein. Provided that, if the importation occurs prior to notification by the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks regarding the existence of the foreign patent, the importer may apply for remission of penalty within ninety days from the date of such notification. Failure to comply with this provision renders the importer liable to a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and the product shall be subject to seizure and forfeiture. Furthermore, any party knowingly assisting in such importation shall face similar penalties as the importer, subject to judicial discretion considering the degree of involvement.

(1) If any difficulty arises in giving effect to the provisions of this Act, the Central Government may, by order published in the Official Gazette, make such provisions not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act as may appear to be necessary for removing the difficulty: Provided that no order shall be made under this section after the expiry of five years from the commencement of this Act. (2) Every order made under this section shall, as soon as may be after it is made, be laid before each House of Parliament.

, and things done by the Registrar .—(1) A copy of any entry in the register or of any document refer red to in sub -section ( 1) of section 148 purporting to be certified by the Registrar and sealed with the seal of the Trade Marks Registry shall be admitted in evidence in all courts and in all proceedings without further proof or production of the original. (2) A certificate purporting to be under the hand of the Registrar as to any entry, matter or thing that he is authorised by this Act or the rules to make or do shall be prima facie evidence of the entry having been made, and of the contents thereof, or of the matter or things having been done or not done.

Any copyright owner aggrieved by an order of the Licensing Authority, or any other person claiming an interest in the subject matter of the copyright, may apply to the Copyrights Appellate Board for review of such order. Such application shall be made within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee. The Appellate Board may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, extend this period. All assignments of copyright interest, whether whole or partial, shall be registered with the Licensing Authority, and a certified copy of such registration may be submitted to the Appellate Board as evidence of ownership. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, subject to verification, accept other demonstrable evidence of valid assignment. The Appellate Board shall, after considering the application and any relevant submissions, issue its reasoned order within one hundred and eighty days, and such order shall be final and binding, save for recourse to writ jurisdiction as provided by law. Any transfer of copyright without prior intimation to the Licensing Authority shall render the assignment voidable at the option of the original copyright owner.

The Central Government may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, grant licenses for the use of copyrighted works in cases where a work is required for purposes of public interest, including but not limited to educational or research institutions lacking commercial viability. Any assignment of copyright relating to cinematograph films intended for public exhibition shall require prior intimation to the Central Government, detailing the scope of rights transferred and the duration of such transfer. Where the assignee fails to adhere to stipulated conditions regarding royalty payments or quality control as determined by the licensor and communicated to the Central Government, the latter may initiate proceedings for revocation of the assignment. Further, the Central Government retains the right to direct compulsory licensing where a copyright holder unreasonably refuses to permit reproduction of a work for national emergency or public health purposes, provided that adequate remuneration is offered and deposited with a designated escrow account maintained by the Reserve Bank of India. All such licenses and assignments shall be registered with the appropriate authority as prescribed under this Act.

An appeal lies to the Appellate Board against any order passed by the Registrar refusing registration of a variety, or revoking such registration, provided that the application for appeal is made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board may, subject to this Act and after giving all parties an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of such decision; however, the High Court shall only entertain appeals based on questions of law arising out of interpretation of provisions relating to distinctness and stability in determining eligibility for registration variety.

Where an application is made for the registration of a trade mark which falsely suggests a connection with any living person, or a person whose death took place within twenty years prior to the date of application for registration of the trade mark , the Registrar may, before he proceeds with the application, require the applicant to furnish him with the consent in writing of such living person or, as the case may be, of the legal representative of the deceased person to the connection appearing on the trade mark, and may refuse to proceed with the application unless the applicant furnishes the Registrar with such consent.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a trade mark on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier trade mark registered in a country other than India, the Trade Marks Registry shall give notice thereof to the applicant. Such notice shall clearly state the particulars of the conflicting mark and the grounds upon which the objection is founded, as provided herein. The applicant may then file its response within the time specified, demonstrating why the marks do not create likelihood of confusion or deception among consumers. Failure to respond adequately shall be deemed an admission of conflict. The Registry may, after considering all submissions, direct registration subject to limitations or refuse it entirely; any such direction is appealable under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Informing international authorities regarding these proceedings is mandatory.

No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie against the Central Government, or against the Chairperson, or members, or the Registrar or any person acting under such Government, Authority or Registrar under the provisions of this Act, for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of this Act or any rule, regulation, scheme or order made thereunder.
(i) “prescribed” means prescribed by rules made under this Act;

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a trade mark on the ground that it is deceptively similar to any prior registered trade mark or any other identifiable trade mark, the Trade Marks Registry shall give notice thereof to the applicant for registration and to the proprietor of the earlier trade mark. The applicant may then file its counter-statement within the time specified in the notice, setting out reasons why the objection should not be sustained. In determining whether a trade mark is deceptively similar, the Registry shall consider all relevant factors including the similarity of the marks, the goods or services for which the respective trade marks are used, and the likelihood of confusion on the part of the public. For the purposes of establishing a “real and effective industrial or commercial establishment”, an applicant must demonstrate continuous activity directly related to the use of the mark in commerce.

(1) No person shall make any representation—
(a) where that word or other expression, symbol or sign is used in direct association with other words delineated in characters at least as large as those in which that word or other expression, symbol or sign is delineated and indicating that the reference is to registration as a trade mark under the law of a country outside India being a country under the law of which the registration r eferred to is in fact in force; or
(b) where that other expression, symbol or sign is of itself such as to indicate that the reference is to such registration as is mentioned in clause (a); or
(c) where that word is used in relation to a mark registered as a trade mark under the law of a country outside India and in relation solely to goods to be exported to that country or in relation to services for use in that country. 108. For the purposes of this Act, “use patented” with reference to a patent shall mean the making, selling, offering for sale, distributing, importing, or hiring out of any process or article claimed in the patent, or the use of such process or article. Such use includes not only direct exploitation but also indirect utilization where the activity contributes substantially to the working of the patented invention. Provided that activities undertaken solely for experimental purposes relating to the patented invention shall not be considered as “use patented” under this Act. Further, the term "use patented" extends to acts performed by a licensee in accordance with the terms of their license agreement, subject to any restrictions stipulated therein.

An application for a register proposed under this Act shall be deemed incomplete unless it is supported by an affidavit verifying the distinctiveness of the mark as against its use in relation to identical or similar goods or services. The Registrar may require further evidence demonstrating acquired reputation, provided that such requirement does not unduly delay processing. Any representation made within the application concerning prior conflicting marks shall be subject to verification through a search report generated under this Act and submitted alongside the application. Furthermore, where the proposed mark incorporates a geographical indication, consent from the relevant authority administering said indication must be obtained and documented as part of the register proposed. The Registrar may reject the register proposed if any condition precedent is not fulfilled.

Where a patent has been granted, any interested person may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. Such opposition shall be limited to the grounds specified in this Act and relating to the novelty, inventive step, or sufficiency of disclosure of the invention claimed in the patent. The Controller may, upon receiving such notice, serve a copy thereof on the patentee and afford both parties an opportunity for reasoned argument and presentation of evidence. Should the opposition be deemed frivolous or manifestly lacking merit, the Controller shall reject it summarily; otherwise, proceedings shall continue as provided herein, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period not exceeding three months from the date of order.

Any individual or entity utilizing a registered act relating to a trademark in a manner that creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services shall be liable for damages. Such liability extends to instances where the unauthorized use dilutes the distinctiveness of the mark, irrespective of actual commercial competition. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint and after due inquiry, issue an injunction restraining further infringing activity. Failure to comply with such an order shall constitute contempt of court and render the offender subject to penalties as provided herein, including fines up to five lakhs rupees and imprisonment for a term not less than six months.

Where a proprietor seeks to register a mark, and such mark incorporates a *trade description* applied by the applicant, the Registrar shall examine whether the use of that description conforms with standards established under this Act. The application may be rejected if the Registrar is satisfied that the inclusion of the *mark trade description* creates confusion likely to mislead the public regarding the nature, quality or geographical origin of goods or services. Any party claiming an interest in opposition to registration may submit evidence demonstrating such misleading potential. Further, the Registrar shall provide a reasonable opportunity for the applicant to present counter-evidence and arguments. The decision of the Registrar concerning the propriety of the *trade description applied* is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This process ensures adherence to principles safeguarding consumer interests and maintaining integrity within the trade mark registry.

Any person alleging infringement of a layout-design right, prior to initiating proceedings before any competent court, shall issue a written notice to the alleged infringer, detailing the specific layout-design right claimed to be infringed and the nature of the infringement. The manner issuing notice shall conform to the regulations prescribed, and failure to adhere to such regulations shall render the notice invalid for the purposes of this Act. Provided that, if the alleged infringer is reasonably identifiable only through publicly available records, service by registered post with acknowledgement due shall constitute sufficient notice. Any person issuing a false or misleading notice, with intent to harass or intimidate another, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, direct the rectification of any improperly issued notice, and any costs associated with such rectification shall be borne by the party at fault. Any appeal against such direction shall lie to the Appellate Board.

Any proprietor of a registered certification mark incorporating a geographical indication shall be entitled to institute proceedings in the High Court for redressal of infringement. Such proceedings may include claims for damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the unauthorized use of the geographical indication applied, taking into account any benefit accruing to the infringing party. The Court shall have power to grant such remedies as it deems just and equitable, including injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and an order requiring the infringer to recall goods bearing the mark from all points of sale. Provided that a claim for damages may be denied if the proprietor failed to exercise due diligence in monitoring use of the geographical indication applied. The Court shall also consider any registered certification marks impacted by the infringing activity when determining appropriate remedies.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement against any person using identical or confusingly similar marks in connection with goods or services identical or closely related to those specified in the registration, provided that such use is likely to cause confusion among the public or to indicate that the goods or services originate from the proprietor. Where an injunction restraining the infringing activity has been granted, damages may be awarded to the proprietor, representing their loss by reason of the infringement; however, the Court shall not award exemplary damages unless it finds that the defendant acted with malice or fraudulent intent. Further, any profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringing use may be recovered by the registered trade mark owner as provided herein, subject to just and equitable considerations.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of a layout-design, makes, imports, sells, hires or offers for sale or hire any product which infringes the design shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such infringement is established when the overall impression created by the infringing product is substantially similar to that formed by viewing the registered layout-design. Where commercial exploitation of a protected layout-design occurs through intermediaries, liability extends to those who knowingly facilitate such acts. The Court may, upon conviction, impose a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees and extendable to two hundred thousand rupees, alongside an order for damages reflecting lost profits attributable to the infringement. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties as provided herein.

Where an inventor, having already obtained a patent under this Act, discovers that the invention for which the original patent was granted includes further inventions not claimed in the initial specification, the controller may grant a patent of addition relating to such new matter. The application for a patent of addition shall be filed within three years from the date of grant of the first patent and shall comply with all requirements applicable to an original patent application, subject to any modifications prescribed herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision granting or refusing a patent of addition may appeal under this Act. Further, the rights conferred by a patent of addition are not assignable independently of the original patent unless the controller permits it in writing, provided that such permission is only granted where public interest so warrants and after due consideration of any opposition filed.

Any person deriving benefit from a patented invention, whether through license granted under this Act or assignment of the patent rights, shall maintain accurate records of royalties paid and received relating to such exploitation. Where an applicant seeks protection for an invention based on a prior application filed in a convention country, they shall furnish a certified copy of that earlier application together with a declaration verifying its filing date and authenticity, as provided herein. The Controller may require translation of any document not in an official language of India. A failure to comply with these requirements relating to convention applications may render the application subject to revocation. Should a licensee fail to remit royalties due to the patentee within ninety days of their becoming payable, the patentee may seek recourse through established legal channels for breach of contract or infringement, subject to the terms of the licensing agreement. Any dispute regarding royalty rates shall be determined by arbitration in accordance with prevailing law.

Where a trade mark is registered in respect of goods manufactured exclusively outside the territory of India, the Registrar shall require the proprietor to furnish, within thirty days of the request, details pertaining to the manufacturing process and location. Such information must be verified by an affidavit confirming adherence to established quality control standards as prescribed under this Act. Failure to provide such particulars or demonstrable non-compliance with said standards may result in a direction for suspension of registration. Furthermore, where goods manufactured outside India are subsequently also produced within India, the proprietor shall notify the Registrar within ninety days, detailing the commencement date and location of domestic manufacture; this constitutes a requirement for goods manufactured notification.

Any party claiming relief against an act of proceeding infringement shall furnish evidence demonstrating substantial similarity between the impugned mark and the registered trade mark, considering both visual appearance and phonetic representation. Where such a claim arises concerning a mark’s registration mentioned clause, the aggrieved party must further demonstrate that the infringing use creates likelihood of confusion amongst relevant consumers regarding origin or sponsorship. Failure to provide satisfactory proof as provided herein shall render the proceeding untenable and subject the claimant to costs incurred by the defendant in defending the action. The Tribunal may, upon finding an unwarranted threat of legal proceedings, impose a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees for each instance of such conduct.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Government undertaking” means any body corporate or other entity owned or controlled by the Central Government or State Governments, either directly or indirectly through holding, management, or control; provided that an entity shall not be deemed a Government undertaking merely by virtue of receiving financial assistance from the government. The expression "control" with reference to a Government undertaking includes the power to appoint the majority of its directors or other governing body members and to direct its policy decisions concerning research and development activities relating to inventions, subject to any specific exemptions as may be notified under this Act.

(1) The Registrar may, on application made in the prescribed manner by the registered proprietor,— (1)(a) correct any error in the name, address or description of the registered proprietor of a layout- design, or any other entry relating to the layout-design; (1)(b) enter any change in the name, address or description of the person who is registered as proprietor of a layout-design; (1)(c) cancel the entry of a layout-design on the register, and may make any consequential amendment or alteration in the certificate of registration, and for that purpose, may require the certificate of registration to be produced to him. (2) The Registrar may, on application made in the prescribed manner by a registered user of a layout- design, and after notice to the registered proprietor, correct any error, or enter any change in the name, address or description of the registered user.
