Any Registrar, upon receiving an application for registration of a layout plan relating to land within a municipal corporation area, shall verify that the applicant has complied with all applicable regulations concerning environmental clearances and building bylaws. Failure to submit requisite documentation demonstrating such compliance, as provided herein, constitutes a deficiency in the application. The Registrar may require the applicant to rectify this deficiency within sixty days; otherwise, the application shall be deemed rejected. Any person who knowingly submits false or misleading information regarding compliance with these regulations is liable for penalty thousand rupees and may face further action under relevant municipal ordinances.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international application designating India, as facilitated by the Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks, any challenge to the registrability of that trade mark under this Act shall be deemed a violation punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, where such a violation is proven to have resulted in demonstrable financial loss to a third party due to confusion or misrepresentation arising from the challenged registration, aggravated penalties, as determined by the relevant court, shall apply. The Registrar may, sua sponte or upon complaint, initiate proceedings against any person found guilty of contravening these provisions, and such proceedings shall be conducted expeditiously.

Any assignment of the right to apply for a patent based upon a provisional specification shall be executed in writing and shall clearly identify the provisional specification to which it relates, including the application number and date of filing. A licensee acquiring rights under such an assignment shall be subject to the same terms and conditions as the assignor, unless otherwise agreed in writing and recorded with the appropriate office. Where a provisional specification discloses an invention which is subsequently found to lack novelty or involve an obvious step, any assignment made prior to the determination of such lack of novelty or obviousness shall not be invalidated, provided that the assignee was not a party to the initial concealment of material facts. The assignee may, subject to the provisions of this Act, proceed with filing a complete specification based on the provisional specification, or may elect to terminate the assignment and seek a refund of any consideration paid. Failure to file a complete specification within the prescribed period following a valid assignment shall, however, render the assignment null and void.

(b) preparing specifications or other documents for the purposes of this Act or of the patent law of any other country;
(c) giving advice other than of a scientific or technical nature as to the validity of patents or their infringement.

For the purposes of this Act, “international application” shall mean an application for a patentable invention filed in accordance with the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of Deposited Microorganisms, and where such an international application designates India, it shall be treated as if it were an application made under this Act. An applicant filing a request for grant of a patent based on an international application shall disclose all priority claims asserted in respect thereof. The Controller may require the furnishing of certified copies of documents relating to the international application and any subsequent proceedings concerning its examination or grant, provided that such requirement is reasonable and necessary for determining novelty and inventive step.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (dd) “broadcast” means communication to the public— (i) by any means of wireless diffusion, whether in any one or more of the forms of signs, sounds or visual images; or (ii) by wire, and includes a re-broadcast; (e) “calendar year” means the year commencing on the 1st day of January; (f) “cinematograph film ” means any work of visual recording and includes a sound recording accompanying such visual recording and “cinematograph” shall be construed as including any work produced by any process analogous to cinematography including video films; (fa) “commercial rental” does not include the rental, lease or lending of a lawfully acquired copy of a computer programme, sound recording, visual recording or cinematograph film for non-profit purposes by a non-profit library or non-profit educational institution. Explanation.—For the purposes of this clause, a “non -profit library or non -profit educational institution” means a library or educational institutio n which receives grants from the Government or exempted from payment of tax under the Income-tax Act, 1961(43 of 1961).

(1) Every applicant shall assign a single and distinct denomination to a variety with respect to which he is seeking registration under this Act in accordance with the regulations. (2) The Authority shall, having regard to the provisions of any international convention or treaty to which India has become a party, make regulations governing the assignment of denomination to a variety.

(1) Any person may apply to the Appellate Board for a licence to produce and publish a translation of a literary or dramatic work in any language after a period of seven years from the first publication of the work. (1A) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub -section ( 1), any person may apply to the Appellate Board for a licence to produce and publish a translation, in printed or analogous forms of reproduction, of a literary or dram atic work, other than an Indian work, in any language in general use in India after a period of three years from the first publication of such work, if such translation is required for the purposes of teaching, scholarship or research: Provided that where such translation is in a language not in general use in any developed country, such application may be made after a period of one year from such publication. (2) Every application under this section shall be made in such form as may be prescribed and sh all state the proposed retail price of a copy of the translation of the work. (3) Every applicant for a licence under this section shall, along with his application, deposit with the Registrar of Copyrights such fee as may be prescribed.

(1) The Authority may, with the previous approval of the Central Government, by notification in the Official Gazette, make regulations consistent with this Act and the rules made thereunder to carry out the provisions of this Act.

(1) Save as provided in sub-section (2), nothing in this Act shall authorise the registration of two or more persons who claim to be the creator of a layout-design. (2) Where the relation between two or more persons claiming to be the creator of layout-design are such that— (2)(a) both of them or all of them have put the combined intellectual effort in creating such design; or (2)(b) in relation to the creation of such layout-design both of them or all of them are connected in such manner that intellectual effort of each of them are not distinguishable in creation of such layout- design, those persons may be registered as joint proprietor of the layout-design and this Act shall have effect in relation to any right to the use of the layout-design vested in those persons as if in those rights vested in a single person.

Any person who—
(a) falsifies any trade mark; or
(b) falsely applies to goods or services any trade mark; or
(c) makes, disposes of, or has in his possession, any die, block, machine, plate or other instrument for the purpose of falsifying or of being used for falsifying, a trade mark; or
(d) applies any false trade description to goods or services; or
(e) applies to any goods to which an indication of the country or place in which they were made or produced or the name and address of the manufacturer or person for whom the g oods are manufactured is required to be applied under section 139, a false indication of such country, place, name or address; or
(f) tampers with, alters or effaces an indication of origin which has been applied to any goods to which it is required to be applied under section 139; or

(d) by any error or defect in any entry in the register, make such order for the making, variation or deletion, of any entry therein as it may think fit.
(2) In any proceeding under this section the 1High Court may decide any question that may be necessary or expedient to decide in connection with the rectification of the register.
(3) Notice of any application to the 1High Court under this section shall be given in the prescribed manner to the Controller who shall be entitled to appear and be heard on the application, and shall appear if so directed by the 2High Court.
(4) Any order of the 1High Court under this section rectifying the register shall direct that notice of the rectification shall be served upon the Controller in the prescribed manner who shall upon receipt of such notice rectify the register accordingly.

The register maintained under this Act shall be open to inspection by any person on payment of the prescribed fee, subject to such conditions as the Controller may deem fit to impose to ensure the confidentiality of sensitive commercial information. Any person who, with intent to deceive, falsely represents themselves as being authorized to inspect the register, or who knowingly makes a false entry into the register, or who fraudulently alters any entry therein, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. Provided that, any amendment to the register necessitated by a judicial order shall be effected expeditiously and without imposition of additional fees beyond those prescribed. Failure by the Controller to comply with such order within sixty days shall constitute a cognizable offence, attracting a penalty of five thousand rupees per day of delay. All fees collected pursuant to inspection of the register shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

The Registering Authority shall record the date patent shall take effect from the date specified in the application for registration, provided that where a request for priority is filed under this Act, the date patent shall be deemed to be the earlier date of filing of the corresponding application in the designated country, subject to verification by the Controller. The applicant shall furnish all necessary documentation substantiating the claim of priority within the prescribed time limit as determined by regulations framed hereunder. Failure to provide such documentation may result in the rejection of the priority claim and a subsequent adjustment of the date patent. This determination is final and binding unless appealed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to applicable timelines.
(2) The Controller may, in case of loss of the original certificate, or in any other case in which he deems it expedient, furnish one or more copies of the certificate.

(1) A person shall be deemed to apply a trade mark or mark or trade description to goods or services who—
(e) in relation to the goods or services uses a trade mark or trade description i n any sign, advertisement, invoice, catalogue, business letter, business paper, price list or other commercial document and goods are delivered or services are rendered to a person in pursuance of a request or order made by reference to the trade mark or trade description as so used. (2) A trade mark or mark or trade description shall be deemed to be applied to goods whether it is woven in, impressed on, or otherwise worked into, or annexed or affixed to, the goods or to any package or other thing.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark relating to “Kashmir Apples,” a geographical indication prescribed under this Act, is opposed, and the opponent dies pending the opposition proceedings, the Registrar shall proceed with the matter notwithstanding such death. Provided that, the applicant or any other interested party may, within sixty days from the date of notice of the death, notify the Registrar of their intention to continue the proceeding. If no such notification is received, or if multiple notifications are received and the Registrar determines a dispute exists regarding representation of interests, the opposition shall be deemed to abate *dies pending proceeding*. The Registrar may require evidence of authority to act on behalf of any continuing party before further action is taken.

The proprietor of an index registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses conferring the right to use the mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee; provided that any such license agreement must explicitly state the geographical territory within which the licensee is authorized to utilize the index registered trade mark. Further, a proprietor intending to assign their entire interest in an index registered trade mark shall provide prior notification to the Registrar, detailing the proposed assignee and the scope of assignment. Such assignments may be facilitated through adherence to procedures consistent with those outlined under the Madrid Protocol concerning the International Registration of Marks, allowing for streamlined international extensions of protection where applicable. The Registrar may require undertakings from assignees regarding continued compliance with this Act.

Where a person alleging infringement of a layout design has suffered damage as a result thereof, such person may institute legal proceedings for redressal under this Act. The measure of damages shall be determined with due regard to the loss of profits reasonably attributable to the infringing activity, taking into account any profit made by the infringer as a consequence of that infringement. It is provided that in determining damages, the court shall consider evidence relating to the extent of the market affected and the prevailing price for similar layout designs. The determination of a *layout design relation* between the original work and the alleged infringing copy shall be a key factor in assessing both liability and the appropriate quantum of compensation. Further, any order restraining the infringer from continuing the infringing activity may include an assessment of costs incurred by the claimant.

(1) There shall be paid in respect of applications and registration and other matters under this Act such fees and surcharge as may be prescribed by the Central Government. (2) Where a fee is payable in respect of the doing of an act by the Registrar, the Registrar shall not do that act until the fee has been paid. (3) Where a fee is payable in respect of the filing of a document at the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry, the document shall be deemed not to have been filed at the Registry until the fee has been paid.

An application for a patent shall be accompanied by a declaration, made by the applicant or by any person authorized by him, stating that the invention disclosed is novel and involves inventive step, and is capable of industrial application. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish such further information as he deems necessary for the purpose of determining whether the claimed invention meets the criteria for patentability under this Act. Where an objection is taken on the ground that the invention lacks novelty or inventive step, the applicant shall be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence in support of his claim. The Board constituted under this Act may hear appeals arising from any decision made by the Controller regarding the grant or refusal of a patent. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to fulfilling prescribed conditions.

The Plant Variety Protection Authority shall maintain a register of all deposited genes forming the basis of a claimed trait in a new plant variety offered for registration under this Act. Any breeder seeking registration of a variety incorporating a compensation deposited gene shall submit, alongside the application for registration, a detailed provenance report outlining the source and conditions of deposit of said gene with a recognized international depositary authority. The Authority may, subject to verification of the provenance report and confirmation from the depositary, grant a registration certificate. 

Where the novelty of a plant variety relies not only on the genetic material but also on a unique layout-design of the plant itself, demonstrably contributing to its distinctiveness, the applicant shall furnish a comprehensive visual representation of said layout-design. Provided that, the layout-design does not contravene any existing intellectual property rights. The Authority shall, in determining the registrability of the variety, consider both the deposited gene and the layout-design as integral components of the claimed invention, and shall ensure equitable benefit sharing with the original source of the deposited gene as provided herein.

(1) Where a patent is granted to two or more persons, each of those persons shall, unless an agreement to the contrary is in force, be entitled to an equal undivided share in the patent.
(2) Subject to the provisions contained in this section and in section 51, where two or more persons are registered as grantee or proprietor of a patent, then, unless an agreement to the contrary is in force, each of those persons shall be entitled, by himself or his agents, to 1the rights conferred by section 4 for his own benefit without accounting to the other person or persons.
(3) Subject to the provisions contained in this section and in section 5 and to any agreement for the time being in force, where two or more persons are registered as grantee or proprietor of a patent, then, a licence under the patent shall not be granted and a share in the patent shall not be assigned by one of such persons except with the consent of the other person or persons.
(4) Where a patented article is sold by one of two or more persons registered as grantee or proprietor of a patent, the purchaser and any person claiming through him shall be entitled to deal with the article in the same manner as if the article had been sold by a sole patentee.

(2) An application under this section may be made by any person notwithstanding that he is already the holder of a licence under the patent and no person shall be estopped from alleging that the reasonable requirements of the public with respect to the patented invention are not satisfied or that the patented invention is not worked in the territory of India or that the patented invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price by reason of any admission made by him, whether in such a licence or otherwise or by reason of his having accepted such a licence.
(3) Every application under sub-section (1) shall contain a statement setting out the nature of the applicant's interest together with such particulars as may be prescribed and the facts upon which the application is based.
(4) The Controller, if satisfied that the reasonable requirements of the public with respect to the patented invention have not been satisfied or that the patented invention is not worked in the territory of India or that the patented invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price, may grant a licence upon such terms as he may deem fit.
(5) Where the Controller directs the patentee to grant a licence he may, as incidental thereto, exercise the powers set out in section 88.

Any person applying a trade description to goods offered for sale or distributed shall ensure such description is conspicuously displayed and accurately reflects the goods’ material characteristics, including but not limited to, quantity, size, composition, and geographical origin. A trade description shall not be deemed to be false or misleading merely because it indicates the goods are in conformity with an industrial standard. However, any claim of conformity must be substantiated by evidence acceptable to the adjudicating officer, as provided herein. Where a trade description incorporates endorsements or testimonials, the source and basis of such endorsements must be clearly stated. The Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require a person applying a trade description to submit samples or other evidence for verification of its accuracy. Failure to comply with these provisions shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment and a fine, and may further invalidate any associated trademark registration. Any aggrieved party may lodge a complaint with the Controller regarding a false or misleading trade description.

(1) At any time after the expiration of three years from the date of the 1grant of patent, any person interested may make an application to the Controller for grant of compulsory licence on patent on any of the following grounds, namely:—
(a) that the reasonable requirements of the public with respect to the patented invention have not been satisfied, or
(b) that the patented invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price, or
(c) that the patented invention is not worked in the territory of India.

(3) Every authorisation under this section shall be in such form as may be specified by regulations. (4) Where an agent or a licensee referred to in sub-section (1) becomes entitled to produce, sell, market, distribute, import or export a variety, he shall apply in the prescribed manner and with the prescribed fees to the Registrar to register his title and the Registrar shall, on receipt of application and on proof of title to his satisfaction, register him as an agent or a licensee, as the case may be, in respect of the variety for which he is entitled for such right, and shall cause particulars of such entitlement and conditions or restrictions, if any, subject to which such entitlement is made, to be entered in the Register: Provided that when the validity of such entitlement is in dispute between the parties, the Registrar may refuse to register the entitlement and refer the matter in the prescribed manner to the Authority and withhold the registration of such entitlement until the right of the parties in dispute so referred to has been determined by the Authority.

Where a trade mark is advertised under this Act following an initial acceptance, any person claiming rights in relation to the proposed trade mark shall have standing to submit objections provided such objection is lodged within the period specified in the official gazette. Any communication from the applicant or any other party indicating agreement with the terms of advertisement, or otherwise demonstrating acquiescence to the advertised acceptance, shall not be construed as a waiver of right to subsequently raise an objection. Further, where an advertised acceptance explicitly references prior use by another entity, such reference shall constitute notice to the applicant of potential conflict and may preclude subsequent claims regarding earlier identical or deceptively similar usage. The Registrar shall consider all submitted objections in accordance with procedures prescribed herein.

For the purposes of this Chapter, unless the context otherwise requires, the expression “owner of copyright” shall include— (a) an exclusive licensee; (b) in the case of an anonymous or pseudonymous literary, dramati c, musical or artistic work, the publisher of the work, until the identity of the author or, in the case of an anonymous work of joint authorship, or a work of joint authorship published under names all of which are pseudonyms, the identity of any of the a uthors, is disclosed publicly by the author and the publisher or is otherwise establishment to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board by that author or his legal representatives.

Where an appeal lies under this Act before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the Board shall have power to entertain appeals from any order passed by the Registrar relating to the rectification of a trademark, including but not limited to disputes concerning dilution and passing off. The Board may, at its discretion, require the appearance of both the appellant and respondent, affording each party an opportunity to present evidence and arguments. Further provided that in cases where technical expertise is deemed necessary for proper adjudication, the Board shall have the power to constitute a bench including a Technical Member possessing relevant qualifications in fields such as chemistry or engineering. Decisions made by the Board are subject to judicial review under law.

Save as otherwise provided in this Chapter, all the provisions of this Act shall apply in relation to a convention application and a patent granted in pursuance thereof as they apply in relation to an ordinary application and a patent granted in pursuance thereof.

Where a mark is registered under this Act, any other mark which identifies goods or services connected to those for which the first-mentioned mark is registered, and which is used or proposed to be used by the proprietor of the first-mentioned mark, may be deemed marks registered associated with the original registration. The Registrar shall, upon application made in the prescribed form and subject to payment of the requisite fee, record such association within the register of trade marks. Any person seeking to assert rights relating to a mark registered associated shall demonstrate that the connection between the marks is clearly established and not misleading to consumers. Failure to do so may result in an action for passing off being dismissed. The proprietor of a mark registered associated retains all rights pertaining to their individual mark, as provided herein.

Where any person residing outside India commits an act infringing copyright under this Act, or abets such an infringement, or participates in such contravention, he shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence within the meaning of this Act. Such offences may be investigated by officers authorized by the Central Government, and they shall possess all powers as are vested in police officers under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, designate such officers for the purposes of investigation. Provided that any evidence obtained during such investigation shall be admissible in accordance with the provisions relating to admissibility of electronic records under the Information Technology Act, 2000. Upon conclusion of the investigation, the officer shall submit a report to the nearest competent court as provided herein. The Court may issue warrants and summons as necessary for further proceedings.

(3) The Registrar may, in any proceeding under this section, decide any question that may be necessary or expedient to decide in connection with the rectification of the Register. (4) The Registrar on his own motion may, after giving notice in the prescribed manner to the parties concerned and after giving them an opportunity of being heard, make any order referred to in sub-section (1) or sub-section (2).

(1) Where any person (whether entitled to or interested in a patent or an application for a patent or not) threatens any other person by circulars or advertisements or by communications, oral or in writing addressed to that or any other person, with proceedings for infringement of a patent, any person aggrieved thereby may bring a suit against him praying for the following reliefs, that is to say—
(a) a declaration to the effect that the threats are unjustifiable;
(b) an injunction against the continuance of the threats; and
(c) such damages, if any, as he has sustained thereby.

(1) An application for the registration of a mark as a certification trade mark shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed manner by the person proposed to be registered as the proprietor thereof, and accompanied by a draft for the regulations to be deposited under section 74.
(2) Subject to the provisions of section 70, the provisions of sections 18, 19 and 22 shall apply in relation to an application under this section as they apply in relation to an application under section 18, subject to the modification that references therein to acceptance of an application shall be con strued as references to authorisation to proceed with an application.
(3) In dealing under the said provisions with an application under this section, the Registrar or the High Court, as the case may be, shall have regard to the like considerations, so far as relevant, as if the application were applications under section 18 and to any other considerations relevant to applications under this section, including the desirability of securing that a certification trade mark shall comprise some indication that it is a certification trade mark.

(1) The reliefs which a court may grant in any suit for infringement include an injunction (subject to such terms, if any, as the court thinks fit) and, at the option of the plaintiff, either damages or an account of profits.
(2) The court may also order that the goods which are found to be infringing and materials and implement, the predominant use of which is in the creation of infringing goods shall be seized, forfeited or destroyed, as the court deems fit under the circumstances of the case without payment of any compensation.

For the purposes of this Act, “person” shall include any individual, firm, company, or association incorporated under the laws for the time being in force and may also extend to bodies politic or corporate. Where an international registration makes a claim for protection within India, the determination of whether such a person is indeed entitled to enforce rights arising from that registration shall be subject to verification by the Controller, considering factors including domicile and place of business at the time of filing the initial application abroad. Any appeal against this determination may be made to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the Controller’s decision; otherwise, such appeals shall be deemed frivolous under this Act.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to use that trade mark throughout India in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and may grant licences permitting such use by third parties. Any licence granted under this Act shall be in writing and specify the territory within which, and the time during which, the licensee is authorized to make use of the registered trade mark. The proprietor may assign any right arising under this Act relating to the use registered trade mark, including any licence agreement, subject to prior approval from the Controller if such assignment involves a foreign entity or concerns goods deemed critical to the security of India. Such approvals shall be granted only after due consideration of national interests and potential economic impact. The proprietor is responsible for ensuring that all licensees adhere to conditions stipulated in their agreements.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor layout design shall enjoy protection for a period of ten years from the date of first commercial exploitation. Any person who, without authorisation from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, sells, hires or offers to sell or hire any integrated circuit embodying a proprietor layout design, shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor. Such damages may include compensation for infringement and recovery of costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies. Further, where an infringing copy is manufactured or imported with intent for commercial gain, the court may order its destruction as provided herein. The proprietor may also seek injunctive relief to restrain further acts of infringement, subject to demonstrating reasonable prospects of success. This protection extends to all forms of reproduction and adaptation of the layout design.

Any person found to be using a registered geographical indication in contravention of this Act shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the court, reflecting the loss suffered by the registered proprietor and detriment to the reputation of the indicated goods. Further, upon complaint made by the Registrar or any registered proprietor, the court may grant an order injunction restraining such use, subject to a hearing where the alleged infringer may present their defense. This power extends to preventing the sale, hire, or offering for sale of goods falsely bearing the geographical indication. Failure to comply with an order injunction shall constitute contempt of court and render the offender liable to further penalties as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by any order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the Appellate Board may, if it considers necessary, require the appellant to furnish security for costs. Failure to comply with a direction issued by the Controller regarding the rectification of a patent shall be deemed an offence and subject the defaulting party to a penalty not exceeding one lakh rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Further, any false representation made in relation to the invention claimed in an application for a patent shall render the applicant liable to prosecution under Indian Penal Code; it is provided that no act patent shall confer rights beyond those specifically defined herein.

Copyright in a work shall be deemed to be infringed— (a) when any person, without a licence granted by the owner of the copyright or the Registrar of Copyrights under this Act or in contraven tion of the conditions of a licence so granted or of any condition imposed by a competent authority under this Act— (i) does anything, the exclusive right to do which is by this Act conferred upon the owner of the copyright, or (ii) permits for profit any place to be used for the communication of the work to the public where such communication constitutes an infringement of the copyright in the work, unless he was not aware and had no reasonable ground for believing that such communi cation to the public would be an infringement of copyright; or (b) when any person— (i) makes for sale or hire, or sells or lets for hire, or by way of trade displays or offers for sale or hire, or (ii) distributes either for the purpose of trade or to such an extent as to affect prejudicially the owner of the copyright, or (iii) by way of trade exhibits in public, or (iv) imports into India, any infringing copies of the work: Provided that nothing in sub -clause (iv) shall apply to the import of one copy of any work for the private and domestic use of the importer. Explanation.—For the purpose s of this section, the reproduction of a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work in the form of a cinematograph film shall be deemed to be an “infringing copy”.

Subject to the provisions contained in this Act, the protection granted to a breeder in respect of a variety may, on the application in the prescribed manner of any person interested, be revoked by the Authority on any of the following grounds, namely:— (a) that the grant of the certificate of registration has been based on incorrect information furnished by the applicant; (b) that the certificate of registration has been granted to a person who is not eligible for protection under this Act; (c) that the breeder did not provide the Registrar with such information, documents or material as required for registration under this Act; (d) that the breeder has failed to provide an alternative denomination of the variety which is the subject matter of the registration to the Registrar in case where the earlier denomination of such variety provided to the Registrar is not permissible for registration under this Act; (e) that the breeder did not provide the necessary seeds or propagating material to the person to whom compulsory licence has been issued under section 47 regarding the variety in respect of which registration certificate has been issued to such breeder; (f) that the breeder has not complied with the provisions of this Act or rules or regulations made thereunder; (g) that the breeder has failed to comply with the directions of the Authority issued under this Act; (h) that the grant of the certificate of registration is not in the public interest: Provided that no such protection shall be revoked unless the breeder is given a reasonable opportunity to file objection and of being heard in the matter.

Where any application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall serve a copy of notice of the opposition on the applicant and the opponent. The applicant and the opponent shall each be given an opportunity to submit their comments and evidence in support of their respective positions. The Registrar shall provide both parties with a reasonable period, not exceeding sixty days from the date of service of the notice, for compliance as provided herein. Following the expiry of this period, the *Registrar shall hearing* all interested parties, including the applicant and the opponent, at a time and place fixed by him, giving them reasonable notice of such hearing. The decision of the Registrar after such hearing shall be final subject to appeal under Chapter VI. Any party failing to appear at the hearing may be deemed to have withdrawn their submissions.
(3) The arrears of fee imposed under sub-section (1) shall be deemed to be the arrears of land revenue and shall be recoverable accordingly.

The registration of a layout-design shall be only for a period of ten years counted from the date of filing an application for registration or from the date of first commercial exploitation anywhere in India or in any country whichever is earlier. CHAPTER IV EFFECT OF REGISTRATION

Subject to any rules made in this behalf, in any proceeding under this Act before the Controller, evidence shall be given by affidavit in the absence of directions by the Controller to the contrary, but in any case in which the Controller thinks it right so to do, he may take oral evidence in lieu of, or in addition to, evidence by affidavit, or may allow any party to be cross-examined on the contents of his affidavit.

Any assignment of a registered layout-design right shall be subject to a written instrument executed by the assignor and the assignee, and such instrument shall clearly identify the layout-design right being assigned, including the registration number and the date of registration. A license to work a registered layout-design, whether sole or non-exclusive, shall be construed as a contractual arrangement governed by the terms specified in the licensing agreement, and such terms may include royalty rates, duration, and territorial scope. However, any license granted must not contravene the provisions of this Act, and any attempt to broaden the scope of the licensed right beyond the originally registered layout-design shall be deemed invalid. The Registrar may, upon application, record such assignments and licenses, and maintain a public register thereof. Any application for registration of assignment or license shall demonstrate a clear nexus between the assigned right and the manner applications clause as it relates to the commercial exploitation of the layout-design. Provided that, the assignee or licensee shall be bound by any existing obligations of the assignor or licensor, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication concerning traditionally crafted placed houses parliament may apply to the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which the rectification is sought, including but not limited to instances of misrepresentation, dilution of distinctiveness, or change in the production method that no longer conforms with established practices. The Tribunal shall afford all interested parties, including producers and legal practitioners representing them, an opportunity to present evidence and arguments. Remedies available under this Act for infringement extend to damages sustained by the registered proprietor, injunctive relief preventing further unauthorized use, and the disposal of infringing goods. Failure to comply with orders issued by the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal may attract penalties as provided herein.

(2) If, before the expiration of the said ten years, application for the extension of the period of copyright is made to the Controller in the prescribed manner, the Controller shall, on payment of the prescribed fee, extend the period of copy-right for a second period of five years from the expiration of the original period of ten years.

The Controller shall, upon reasonable grounds believing that disclosure of a design’s particulars would be prejudicial to the security of India, refuse registration or impound any design application as provided herein. Any design incorporating features directly relating to defense installations, strategic materials, or technologies critical to national security shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny. An applicant seeking registration must submit a detailed declaration affirming the design’s non-detrimental impact on India’s security interests. The Controller may, prior to registration, request further clarification or evidence from the applicant regarding the design’s potential implications. Provided that, if the design is demonstrably for civilian applications and poses no discernible threat, registration may proceed. Failure to accurately disclose relevant security concerns shall render the registration voidable and may attract penalties. The Controller’s decision regarding security india explanation is final and not subject to appeal, except before the High Court.

(1) When the court has to form an opinion upon any question of fact or a scientific issue, such court may appoint an independent scientific adviser to suggest it or to inquire into and report upon the matter to enable it to from the desired opinion. (2) The scientific adviser may be paid such remuneration or expenses as the court may fix. Offences, penalties and procedure

Where an applicant seeks to introduce an amendment claim specification in respect of a patent application already published under this Act, such amendment shall only be permissible if it clarifies the subject matter disclosed in the original specification and does not substantially alter the nature of the invention. Any attempt to broaden the scope of protection beyond that initially described will be deemed invalid and may render the granted patent liable for revocation proceedings. Furthermore, any party demonstrating prejudice arising from a late or unduly expansive amendment claim specification shall have standing to petition the Controller for appropriate remedies, including damages proportionate to the infringement suffered due to the extended exclusive rights afforded by the amended claim. The Controller shall impose penalties as provided herein upon finding such an infraction.

(1) The Authority shall, while determining the terms and conditions of a compulsory licence under the provisions of this Chapter, endeavour to secure— (i) reasonable compensation to the breeder of the variety relating to the compulsory licence having regard to the nature of the variety, the expenditure incurred by such breeder in breeding the variety or for developing it, and other relevant factors; (ii) that the compulsory licensee of such variety possesses the adequate means to provide to the farmers, the seeds or other propagating material of such variety, timely and at reasonable market price. (2) No compulsory licence granted by the Authority shall authorise the licensee to import the variety relating to such licence or any seed or other propagating material of such variety from abroad where such import would constitute an infringement of the rights of the breeder of such variety.

The reports of examiners to the Controller under this Act shall not be open to public inspection or be published by the Controller; and such reports shall not be liable to production or inspection in any legal proceeding unless the court certifies that the production or inspection is desirable in the interests of justice, and ought to be allowed.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no person shall commercially exploit a registered layout design without the prior written consent of the registered proprietor. Such consent may be granted upon such terms and conditions as the proprietor deems fit, including but not limited to limitations on geographical area, field of use, or duration of exploitation. Where consent is given for the use layout design, the licensee shall ensure that any integrated circuit manufactured pursuant to such license adheres strictly to the registered layout design specifications as filed with the Controller General. Any alteration to the registered layout design during manufacturing, without express written permission from the proprietor, constitutes a violation under this Act and renders the manufacturer liable for damages. The right to use layout design is deemed infringed if it involves reproduction or adaptation that substantially replicates the original design’s features.
Subject to the other provisions contained in this Act, a patent shall have to all intents the like effect as against Government as it has against any person.

(1) For the purposes of this Act, a Register called the National Register of Plant Varieties shall be kept at the head office of the Registry, wherein shall be entered the names of all the registered plant varieties with the names and addresses of their respective breeders, the right of such breeders in respect of the registered varieties, the particulars of the denomination of each Registered variety, its seed or other propagating material along with specification of salient features thereof and such other matters as may be prescribed. (2) Subject to the superintendence and direction of the Central Government, the Register shall be kept under the control and management of the Authority.

Any proprietor who utilizes a registered geographical indication in contravention of the provisions as provided herein, or engages in any activity prejudicial to the public interest concerning such indication, shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Geographical Indications Registry. Further, where it is established that the proprietor has misrepresented facts during registration, or subsequently employed the indication to deceive consumers regarding the origin and quality of goods, the Registrar may order the cancellation of the registration. In such instances, any profits derived from the unauthorized use of the geographical indication shall be recoverable as damages. The court may also direct the aforesaid committed forfeiture of all assets acquired through these unlawful activities, subject to appeal before a designated appellate authority.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any owner of an integrated circuit layout design may grant a transmissible use layout license conferring upon the licensee the right to perform acts which would otherwise constitute infringement of the layout-design. Such licenses shall be assignable in accordance with the principles of general law and may be granted for a term not exceeding five years, renewable by agreement between the licensor and licensee. Provided that where a transmissible use layout license is granted relating to a layout-design incorporated within a larger integrated circuit, the scope of such license shall be clearly defined, specifying the permitted acts and any restrictions on their performance. The owner granting such a license shall provide a written record detailing the terms and conditions thereof, accessible for inspection under this Act upon reasonable notice.

(1) Where it is proposed that a person should be registered as a registered user of a layout-design, the registered proprietor and the proposed registered user shall jointly apply in writing to the Registrar in the prescribed manner and every such application shall be accompanied by— (1)(a) the agreement in writing or a duly authenticated copy thereof, entered into between the registered proprietor and the proposed registered user with respect to the permitted use of the layout- design; and (1)(b) an affidavit made by the registered proprietor or by some person authorised to the satisfaction of Registrar to act on his behalf— (1)(i) giving particulars of the relationship, existing or proposed, between the registered proprietor and the proposed registered user, including particulars showing the degree of control by the proprietor over the permitted use which the relationship will confer and whether it is a term of their relationship that the proposed registered user shall be sole registered user or that there shall be any other restriction as to persons for whose registration as registered user application may be made; (1)(ii) stating the conditions or restrictions, if any, proposed with respect to the place of permitted use or any other matter;

(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, no registration of a variety shall be made under this Act in cases where prevention of commercial exploitation of such variety is necessary to protect public order or public morality or human, animal and plant life and health or to avoid serious prejudice to the environment. (2) The Central Government shall, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify the genera or species for the purposes of registration of varieties other than extant varieties and farmers' varieties under this Act.

Provided that the applicant shall not be entitled to institute any proceedings for infringement until the patent has been granted:
Provided further that the rights of a patentee in respect of applications made under sub-section (2) of section 5 before the 1st day of January, 2005 shall accrue from the date of grant of the patent:
Provided also that after a patent is granted in respect of applications made under sub-section (2) of section 5, the patent-holder shall only be entitled to receive reasonable royalty from such enterprises which have made significant investment and were producing and marketing the concerned product prior to the 1st day of January, 2 and which continue to manufacture the product covered by the patent on the date of grant of the patent and no infringement proceedings shall be instituted against such enterprises.

Where a registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design has been granted, such registration shall remain valid subject to the provisions herein. However, the Registrar may, acting upon an application made in the prescribed form by any interested party, initiate proceedings for cancelling registration registered if it is established that the assignor had not obtained prior consent from the original registrant before assigning rights pertaining to the layout-design. Further, a licensee of a registered layout-design shall be deemed an interested party for the purpose of such application. The Registrar may also entertain applications seeking cancellation where evidence demonstrates a material alteration of the layout-design post-registration without proper notification and consent as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order cancelling registration registered may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

For the purposes of this Act, a “copy thereof court” shall be deemed to exist where an infringement of copyright subsists in respect of works comprising literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works, and such infringement is alleged to have occurred within the territorial jurisdiction of a civil court. The determination of whether a work constitutes a substantial copy for the purposes of establishing infringement shall be undertaken by said copy thereof court, applying principles of originality and access as provided herein. Any person found guilty of copyright infringement before a copy thereof court may, subject to appeal under this Act, be liable to impose sentence imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, any person claiming to be a producer of a cinematograph film shall submit a duly completed Form-V, accompanied by the prescribed fee, to the designated Registrar of Copyrights. The application shall clearly identify the film, including its title, duration, and language, and shall state the name and address of the producer. A producer, for the purposes of this registration, includes any person who owns the rights to produce or has undertaken the responsibility for the making of the film. Should the application be incomplete or contain inaccuracies, the Registrar may require the applicant to provide further information or clarification within a period of thirty days. Registration shall be conclusive evidence of ownership, subject to any existing rights or valid claims. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered cinematograph films, accessible for inspection as provided herein. Any alteration to the particulars of a registered film shall necessitate a fresh application for amendment.

Where an audiovisual work incorporates elements originating from multiple sources, including literary, dramatic, musical, artistic, and cinematographic works, determination of ownership shall be predicated upon the contribution of each party involved in its creation. For the purposes of this Act, the term "director" signifies the individual exercising primary creative control over the direction and execution of an audiovisual work, irrespective of their formal contractual designation; such authority extends to decisions concerning script adaptation, musical composition selection, and artistic rendering. Any dispute regarding ownership arising from a directorial contribution may be referred to the Controller for adjudication, following established procedures as provided herein. The Controller shall consider evidence pertaining to the extent of the director’s involvement in shaping the work's overall form and content, particularly with regard to elements classifiable under international classification goods relating to artistic expression.

For the purposes of this Act, “description means trade” shall be interpreted liberally and with due regard to consumer perception; provided that, where an entity utilizes a visual representation purporting to indicate the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods, such representation constitutes a description within the meaning of this Act even if lacking explicit textual claims. An appeal against any order determining whether a particular depiction qualifies as a misleading trade description may be made to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal; however, such appeal shall only be entertained where it is demonstrated that the original determination was manifestly arbitrary or based on an erroneous interpretation of established legal principles concerning deceptive advertising practices and consumer detriment.

No suit for a declaration under section 1 or for any relief under section 1 or for infringement of a patent shall be instituted in any court inferior to a district court having jurisdiction to try the suit:
Provided that where a counter-claim for revocation of the patent is made by the defendant, the suit, along with the counter-claim, shall be transferred to the High Court for decision.

The registrar shall maintain a register of trade marks in accordance with the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, ensuring its accessibility to public inspection subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any person desiring to inspect the register or obtain certified copies thereof may apply to the registrar in writing, specifying the class and mark details for which inspection is sought. The registrar may require such applicant to furnish reasonable proof of identity before granting access. Where an application for registration is deemed defective by the registrar, notice of such deficiency shall be served upon the applicant, affording a period not less than thirty days for rectification; provided that failure to rectify within said timeframe may result in abandonment of the application. All decisions of the registrar relating to examination, advertisement or refusal of trade marks shall be reasoned and communicated in writing to the concerned party. The registrar’s functions are subject to appeal before the appropriate appellate authority as provided herein.

Any dispute relating to the registration or validity of a trade mark, or any infringement thereof, arising within the territories of India, shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the High Court having local jurisdiction over the place where the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business. Provided that, in cases where the defendant has no place of business within India but actively targets the Indian market through commercial activity, the High Court in Delhi shall, notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere, have jurisdiction to entertain and adjudicate upon such disputes. 

Where a plaintiff seeks to enforce rights in a registered trade mark against a party located outside India, evidence of substantial connection between such party and India, including but not limited to, sales, advertising, or the maintenance of a website accessible within India, shall be presented to establish jurisdiction. The Registrar, as provided herein, may direct service of process on such foreign party through established diplomatic channels or in accordance with international treaties to which India is a party. Any order issued by a court regarding jurisdiction india trade shall be enforceable as if made by a court within its ordinary territorial limits.

(1) Any person who— (a) applies any false denomination to a variety; or (b) indicates the false name of a country or place or false name and address of the breeder of a variety registered under this Act in the course of trading such variety, shall, unless he proves that he acted, without intend to defraud, be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three months but which may extend to two years, or with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to five lakh rupees, or with both.

(1) No ap plication for the registration of a trade mark in respect of any goods or services shall be refused nor shall permission for such registration be withheld, on the ground only that it appears that the applicant does not use or propose to use the trade mark if the Registrar is satisfied that— (a) a company is about to be formed and registered under the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956) and that the applicant intends to assign the trade mark to that company with a view to the use thereof in relation to those goods or services by the company, or (b) the proprietor intends it to be used by a person, as a registered user after the registration of the trade mark.
(2) The provisions of section 47 shall have effect, in relation to a trade mark registered under the powers conferred by this sub -section, as if for the reference, in clause ( a) of sub -section ( 1) of that section, to the intention on the part of an applicant for registration that a trade mark should be used by him there were substituted a reference to the intention on his part that it should be used by the company or registered user concerned.
